LU-1.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the chest wall, at the level of the first intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline and 1 cun below Yunmen LU-2. Located slightly medial to the caudal border of the coracoid process.
howToFind: Seated with the hand resting on the hip, locate Yun Men (LU-2) in the depression below the lateral segment of the clavicle (at the acromioclavicular extremity). The point lies 1 cun directly below Yun Men (LU-2), at the level of the first intercostal space.
In the supine position, locate the point 2 cun lateral to the nipple (in males) at the first intercostal space.
LU-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraclavicular nerve branch, pectoralis major muscle, thoracoacromial artery, cephalic vein, lateral pectoral nerve, and lateral intercostal muscle.
LU-1.needling: Oblique insertion 0.5–1 cun directed cranially (approximately 45°) and laterally toward the coracoid process, or transverse-oblique insertion of 0.5 to 1 cun medially along the intercostal space.
LU-1.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular or medially directed insertion carries substantial risk of pneumothorax. Caution: deep perpendicular, medial, or oblique insertion poses a real risk of pneumothorax. The needle must be directed only laterodorsally or tangentially to the coracoid process.
actions: clears Heat in the Upper Jiao
moves Qi locally and in the tendinomuscular channel
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and back
sensation of oppression and tightness in the chest
expectoration of turbid Phlegm or Phlegm with blood and pus
sensation of heat in the palms
running piglet Qi with low back pain
LU-1.etymology: Zhong (中), chest; Fu (府), site. Meeting point of the Qi of Fei (Lung).
LU-1.clinicalNotes:
Front Mu point of Fei (Lung), routinely used in the treatment of pulmonary diseases. Cupping over Zhong Fu (LU-1) is effective in treating bronchitis and pneumonia.

The Lung Meridian, Hand Tai Yin, originates in the epigastric region; for this reason it can be used in the treatment of stomach disorders related to exogenous pathogenic factors.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-2.category: Point of the Lung primary channel.
LU-2.locationClassical: On the superolateral aspect of the chest, above the coracoid process of the scapula, in the depression of the infraclavicular fossa (in the center of the deltopectoral triangle), 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Seated with the hand on the hip, locate the point in the center of the inferior triangular depression of the infraclavicular fossa.
LU-2.anatomy: Pectoralis major muscle, anterior fibers of the deltoid. Innervated by the supraclavicular nerve and the lateral and medial pectoral nerves.
LU-2.needling: Oblique insertion to a maximum depth of 0.8 cun, or transverse-oblique insertion of 0.5 to 1 cun.
LU-2.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular or medial insertion carries substantial risk of pneumothorax. Caution: do not direct the needle medially, as deep perpendicular or oblique insertion can cause pneumothorax.
actions: opens the channel and the tendinomuscular channel
tcmIndications: pain in the chest, shoulder, and arm
dyspnea with inability to lie down
oppressive and agitated sensation in the chest
ascent of Qi to the Heart
sudden pain in the Heart and abdomen
pain in the lateral costal region, back, and shoulders
LU-2.etymology: Yun (雲), cloud; Men (門), gate. Yun refers to Lung Qi. The point sits on the upper part of the chest, like a gateway for Qi of the Lung.
LU-2.clinicalNotes: Needling Yun Men (LU-2) improves the flow of Qi of Fei (Lung) and relieves the sensation of heat in the four limbs. It is used to treat shoulder pain, frozen shoulder, pain in the supraclavicular fossa, and the sensation of heat in the extremities caused by infection and pulmonary disease. Cold in the four limbs from obstruction of Lung Qi, and diseases caused by pathogenic Heat, can also be treated by needling Yun Men (LU-2).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-3.locationClassical: On the anterolateral aspect of the upper arm, 3 cun below the axillary fold and 6 cun above the cubital crease, in the depression between the lateral border of the biceps brachii and the shaft of the humerus.
howToFind: Seated, raise the arm forward and tilt the head. Locate the point where the tip of the nose touches the anterior aspect of the arm.
Seated with the elbow slightly flexed, locate the point 6 cun above the cubital crease.
LU-3.anatomy: Biceps brachii and brachialis muscles. Innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve and the radial nerve.
LU-3.safetyWarning: No special precautions; avoid the cephalic vein. Moxibustion is contraindicated according to some classics, as it may provoke counterflow and Qi disorder.
actions: cools the Blood and stops bleeding
opens the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: pain and swelling on the medial aspect of the arm
westernIndications: local treatment for biceps tendinopathy or brachialis myofascial pain
LU-3.etymology: Tian (天), heaven; Fu (府), mansion. Tian refers to what is above. The point bears this name because Fei (Lung) is the Mansion of bodily Qi, which communicates with celestial Qi through the nose.
LU-3.clinicalNotes: This point of the Lung Meridian promotes the flow of Qi of Fei (Lung) and therefore calms the mind. Nasal, pulmonary, and mental disorders caused by disturbances of Lung Qi can be treated through this point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-4.category: Point of the Lung primary channel.
LU-4.locationClassical: On the inner (anterolateral) aspect of the upper arm, along the radial border of the biceps brachii, 4 cun distal to the anterior axillary fold (or 5 cun above the cubital crease).
howToFind: Seated, locate the point 5 cun above the cubital crease, lateral to the tendon of the biceps brachii.
LU-4.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, cephalic vein, biceps brachii and brachialis muscles, radial collateral artery.
LU-4.safetyWarning: No special precautions; avoid the cephalic vein.
actions: regulates Qi and Blood in the chest
moves Qi and Blood in the chest
opens the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: pain on the medial aspect of the arm
LU-4.etymology: Xia (俠), to clasp on both sides; Bai (白), white. The color white relates to the Lung. With the arms relaxed, the Lung is encircled by the two Xia Bai (LU-4) points.
LU-4.clinicalNotes: Xia Bai (LU-4) is a regional point of the Lung Meridian on the anteromedial upper arm, with no major classifying category — it is neither Yuan, Luo, Xi-Cleft, He-Sea, Jing-Well, Back-Shu, nor Front-Mu. Its classical indications in the Jia Yi Jing (cough with shortness of breath, cardiac pain, pain along the medial aspect of the arm) have been absorbed, in modern practice, by Tian Fu (LU-3) for the shen component and by Chi Ze (LU-5), the He-Sea point, for elbow and forearm complaints (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 76; Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). It is rarely needled in isolation today; it serves mainly as a local point on the biceps brachii. Perpendicular insertion of 0.5–1.0 cun. See Tian Fu (LU-3) and Chi Ze (LU-5).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-5.locationClassical: On the cubital crease, in the depression at the radial margin of the biceps brachii tendon. Located with the elbow slightly flexed.
howToFind: With the elbow slightly flexed and the palm facing up, locate the point in the cubital crease, in the depression immediately lateral (radial) to the tendon of the biceps brachii muscle (WHO 2008, §LU-5).
LU-5.anatomy: Brachioradialis muscle, lateral to the biceps tendon. Innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve and the radial nerve.
actions: clears Heat in the Upper Jiao
descends Lung Qi and rebellious Qi
opens the channel and the Luo vessels to relieve pain
tcmIndications: spasmodic pain in the elbow and arm
LU-5.etymology: Chi (尺), cubit, forearm (the classical body-measure of the forearm); Ze (澤), marsh, low boggy land. The point lies in the cubital crease, in a moist depression that collects the descending flow of the Lung channel as a marsh collects rain water — the classical image of a He-Sea point, where channel Qi "enters" as a river reaches the sea (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 69; Ling Shu, chapter 1).
LU-5.clinicalNotes: Chi Ze (LU-5) is the He-Sea (Water) point of the Lung Meridian, Hand Tai Yin, and the Sedation point (the child draining excess from the mother-organ) by the mother-child rule of the Five Shu (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 69–71). Its central clinical function is to clear Lung Heat, descend rebellious Qi, and regulate the water passages of the Upper Jiao. It is a first-line choice in Lung Heat-Excess patterns with loud cough, dyspnea, thick yellow sputum, hemoptysis, and acute-onset chest pain — patterns corresponding to pneumonia and acute bronchitis in contemporary practice (Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). By the He-Sea/Water-on-Metal correspondence it also treats patterns in which Lung Qi obstructs the descent of water, producing acute facial and upper-limb edema. As a local point it is effective in medial epicondylitis and pain of the cubital crease. Common combinations: Chi Ze (LU-5) + Kong Zui (LU-6) for acute cough with Lung Heat; with Wei Zhong (BL-40) (bloodletting) for acute heatstroke with high fever; with Lie Que (LU-7) and He Gu (LI-4) for common cold with dry cough from Wind-Heat. Caution: the median cubital vein crosses the region — avoid venous puncture by keeping perpendicular insertion at 0.5–1.0 cun (WHO 2008, §LU-5).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-6.locationClassical: On the radial border of the posterior aspect of the forearm, 5 cun distal to LU-5 (or 7 cun proximal to the wrist joint space / LU-9), on the line connecting LU-5 and LU-9.
howToFind: On the forearm with the palm facing up, locate the point 5 cun distal to Chi Ze (LU-5) (or 7 cun proximal to the wrist crease / Tai Yuan LU-9), on the line connecting Chi Ze (LU-5) to Tai Yuan (LU-9), on the medial border of the radius (WHO 2008, §LU-6).
LU-6.anatomy: Brachioradialis muscle, pronator teres muscle. Innervated by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
actions: clears Heat and stops bleeding in acute conditions
cools Blood Heat and stops bleeding
tcmIndications: pain in the elbow and arm
swelling and pain in the throat
obstruction of the elbow, arm, and fingers
westernIndications: useful for pronator teres syndrome and forearm flexor strain
inflammation of the elbow joint and periarticular soft tissues
LU-6.etymology: Kong (孔), opening, aperture; Zui (最), the supreme, the maximum. As the Xi-Cleft point of the Lung Meridian, it is the maximum aperture where the channel Qi gathers most deeply — the best point for releasing blocked flow of Lung Qi (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 74).
LU-6.clinicalNotes: Kong Zui (LU-6) is the Xi-Cleft point of the Lung Meridian, Hand Tai Yin. The Xi-Cleft points of the Yin meridians are particularly effective for Xue (Blood) patterns: needling Kong Zui is the classical indication for hemoptysis, especially that associated with bronchiectasis and pulmonary tuberculosis (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 74–75). As a Yin-meridian Xi-Cleft point it also addresses acute disorders of the channel and organ — acute asthma attacks, acute cough with dyspnea, and sudden-onset chest pain. The Lung Meridian is paired with the Large Intestine Meridian; through this Biao-Li relationship, Kong Zui has traditionally also been used to treat bleeding hemorrhoids with anal pruritus. Common combinations: Kong Zui (LU-6) + Chi Ze (LU-5) for acute cough with Lung Heat; with Yu Ji (LU-10) and Shao Shang (LU-11) for acute febrile pharyngitis with hemoptysis; with Cheng Shan (BL-57) for hemorrhagic hemorrhoids (Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-7.locationClassical: On the radial aspect of the forearm, directly above the styloid process of the radius, approximately 1.5 cun proximal to the wrist joint space, in a V-shaped cleft between the tendons of the brachioradialis and the abductor pollicis longus.
howToFind: Interlock the index finger and thumb of both hands; the point is located at the tip of the index finger resting over the styloid process of the radius of the opposite hand.
With the hand loosely closed and the thumb extended, locate Yang Xi (IG 5) in the anatomical snuffbox. Lie Que (P 7) lies
5 cun proximal to Yang Xi (IG 5), in the depression over the styloid process of the radius.
LU-7.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, superficial branch of the radial nerve, brachioradialis muscle, between the tendons of the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis and the abductor pollicis longus, radial artery, and supinator muscle.
LU-7.needling: Transverse (subcutaneous) insertion, directed proximally or distally, 0.5–1 cun.
actions: promotes the descending function of the Lung
opens and regulates the Conception Vessel
activates the channel to relieve pain
tcmIndications: cold sensation in the chest and back
sudden edema of the four limbs
deviation of the mouth and eye
pain in the thumb and wrist
westernIndications: primary point for De Quervain tenosynovitis and osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint
LU-7.etymology: Lie (列): crack, divergence; Que (缺): depression. The collateral branch of the Hand Tai Yin Meridian emerges from this point, which sits in the depression just above the styloid process of the radius.
LU-7.clinicalNotes:
The Fei (Lung) governs Qi. By promoting the flow of Lung Qi, this point is used in treating throat inflammation and respiratory disease.

The Lung Meridian originates in the Middle Jiao. It supports diuresis and the respiratory function of the Fei (Lung), and is indicated for diseases of the urogenital system. By strengthening the Qi of the Fei (Lung) and Wei (Stomach), it addresses abdominal pain, diarrhea, dysentery, and hematemesis. The Xin (Heart) and Fei (Lung) both reside in the Upper Jiao and are closely related. This point strengthens Lung Qi and relieves thoracic discomfort; it is indicated for hypertension, precordial pain, and chest pain.

Lie Que (P 7) connects to the Ren Mai and may be used in the treatment of infertility.

Figure 8.4 Points of the Hand Tai Yin (wrist and hand).

The Lung Meridian does not reach the head directly, but its divergent meridian does. Lie Que (P 7) is the Luo point of the Lung Meridian; it connects to the Large Intestine Meridian at Da Zhui (DM 14) and meets all the Yang meridians. It is an effective point for neuropsychiatric disorders. The "Poem of the Four Key Points" states that "Lie Que (P 7) should be used to treat diseases of the head and neck."

Dorsolumbar disorder: Lie Que (P 7) + Wei Zhong (B 40). Head and neck disorder: Lie Que (P 7).

Face and mouth disorder: Lie Que (P 7) + He Gu (IG 4).

The Fei (Lung) governs the skin and body hair; this point may be used to treat urticaria by eliminating exogenous Wind from the body surface.

combinations.indication: Common cold, headache, nasal congestion, facial disorders
Throat disorders, chest tightness, respiratory and urogenital conditions

LU-8.locationClassical: Above the wrist joint space, 1 cun proximal to the palmar carpal crease (Taiyuan LU-9), on the radial border of the radial artery, in the depression at the base of the styloid process of the radius.
howToFind: With the hand extended and the palm facing up, locate the point 1 cun above the transverse wrist crease, where the artery lies, or where the radial pulse is examined. Jing Qu (LU-8) sits where the examiner's finger reaches on the radial side of the artery.
LU-8.anatomy: Tendon of the flexor carpi radialis muscle, brachioradialis muscle. Innervated by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the radial nerve.
LU-8.needling: Perpendicular (vertical) or proximally directed insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun.
LU-8.safetyWarning: Avoid puncturing the radial artery — gently displace it to the side during palpation. Moxibustion is contraindicated according to some classics.
actions: opens the pores and expels Wind
tcmIndications: distension and pain in the chest and upper back
pain in the Heart with vomiting
westernIndications: local application for radial wrist pain
wrist joint or soft tissue injuries
LU-8.etymology: Jing (經), passage; Qu (渠), gutter, valley. It is like a gutter through which the artery runs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-9.locationClassical: At the wrist joint space, in the depression between the radial artery and the tendon of the abductor pollicis longus, at the level of the wrist crease.
howToFind: With the palm facing up, locate the point on the transverse wrist crease where the pulsation is felt.
LU-9.anatomy: Tendon of the flexor carpi radialis muscle, abductor pollicis longus muscle. Innervated by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the radial nerve.
LU-9.needling: Perpendicular (vertical) insertion 0.2–0.5 cun, or 2 to 3 mm.
LU-9.safetyWarning: Strictly avoid the radial artery. If the needle pulses (the desired effect), do not apply additional stimulation.
actions: Tonifies the Lung and transforms Phlegm
promotes the descending function of the Lung
regulates and harmonizes the hundred vessels
activates the channel and relieves pain
tonifies and replenishes Lung Qi and Lung Yin
promotes the circulation of Qi and Blood
opens the channel to relieve pain
tcmIndications: pain in the chest and back
pulmonary distension and shortness of breath
pain in the shoulder and back radiating to the arms
LU-9.etymology: Tai (太), great; Yuan (淵), deep well. Tai means abundance. At this point, the Qi of the meridian is abundant.
LU-9.clinicalNotes:
1. The Lung Meridian, Hand Tai Yin, is paired with the Hand Yang Ming and communicates with the Ren Mai. The points of the Large Intestine Meridian are commonly used to treat the sense organs. According to the therapeutic property of the five Shu points, this point is commonly used to treat the sense organs.

2. The heart governs blood circulation, and this is the Influential Point of the Vessels; it is therefore used to treat precordial pain.

3. The Tendinomuscular Meridian of the Hand Tai Yin "runs downward, gathers in the chest, and reaches the hypochondriac region," so it is indicated in the treatment of intercostal neuralgia.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-10.locationClassical: On the thenar eminence of the hand, in the depression between the midpoint of the shaft of the first metacarpal bone and the thenar muscles, along the border between the palmar and dorsal aspects of the hand.
howToFind: With the palm facing up, locate the point on the thenar eminence, at the midpoint of the first metacarpal bone, at the transition from palmar (light) skin to dorsal (dark) skin — the border of the thenar muscle (WHO 2008, §LU-10).
LU-10.anatomy: Abductor pollicis brevis muscle, opponens pollicis muscle. Innervated by the superficial branch of the radial nerve and the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve.
LU-10.safetyWarning: Needling can be highly sensitive. Caution: this point can be quite painful.
actions: expels pathogenic factors from the throat
tcmIndications: shortness of breath with painful obstruction of the Heart
pain in the palm and wrist
LU-10.etymology: Yu (魚), fish; Ji (際), border, edge. The thenar muscle has the appearance of a fish belly ("yu fu"), and the point lies on the border of that fleshy ridge, exactly at the transition from palmar (light) skin to dorsal (dark) skin — hence the name "fish border" (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 84; Ling Shu, chapter 1).
LU-10.clinicalNotes: Yu Ji (LU-10) is the Ying-Spring (Fire) point of the Lung Meridian, Hand Tai Yin. By Five-Shu theory, Ying-Spring points are classical for treating Heat — especially Heat ascending the channel to the throat — and this is, together with Shao Shang (LU-11), the point of choice for acute pharyngitis and tonsillitis with intense pain and fever (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 84–85). Its central clinical function is to clear Lung Heat, benefit the throat, and descend rebellious Qi, with indications for acute sore throat, loss of voice from Wind-Heat, cough with hemoptysis from Lung Heat, and fever without sweating (Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, Foreign Languages Press, Beijing). In pediatrics, the color of the thenar — red, pale, or cyanotic — is used as a classical diagnostic sign of the state of Lung and Stomach Qi ("thenar venule"). Common combinations: Yu Ji (LU-10) + Shao Shang (LU-11) for acute febrile pharyngotonsillitis (bloodletting at Shao Shang combined with needling of Yu Ji); with Lie Que (LU-7) and He Gu (LI-4) for loss of voice from Wind-Heat; with Chi Ze (LU-5) for cough with hemoptysis. Caution: the point can be quite painful on insertion; keep perpendicular insertion at 0.5–1.0 cun (WHO 2008, §LU-10).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LU-11.locationClassical: On the radial/extensor aspect of the thumb, approximately 0.1 cun from the radial corner of the nail (at the junction of lines drawn along the radial border and the base of the nail).
howToFind: With the hand half-closed and the thumb extended, palm facing up, locate the point on the radial side of the thumb,
1 cun from the radial corner of the nail, at the intersection of the lines extending the radial border of the digit and the base of the nail (WHO 2008, §LU-11).
LU-11.anatomy: On the tip of the thumb, between the radial corner of the nail and the radial border of the digital pulp.
LU-11.needling: Perpendicular or proximally directed oblique insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun, or puncture for bloodletting.
LU-11.safetyWarning: Extremely painful point. Avoid puncturing the perionychium.
actions: clears Heat and benefits the throat
tcmIndications: heat and pain in the palms
contracture of the wrist and thumb
westernIndications: acute pain at the thumb joint
LU-11.etymology: Shao (少), lesser, small; Shang (商), one of the five notes of the ancient pentatonic musical scale, corresponding to the Metal element and therefore to the Lung (Fei). Because it lies at the tip of the thumb — the most distal point along the Lung channel — this point is called "Lesser Shang," designating the Jing-Well (Wood) point of the Lung Meridian (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 86).
LU-11.clinicalNotes: Shao Shang (LU-11) is the Jing-Well (Wood) point of the Lung Meridian and one of Sun Si Miao's Thirteen Ghost (Gui) points (Qian Jin Yao Fang, ~650 CE), traditionally indicated for acute patterns with Shen disturbance — coma, infantile convulsions, sudden psychiatric disorders (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 85–87). In contemporary practice its primary use is bloodletting with a three-edged needle (1–2 drops) in acute febrile pharyngotonsillitis, in which it rapidly reduces sore throat and fever by dispersing Heat (Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, Foreign Languages Press, Beijing). The same bloodletting technique is also applied in acute heatstroke, febrile convulsions of infancy, and loss of consciousness from stroke, in order to "open the orifices" and restore the Shen. Common combinations: Shao Shang (LU-11) + Shang Yang (LI-1) for acute pharyngotonsillitis with high fever (bilateral bloodletting at the four points); with Ren Zhong (GV-26) and the Twelve Hand Jing points for coma and acute stroke; with Yu Ji (LU-10) for cough with hemoptysis from Lung Heat.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-1.locationClassical: On the lateral (radial) aspect of the tip of the index finger, midway between the radial nail corner and the radial border of the digital pulp, approximately 0.1 cun from the corner of the nail.
howToFind: With the fingers slightly flexed and the index finger held in extension, locate the point at the intersection of the lines passing along the radial border and the base of the nail of the index finger.
LI-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, dorsal digital nerves and veins, dorsal branches of the proper palmar digital arteries and nerves, distal interphalangeal joint.
LI-1.needling: Lancet puncture for bloodletting (indicated in acute pharyngitis). Perpendicular or proximally directed oblique insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
tcmIndications: agitation and restlessness (disorder of the restless organs)
spasms and pain in the fingers
LI-1.etymology: Shang (商), one of the five musical notes, belongs to the Metal element; Yang (阳), yang (of Yin-Yang). The Large Intestine is paired with the Lung, which belongs to Metal in Five Element theory and is associated with the Shang note. Yang relates to the Yang Meridian.
LI-1.clinicalNotes: See Shao Shang (LU-11) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-2.locationClassical: On the radial aspect of the index finger, in the depression anterior and inferior to the metacarpophalangeal joint, at the junction between the shaft and base of the proximal phalanx.
howToFind: With the wrist slightly flexed and the palm facing up, locate the point on the radial border anterior to the metacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger, at the junction of light and dark skin of the first phalanx of this finger.
LI-2.anatomy: First lumbrical muscle, tendon of the extensor digitorum. Innervated by the proper palmar digital nerve (median nerve) and the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
tcmIndications: febrile diseases from Cold without sweating
LI-2.etymology: Er (二), two, second; Jian (間), free space. It is the second point of the Large Intestine Meridian.
LI-2.clinicalNotes: The point is mainly used to treat somnolence and jaundice due to internal heat accumulation and damp-heat of Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach). Its action is similar to that of He Gu (LI-4). See He Gu (LI-4) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-3.locationClassical: On the radial aspect of the index finger, proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joint, at the junction between the shaft and head of the second metacarpal bone.
howToFind: With the fingers gently flexed, locate the point at the metacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger, at the transition between light and dark skin, posterior to the head of the second metacarpal.
LI-3.anatomy: First dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the proper palmar digital nerve and the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
LI-3.needling: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–2.0 cun (may be directed toward PC-8).
tcmIndications: redness and swelling of the fingers and the dorsum of the hand
westernIndications: Rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis of the hand
LI-3.etymology: San (三), three, third; Jian (間), free space. This is the third point of the Large Intestine Meridian.
LI-3.clinicalNotes: San Jian (LI-3) is the Shu-Stream and Wood point of the Large Intestine Meridian, classified in Ling Shu chapter 1 (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, pp. 105–106). Its central clinical function is to clear Heat from the channel — particularly Heat manifesting on the face, teeth, and gums — and to resolve swelling of the throat and gums. The classical indications listed in the Jia Yi Jing include throat painful obstruction, eye pain, deafness, and mania. In modern practice San Jian is used mainly as a local point: joint pain at the second metacarpophalangeal joint (especially of the index finger), finger numbness, and dental analgesia. Common combinations: San Jian (LI-3) + He Gu (LI-4) + Nei Ting (ST-44) for toothache; San Jian (LI-3) + Lie Que (LU-7) + He Gu (LI-4) for occipital headache. It is eclipsed by He Gu (LI-4), the Yuan-Source and most-used point of the entire meridian, which concentrates nearly all systemic Large Intestine indications — hence San Jian is preferred as a local distal point for the hand and index finger. Perpendicular insertion of 0.5–1.0 cun, optionally directed toward He Gu (LI-4); respect the proper palmar digital nerve branch and the superficial branch of the radial nerve.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-4.locationClassical: On the radial aspect of the hand, between the first and second metacarpal bones, closer to the second metacarpal and approximately at its midpoint — corresponds to the apex of the muscular bulge when the thumb and index finger are brought together.
howToFind: With the thumb in abduction, place the crease of the distal interphalangeal joint of the contralateral thumb pressing the area between the thumb and index finger of the first hand. Locate the point where the tip of the thumb reaches.
With the thumb in abduction, locate the point at the apex of the muscles on the dorsum of the hand, between the thumb and index finger.
With the thumb in abduction, locate the point at the center of the line connecting the midpoints of the first and second metacarpal bones.
LI-4.anatomy: First dorsal interosseous muscle, adductor pollicis muscle. Innervated by the superficial branch of the radial nerve and the palmar digital branch of the median nerve.
LI-4.safetyWarning: Strictly contraindicated in pregnancy (may induce labor).
actions: supports the descending function of Lung Qi
tcmIndications: pain in any region of the body
trismus with inability to speak — treats diseases of the face and oropharynx
westernIndications: idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (in combination with other points)
LI-4.etymology: He (合), joining; Gu (谷), valley. This point lies between the first and second metacarpal bones. The site is a depression resembling a valley.
LI-4.clinicalNotes:
1. The indications follow the principle of treating with the local point. The point is effective in harmonizing meridians and collaterals; it can therefore be used to treat Wei (flaccidity) syndrome, Bi syndrome (arthralgia), paralysis, and pain in the upper limbs.

2. The Hand and Foot Yang Ming meridians connect with each other at Ying Xiang (LI-20). The Yang Ming meridians and tendinomuscular meridians distribute over nearly the entire face. The point is therefore highly effective in the treatment of disorders of the head, face, and sense organs.

3. The Lung and Large Intestine Meridians are internally and externally related; this point is therefore important in the treatment of respiratory disorders.

4. He Gu (LI-4) may be used to remove obstructions, reduce fever, neutralize convulsions, and as an analgesic.

5. It is therefore effective in the treatment of urinary retention, constipation, agalactia, amenorrhea, labor, and anhidrosis related to Qi stagnation.

6. In neuropsychiatric disorders such as stroke sequelae, infantile convulsions, and opisthotonos, the point acts to neutralize the convulsions.

7. The point can be used as an analgesic in headache, epigastralgia, dysmenorrhea, and precordial pain.

8. He Gu (LI-4) may be used not only to control excess syndromes but also to recover deficiency of exhausted Yang.

9. It is also indicated in the treatment of loss of consciousness from stroke, heatstroke, fainting, and hemorrhage.

10. Ancient literary citations contraindicate the use of this point in pregnant women, as it may alter fetal Qi (Ton Ren). This warrants further investigation, since such an effect has not been observed in clinical practice. (Editor's note.)

combinations.indication: Pain, stress, emotional regulation, headache
Common cold, headache, nasal congestion, facial disorders

LI-5.locationClassical: With the thumb in abduction, in the depression between the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis (anatomical snuffbox), on the radial aspect of the wrist.
howToFind: With the thumb abducted, locate the point on the radial border of the wrist joint, between the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and brevis.
LI-5.anatomy: Between the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. Cephalic vein, radial artery. Innervated by the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
LI-5.safetyWarning: Avoid the cephalic vein and the radial artery.
tcmIndications: redness, pain, and swelling of the eye
LI-5.etymology: Yang (阳), Yang (dorsum of the wrist); Xi (溪), stream, depression between two tendons. The local depression resembles a stream between mountains.
LI-5.clinicalNotes: Yang Xi (LI-5) is the Jing-River and Fire point of the Large Intestine Meridian, classified in Ling Shu chapter 1. As a Jing-River, its central modern clinical indication is wrist tenosynovitis and radial wrist pain — including the anatomical region of de Quervain disease (stenosing tenosynovitis of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis) — favored by the point’s direct proximity to the anatomical snuffbox (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 107–108). Its classical role in the Jia Yi Jing also includes tinnitus, deafness, frontal headache, and laryngopharyngitis. Common combinations: Yang Xi (LI-5) + Lie Que (LU-7) + Yang Chi (TE-4) for radial tenosynovitis and wrist pain; with Ting Gong (SI-19) and Yi Feng (TE-17) for acute Heat-pattern tinnitus; and with He Gu (LI-4) along the meridian for frontal headache. It is eclipsed by He Gu (LI-4), the Yuan-Source point and the most-used point of the entire meridian, which concentrates nearly all systemic indications — hence Yang Xi is preferred mainly as a local wrist point. Perpendicular insertion of 0.5 cun in the anatomical snuffbox; respect the radial artery and superficial branches of the radial nerve.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-6.locationClassical: 3 cun proximal to LI-5 (in the center of the anatomical snuffbox), on the line connecting LI-5 and LI-11, between the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis muscles, at the level of the musculotendinous junction.
howToFind: With the elbow slightly flexed, locate the point 3 cun above Yang Xi (LI-5), on the lateral border of the radius.
LI-6.anatomy: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis muscles, abductor pollicis longus muscle. Innervated by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
actions: regulates and opens the water passages
opens the channel and the Luo vessels
tcmIndications: pain and fatigue in the arm and elbow — major point for regulating the water passages; treats auricular disorders such as tinnitus and deafness
westernIndications: mild edema of the upper limbs
tags: mild edema of the upper limbs
LI-6.etymology: Pian (偏), divergence; Li (歴), passage. A collateral of the Large Intestine Meridian separates from the Lung Meridian at this point.
LI-6.clinicalNotes: Luo (connecting) point, which connects to the Lung Meridian. The Fei (Lung) maintains normal water metabolism and has the function of draining the water passages. The point can be used to regulate the Qi of Fei (Lung) through the Luo collateral; it can therefore be used in the treatment of urinary retention and edema. See He Gu (LI-4) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-7.locationClassical: On the posterolateral aspect of the forearm, 5 cun proximal to LI-5, on the line connecting LI-5 and LI-11.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed, locate the point 5 cun above Yang Xi (LI-5), on the lateral border of the radius.
LI-7.anatomy: Extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle, extensor digitorum muscle. Innervated by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the deep branch of the radial nerve.
actions: clears the Yangming and calms the Shen
regulates the Stomach and Large Intestine
westernIndications: parotitis — local musculoskeletal pain in the radial forearm
LI-7.etymology: Wen (温), to warm; Liu (溜), circulation. The point has the function of warming the meridian and promoting the circulation of Qi.
LI-7.clinicalNotes: Xi (Cleft) point of the Large Intestine Meridian, Hand Yang Ming. The Xi (Cleft) points of the Yang meridians are used to treat acute pain syndromes.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-8.category: Point of the Large Intestine primary channel.
LI-8.locationClassical: 4 cun distal to LI-11 (equivalent to two-thirds proximal to LI-5 and one-third distal to LI-11, on the line connecting LI-5 and LI-11).
howToFind: With the hand closed, locate the point 4 cun below Qu Chi (LI-11), on the lateral border of the radius.
LI-8.anatomy: Extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle, supinator muscle. Innervated by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the radial nerve.
tcmIndications: pain in the elbow and arm
LI-8.etymology:
Xia (下), lower; Lian (廉), edge, ridge. The point is located 1 cun below Shang Lian (LI-9), on the dorsal aspect of the forearm, near the radial border, on a prominence formed by the extensor carpi radialis longus when the hand is firmly clenched.

[Location] On the radial border of the dorsal surface of the forearm and on the line connecting Yang Xi (LI-5) and Qu Chi (LI-11), 4 cun below the cubital crease.
LI-8.clinicalNotes: See Shou San Li (LI-10), Wen Liu (LI-7), and Qu Chi (LI-11) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-9.category: Point of the Large Intestine primary channel.
LI-9.locationClassical: On the posterolateral aspect of the forearm, 3 cun distal to LI-11, on the line connecting LI-5 and LI-11.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed, locate the point on the lateral border of the radius, 3 cun below Qu Chi (LI-11).
LI-9.anatomy: Extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle, supinator muscle. Innervated by the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the radial nerve.
tcmIndications: Pain and fatigue in the shoulder and arm
numbness in the arm and hand
westernIndications: motor rehabilitation of the upper limb after stroke
LI-9.etymology: Shang (上), upper; Lian (廉), edge, ridge. The point lies 1 cun above Xia Lian (LI-8), on the dorsal aspect of the forearm, near the proximal end of the radius.
LI-9.clinicalNotes: See Shou San Li (LI-10) and Qu Chi (LI-11) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-10.locationClassical: 2 cun distal to LI-11, on the line connecting LI-5 and LI-11, over the extensor carpi radialis longus muscle.
howToFind: Position the wrist laterally, with the elbow flexed. Locate the point on the line between Yang Xi (LI-5) and Qu Chi (LI-11), one-sixth from Qu Chi (LI-11) and five-sixths from Yang Xi (LI-5).
LI-10.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, accessory cephalic vein and posterior branch of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, brachioradialis muscle, extensor carpi radialis longus and extensor carpi radialis brevis, superficial branch of the radial nerve and a branch of the radial artery, radius — deeper insertion reaches the supinator muscle.
actions: activates the channel and relieves pain
regulates Qi and Blood in the upper limb
opens the channel and the Luo vessels
tcmIndications: pain and limited movement in the arm and shoulder
pain and hypersensitivity in the elbow and arm
westernIndications: generalized tendinopathy of the forearm extensors
inflammation of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
LI-10.etymology: Shou (手), hand; San (三), three; Li (里), considered as 1 cun in ancient times, equivalent to a distance of 1 kilometer. This point lies on the forearm, 3 cun below Qu Chi (LI-11).
LI-10.clinicalNotes:
1. The points located between the elbow and the wrist are mainly used in the treatment of disorders of the Zang Fu organs. This point belongs to the Large Intestine Meridian and is therefore effective in treating intestinal problems, especially abdominal distension, vomiting, and diarrhea.

2. The indications follow the principle of treatment along the meridian course, so it can be used to treat disorders of the head and sense organs, pain in the shoulder and arm, and hemiplegia.

3. Technical errors in handling acupuncture needles can cause pain and a sensation of heaviness in the upper limbs. Rocking the handle of the needle at this point can relieve the local discomfort. The point can treat low back pain because the tendinomuscular meridian passes alongside the spine.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-11.locationClassical: With the elbow flexed at a right angle, at the lateral end of the cubital crease, in the depression between the end of the crease and the lateral epicondyle of the humerus, over the extensor carpi radialis longus muscle.
howToFind: When the elbow is flexed at a 90° angle, the point can be located at the radial end of its crease. (Fig.
When the elbow is flexed, Qu Chi (LI-11) is located at the midpoint of the line connecting Chi Ze (LU-5) and the lateral epicondyle.
LI-11.anatomy: Origin of the extensor carpi radialis longus muscle, brachioradialis muscle. Innervated by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the radial nerve.
tcmIndications: pain and motor impairment of the shoulder and arm
hemiplegia with inability to close the hand
flaccidity of the tendons preventing combing the hair
painful obstruction of the throat with sensation of impending death
loose or watery foul-smelling stools (traveler's diarrhea) — bloodletting is permitted in pharyngitis and laryngitis
westernIndications: eczema — essential orthopedic point in lateral epicondylitis
myofascial pain syndrome of the brachioradialis and supinator
lateral epicondylitis of the humerus (tennis elbow)
LI-11.etymology: Qu (曲), bent, curved; Chi (池), shallow pool. With the elbow flexed, a depression resembling a shallow pool appears at the location of the point.
LI-11.clinicalNotes:
1. It is an effective point for circulating Qi in the meridians and collaterals. It may be used to treat painful cramping of the upper limbs, inflammation, joint and muscular pain, Bi syndrome, and Wei (flaccidity) syndrome of the whole body.

2. It can be used to expel Wind and regulate Ying Wei (nutrition-defense). It is one of the principal points in the treatment of fever, common cold, and dermatologic diseases.

3. It can also be used to regulate the function of the Chang (intestine). It is widely used in the treatment of infectious diarrhea. Recent research has confirmed its efficacy in lowering fever, expelling wind, regulating the functions of Ying Wei (nutrition-defense), and improving homeostasis (a tonifying effect, since it is a tonification point. Despite having a strong sedative effect, it cannot be regarded as a sedation point).

Figure 9.3 — Qu Chi point.

combinations.indication: Fever, skin disorders, immune regulation
High fever, heat clearing, immune regulation

LI-12.category: Point of the Large Intestine primary channel.
LI-12.locationClassical: 1 cun proximal (obliquely superior) to the lateral end of the cubital crease (LI-11), on the anterior border of the humerus.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed, locate the point 1 cun directly above Qu Chi (LI-11), on the lateral border of the triceps brachii tendon.
LI-12.anatomy: Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, origin of the brachioradialis and triceps brachii muscles. Innervated by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the radial nerve.
LI-12.needling: Vertical insertion 0.5–1 cun; the needle is introduced between the border of the humerus and the flexor muscles in a medial direction.
tcmIndications: Pain, numbness, and contracture in the elbow and arm
westernIndications: lateral epicondylalgia of the humerus (tennis elbow)
LI-12.etymology: Zhou (肘), elbow; Liao (髎), bone hole. The point lies on the elbow, near the bone hole.
LI-12.clinicalNotes: The indications follow the principle of the local point and the meridian course.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-13.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the upper arm, 3 cun proximal to LI-11, on the line connecting LI-11 and LI-15.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed, locate the point 3 cun directly above Qu Chi (LI-11), on the lateral aspect of the triceps brachii tendon.
LI-13.anatomy: Lateral border of the brachialis and triceps brachii muscles. Innervated by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm and the radial nerve.
actions: Activates the channel and relieves pain
clears the channels and transforms Phlegm
tcmIndications: pain and contracture in the elbow and arm
westernIndications: myofascial pain of the brachialis muscle
rehabilitation after a fracture of the humeral shaft
LI-13.etymology: Shou (手), arm; Wu (五), five; Li (里), considered as cun in ancient times. The point lies on the lower portion of the upper arm, 5 cun below Tian Fu (LU-3).
LI-13.clinicalNotes:
The point is mainly used in the treatment of disorders of the shoulder and arm, since it acts to improve the flow of Qi in the meridians and to activate the collaterals.

[Figure missing — Fig. 9.4: Hand Yang Ming points (arm and shoulder).]

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-14.category: Meeting Point of the Large Intestine channel with the Small Intestine and Bladder channels
LI-14.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the upper arm, on the line connecting LI-11 and LI-15, 7 cun proximal to LI-11 and slightly above the distal insertion of the deltoid muscle.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed, locate the point at the lower end of the deltoid muscle, on the line connecting Qu Chi (LI-11) and Jian Yu (LI-15).
LI-14.anatomy: Insertion of the deltoid muscle, brachialis muscle. Innervated by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm and the radial nerve.
LI-14.needling: Vertical insertion 0.5–1 cun; also obliquely directed toward the shoulder for ocular disorders.
actions: Activates the channel and relieves pain
regulates Qi and dissolves Phlegm nodules
opens the channel and the Luo vessels
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and arm
westernIndications: myofascial trigger points in the deltoid
LI-14.etymology: Bi (臂), upper limb; Nao (臑), upper arm. The point lies over the prominence of the upper arm muscle.
LI-14.clinicalNotes: The point may be employed to improve the circulation of Qi in the collaterals and to provide better visual acuity; it can therefore be used in the treatment of ocular diseases.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-15.category: Meeting Point of the Large Intestine channel with the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
LI-15.locationClassical: In the depression anterior and inferior to the acromion. With the arm abducted to 90°, two depressions appear at the anterior and posterior borders of the acromion; LI-15 is located in the anterior depression.
howToFind: With the arm abducted, locate the point in the anterior depression of the shoulder joint.
With the shoulder relaxed, locate the point 2 cun directly below the acromial extremity of the clavicle, on the Large Intestine Meridian, Hand Yang Ming. (Fig.
LI-15.anatomy: Anterior and middle fibers of the deltoid muscle, supraspinatus tendon. Innervated by the lateral supraclavicular nerve and the axillary nerve.
LI-15.needling: Perpendicular insertion (with the arm abducted) 1.0–1.5 cun, or downward oblique insertion (with the arm at rest) 0.8–1.5 cun.
LI-15.safetyWarning: Avoid deep medial insertion into the joint capsule without specific indication — there is risk of penetrating the glenohumeral joint with vertically directed needling.
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and arm
motor impairment of the upper limbs
scrofula — master point for paresis of the upper limb; prophylactic moxa is used to prevent muscular atrophy in hemiplegia
westernIndications: rotator cuff tendinopathy (especially of the supraspinatus)
myofascial pain syndrome of the anterior deltoid
LI-15.etymology: Jian (肩), shoulder; Yu (髃), corner, angle. The point lies at the corner of the shoulder.
LI-15.clinicalNotes: The point is used in the treatment of shoulder and upper limb pathology. With its function of promoting the circulation of Qi, it is used in the treatment of Bi syndrome, flaccidity, hemiplegia, and Wei syndrome.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-16.category: Meeting Point of the Large Intestine channel with the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
LI-16.locationClassical: On the upper aspect of the shoulder, in the depression between the acromial extremity of the clavicle and the spine of the scapula (acromioclavicular joint space).
howToFind: Seated with the shoulder relaxed, locate the point at the posterior border of the acromioclavicular joint, in the depression between the clavicle and the spine of the scapula.
LI-16.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, thoracoacromial vein, supraclavicular nerve (lateral branch), trapezius muscle, supraspinatus muscle, suprascapular nerve and artery, scapula.
LI-16.safetyWarning: Deep medially directed insertion carries a risk of pneumothorax.
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and back
motor impairment of the upper limb
difficulty flexing and extending the shoulders and arms
difficulty extending and raising the arms
westernIndications: tendinopathy and trigger points in the supraspinatus
myofascial pain of the upper trapezius
LI-16.etymology: Ju (巨), great; Gu (骨), bone. In ancient times, the clavicle was called Ju Gu. The point lies posterior to the clavicle.
LI-16.clinicalNotes: See Jian Yu (LI-15) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-17.category: Point of the Large Intestine primary channel.
LI-17.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the neck, along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (at the level of the laryngeal prominence), 1 cun inferior to LI-18.
howToFind: Seated with the neck slightly tilted laterally and extended, first locate Fu Tu (LI-18), 3 cun lateral to the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). Locate the point at the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, 1 cun directly below Fu Tu (LI-18).
LI-17.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, platysma, cervical fascia, posterior aspect of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, lateral border of the external jugular vein, supraclavicular nerve (C3 and C4), transverse cervical nerve (C2 and C3), transverse cervical artery, levator scapulae muscle, scalene muscle, cervical plexus.
LI-17.safetyWarning: Deep insertion carries a risk of puncturing the jugular vein or the carotid artery — the common carotid artery must be strictly avoided.
LI-17.etymology: Tian (天), heaven; Ding (鼎), an ancient vessel with two handles and three feet. Tian Ding (LI-17) together with Que Pen (ST-12) and Qi She (ST-11) form a triangle.
LI-17.clinicalNotes: The indications follow the principle of treatment with the local point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-18.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the neck, at the level of the tip of the laryngeal prominence, between the sternal and clavicular heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (SCM).
howToFind: Seated with the neck slightly tilted laterally and extended, first locate Lian Quan (CV-23), in the depression above the hyoid bone. Locate the point 3 cun lateral to Lian Quan (CV-23).
LI-18.anatomy: Sternocleidomastoid muscle, platysma. Innervated by the great auricular nerve, cervical plexus, and spinal accessory nerve.
LI-18.needling: Vertical insertion 0.3–0.5 cun or oblique up to 0.8 cun.
LI-18.safetyWarning: Deep insertion carries a risk of puncturing the jugular vein or the carotid artery. Reposition the head to neutral before insertion. Caution: carotid artery and jugular vein.
tcmIndications: indicated when swallowing is impaired (e.g., after stroke) and in acute aphonia
westernIndications: dysphagia — direct access to the primary trigger points of the SCM, very effective for pain referred to the forehead, ear, and sinus region, as well as for atypical facial pain, dizziness, and vertigo
LI-18.etymology: Fu (扶), equivalent to 3 cun; Tu (突), prominence. Tu refers to the prominence of the larynx. The point lies lateral to the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple).
LI-18.clinicalNotes: The point is located beside the throat and trachea. It can be used in the treatment of local disorders such as goiter symptoms. The effect can be obtained by activating and circulating Qi and Xue (Blood), by clearing heat, and by activating the Qi of Fei (Lung), dissolving "tumoral masses."

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-19.category: Point of the Large Intestine primary channel.
LI-19.locationClassical: On the upper lip, immediately below the lateral margin of the nostril, at the level of GV-26 (Shuigou).
howToFind: Seated with the neck extended or in an upright posture, first locate Shui Gou (GV-26). Locate LI-19
5 cun lateral to it.
LI-19.anatomy: Orbicularis oris muscle, levator labii superioris muscle. Innervated by the superior labial branches of the facial nerve and the infraorbital nerve (a branch of the trigeminal).
LI-19.etymology: Kou (口), mouth; He (禾), refers to bamboo, the area around the lips where the mustache and beard grow; Liao (髎), bone hole. The point lies near the incisor tooth.
LI-19.clinicalNotes: The point is used in the treatment of nasal disorders, by the principle of the local point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LI-20.category: Meeting Point of the Large Intestine and Stomach channels
LI-20.locationClassical: On the outer border of the wing of the nose, in the nasolabial groove, approximately 0.5 cun lateral to the midpoint of the lateral border of the nasal wing.
howToFind: Seated with the neck extended, locate the point in the nasolabial groove, at the level of the lateral border of the wing of the nose.
LI-20.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, second branch of the trigeminal nerve, nasalis muscle and levator labii superioris muscle, branches of the facial arteries and veins, angular vein, mandible.
LI-20.needling: Insertion of 0.3–0.5 cun — vertical, oblique, or transverse (subcutaneous) directed medially and superiorly toward EX-HN-8, or 3–8 mm obliquely directed craniomedially.
LI-20.safetyWarning: According to some authors, moxibustion is contraindicated at this point. Hygiene is particularly important. Infected regions must never be needled under any circumstances, given the proximity of the angular vein and its anastomosis with the ophthalmic vein — there is a risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis and central inflammatory processes.
tcmIndications: facial paralysis — when this point is pressed, the patient should feel distension and heaviness radiating into the interior of the nose
LI-20.etymology: Ying (迎), to meet; Xiang (香), fragrance. Used in the treatment of nasal problems and to restore the sense of smell, enabling the nose to "perceive fragrances."
LI-20.clinicalNotes: The indications follow the principle of treatment with the local point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-1.locationClassical: With the eyes looking straight ahead, directly below the center of the pupil, in the depression between the eyeball and the infraorbital margin.
howToFind: Seated or supine, with the patient looking straight ahead, locate the point directly below the pupil, between the eyeball and the infraorbital margin.
ST-1.anatomy: Orbicularis oculi muscle. Innervated by the infraorbital nerve (second division of the trigeminal nerve) and the facial nerve. Infraorbital artery and vein.
ST-1.needling: Ask the patient to close the eyes. Gently push the eyeball upward. Insert slightly downward, then perpendicularly 0.5–1.0 cun (or 0.2–0.4 cun) between the eyeball and the inferior wall of the orbit.
ST-1.safetyWarning: High Risk. Do not lift, thrust, or rotate the needle, in order to avoid hemorrhage or injury to the optic nerve and eyeball. Press firmly with cotton for one minute when withdrawing the needle to prevent hematoma. Classical texts contraindicate moxibustion at this point.
tcmIndications: Redness and pain in the eyes
deviation of the mouth and eyes
ST-1.etymology: Cheng (承), to receive; Qi (泣), tears. The point lies below the eye, in the place where tears are received.
ST-1.clinicalNotes: The point improves vision and eliminates Wind; commonly used to treat ocular disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-2.category: Meeting Point with the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
ST-2.locationClassical: With the eyes looking straight ahead, 1 cun directly below the center of the pupil, in the depression at the infraorbital foramen.
howToFind: Seated or supine, with the patient looking straight ahead, locate the point below the pupil, in the depression of the infraorbital foramen.
ST-2.anatomy: Orbicularis oculi muscle. Located at the exit of the infraorbital nerve. Infraorbital artery and vein.
ST-2.needling: Perpendicular insertion 0.3–0.5 cun, or transverse (subcutaneous) insertion toward neighboring points (e.g., ST-4, SI-18).
ST-2.safetyWarning: Deep oblique or upward insertion is contraindicated. Avoid lifting and thrusting movements to prevent injury to the infraorbital nerve.
tcmIndications: Redness and pain in the eyes
deviation of the mouth and eyes
westernIndications: biliary ascariasis (roundworm in the bile duct)
ST-2.etymology: Si (四), four; Bai (白), white, brightness. The point lies below the eye and is indicated for ocular disorders. It improves vision in the four directions.
ST-2.clinicalNotes: This point is used to improve vision, eliminate Wind, and treat ocular disorders, facial palsy, and trigeminal neuralgia.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-3.category: Meeting Point with the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
ST-3.locationClassical: Directly below the pupil, at the level of the inferior border of the ala of the nose, on the lateral side of the nasolabial groove.
howToFind: Seated or supine, with the patient looking straight ahead, locate the point at the intersection of the vertical line through the pupil and the horizontal line through the inferior border of the ala of the nose.
ST-3.anatomy: Levator labii superioris muscle. Innervated by branches of the facial nerve and the infraorbital nerve.
ST-3.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion 0.3–0.5 cun. Alternatively, transverse insertion toward ST-4 or SI-18 for facial palsy.
ST-3.safetyWarning: Avoid the facial artery and vein.
tcmIndications: Deviation of the mouth and eyes
swelling of the lips and cheeks
ST-3.etymology: Ju (巨), huge; Liao (髎), foramen. The point lies in a foramen, at the junction of the maxilla and the zygomatic bone.
ST-3.clinicalNotes:
1. This point is used to treat local disorders such as headache and trigeminal neuralgia. Insert the needle deeply, directing it toward the inner canthus of the contralateral eye.

2. According to the principle of "where the meridian passes, the indications follow," the point is also used to treat knee swelling and inflammation.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-4.category: Meeting Point with the Large Intestine channel
ST-4.locationClassical: With the eyes looking straight ahead, 0.4 cun lateral to the angle of the mouth, directly below the pupil.
howToFind: Seated or supine, with the patient looking straight ahead, locate the point at the intersection of the vertical line through the pupil and the horizontal line through the angle of the mouth.
ST-4.anatomy: Orbicularis oris muscle. Innervated by branches of the facial nerve and the infraorbital nerve. Network of facial artery and vein.
ST-4.needling: Transverse (subcutaneous) insertion 0.5–1.0 cun, frequently directed toward ST-6.
ST-4.etymology: Di (地), earth; Cang (倉), granary. The five grains grow from the earth. Grains enter the Wei (Stomach) through the mouth, as if entering a granary. The point lies at the corner of the mouth.
ST-4.clinicalNotes: Facial palsy and sialorrhea can be treated by needling Di Cang (ST-4) toward Jia Che (ST-6).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-5.category: Meeting Point with the Gall Bladder channel (per some classical texts)
ST-5.locationClassical: On the lateral mandible, anterior to the masseter muscle. Located in a shallow depression slightly above the angle of the mandible.
howToFind: Seated or supine, with the mouth closed and the cheeks puffed out, locate the point at the border of the mandibular fossa, where the pulse is palpable.
ST-5.anatomy: Anterior border of the masseter muscle. Facial nerve (mandibular branch). The facial artery is directly palpable here.
ST-5.needling: Oblique or transverse (subcutaneous) insertion 0.3–0.5 cun, generally directed toward ST-6.
ST-5.safetyWarning: Take care to avoid the facial artery and vein.
ST-5.etymology: Da (大), great; Ying (迎), reception. The point lies beside the mandibular artery.
ST-5.clinicalNotes: The point eliminates Wind and drains the meridian. It is one of the major points for treating disorders of the facial region.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-6.locationClassical: With the teeth clenched, at the highest prominence of the masseter muscle, approximately one finger-breadth anterior and superior to the angle of the mandible.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point
4 cun from the angle of the mandible. With the teeth clenched, the masseter muscle becomes prominent.
ST-6.anatomy: Masseter muscle. Innervated by the masseteric nerve (a branch of the trigeminal) and the facial nerve.
ST-6.needling: Insert with the patient's mouth closed. Perpendicular insertion 0.3–0.5 cun, or transverse insertion 1.0–1.5 cun directed toward ST-4, SI-18, or SI-19.
actions: benefits the jaw and the teeth
westernIndications: parotitis. Extremely important local trigger point
ST-6.etymology: Jia (頰), cheek region; Che (車), vehicle. Che refers to the mandible. The point lies in the cheek region near the angle of the mandible.
ST-6.clinicalNotes: Jia Che (ST-6) is used to treat deviation of the mouth by needling from Jia Che (ST-6) toward Di Cang (ST-4), or vice versa. It eliminates pathogenic Wind and is indicated for parotitis. The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, enters the upper dental arch, so digital pressure on this point can relieve toothache.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-7.category: Meeting Point with the Gall Bladder channel
ST-7.locationClassical: On the inferior border of the zygomatic arch, in the depression anterior to the condylar process of the mandible. Locate and needle with the mouth closed.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, with the mouth closed, locate the point in the depression below the zygomatic arch. The depression becomes more pronounced when the mouth is opened.
ST-7.anatomy: Masseter and lateral pterygoid muscles. Branches of the facial nerve and the mandibular nerve. Superficial temporal artery in the vicinity.
ST-7.safetyWarning: Deep needling reaches the lateral pterygoid muscle. Some classical texts contraindicate moxibustion.
actions: Eliminates Wind from the head and face
benefits the ears and the jaw
tcmIndications: deviation of the mouth and eyes
westernIndications: facial palsy. Provides direct access to the lateral pterygoid
ST-7.etymology: Xia (下), below; Guan (关), passage, joint. Guan refers to the zygomatic arch: the point lies below the zygomatic arch.
ST-7.clinicalNotes: This point is used to treat disorders of the ear and mouth, such as temporomandibular occlusion disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-8.category: Meeting Point with the Gall Bladder channel and Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
ST-8.locationClassical: 0.5 cun within the anterior hairline, at the frontal angle, 4.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (GV-24).
howToFind: Seated, first locate Tou Lin Qi (GB-15),

5 cun posterior to the anterior hairline, on the vertical line through the pupil. Locate Tou Wei (ST-8) lateral to Tou Lin Qi (GB-15), at the same distance from Tou Lin Qi (GB-15) as that point lies from Shen Ting (GV-24).
ST-8.anatomy: Border of the temporalis muscle. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve and branches of the facial nerve.
ST-8.needling: Transverse (subcutaneous) insertion 0.5–1.0 cun along the scalp.
actions: benefits the head and the eyes
ST-8.etymology: Tou (頭), head; Wei (維), corner or angle. The point lies at the lateral angle of the frontal hairline.
ST-8.clinicalNotes: The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, and the Bladder Meridian, Tai Yang of the Foot, connect at the medial canthus of the eyelid and cross at Shen Ting (GV-24). For this reason the point is commonly used to treat migraine, headache, vertigo, and ocular disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-9.category: Point of the Sea of Qi
ST-9.locationClassical: On the anterior aspect of the neck, at the level of the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple), 1.5 cun lateral to the midline, on the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle.
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest, locate the point
5 cun lateral to the cricoid cartilage.
ST-9.anatomy: Platysma, SCM muscle. Bifurcation of the common carotid artery (internal/external), internal jugular vein. Innervated by the cervical plexus and branches of the vagus nerve.
ST-9.needling: Perpendicular insertion 0.5–1.0 cun between the artery and the thyroid cartilage.
ST-9.safetyWarning: HIGH-DANGER POINT. The carotid artery must be manually isolated and held laterally before inserting the needle anterior to the pulse. Deep insertion can puncture the carotid artery or the internal jugular vein. Irritation of the carotid sinus may cause acute hypotension and syncope.
ST-9.etymology: Ren (人), person; Ying (迎), welcoming, motion. The point lies beside the common carotid artery.
ST-9.clinicalNotes:
1. According to the location of the point and the course of the meridian, this point is used to treat headache and vertigo caused by excess Heat in the Yang Ming.

2. The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, belongs to the Wei (Stomach) and is used to treat vomiting and diarrhea.

3. As a local point, it is used to treat sore throat with difficulty swallowing, asthma, and acute pharyngitis.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-10.locationClassical: On the anterior border of the SCM muscle, at the midpoint of a line connecting ST-9 and ST-11.
howToFind: Seated, with the head erect, locate the point inferior to Ren Ying (ST-9), on the anterior aspect of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the level of the inferior margin of the cricoid cartilage, at the midpoint of a line connecting Ren Ying (ST-9) and Qi She (ST-11).
ST-10.anatomy: Platysma, SCM muscle. Innervated by the transverse cervical nerve.
ST-10.needling: Oblique medially-directed insertion 0.5–1.0 cun, angled away from the carotid artery.
ST-10.safetyWarning: Avoid the carotid artery and the jugular veins.
ST-10.etymology: Shui (水), water; Tu (突), prominence, projection. The point lies on the neck, near the esophagus. It treats dysphagia and asthma.
ST-10.clinicalNotes: The point lies near the trachea, where lymphadenitis and goiter often occur. Its local indications are therefore to relieve thoracic discomfort and throat inflammation, regulate the flow of Qi, and reduce phlegm.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-11.locationClassical: At the base of the neck, directly below ST-9, at the superior border of the clavicle, in the depression between the sternal and clavicular heads of the SCM muscle.
howToFind: Seated, with the head erect, locate the point immediately inferior to Ren Ying (ST-9), at the upper margin of the proximal end of the clavicle,
5 cun lateral to Tian Tu (CV-22).
ST-11.anatomy: Between the heads of the SCM. The apex of the lung, the common carotid artery, and the internal jugular vein lie deep.
ST-11.safetyWarning: Deep insertion carries a risk of puncturing the lung (causing pneumothorax) or injuring the great cervical vessels.
ST-11.etymology: Qi (气), air; She (舍), abode. Qi refers to the vital energy of Fei (Lung) and Wei (Stomach).
ST-11.clinicalNotes: The point lies near Fei (Lung). It regulates the flow of Qi and relieves respiratory discomfort and asthma; it is indicated for respiratory disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-12.category: Meeting Point with the Large Intestine
ST-12.locationClassical: In the supraclavicular fossa, superior to the midpoint of the clavicle, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Seated, with the head erect, locate the point in the middle of the supraclavicular fossa, on the superior aspect of the lateral depression of the clavicular insertion of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
ST-12.anatomy: Platysma. Supraclavicular nerve, brachial plexus, subclavian artery and vein.
ST-12.safetyWarning: High Risk of Pneumothorax. Deep insertion can puncture the apex of the lung. Also avoid the subclavian vessels.
ST-12.etymology: Que (缺), defective; Pen (盆), basin. Que Pen refers to the supraclavicular fossa, where the point is located.
ST-12.clinicalNotes: The indications follow the principle of treatment with the local point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-13.locationClassical: On the chest, directly below ST-12, on the inferior border of the clavicle, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point at the midpoint of the inferior border of the clavicle, 4 cun lateral to the sternal midline, directly above the nipple.
ST-13.anatomy: Pectoralis major muscle. Subclavius muscle. Innervated by the supraclavicular and pectoral nerves.
ST-13.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the rib 0.5–0.8 cun.
ST-13.safetyWarning: Perpendicular or deep insertion carries substantial risk of pneumothorax.
tcmIndications: fullness and distension of the chest
ST-13.etymology: Qi (氣), air; Hu (戶), door. The point lies in the upper chest region, like a door for Qi and for the vital energy of Fei (Lung) and Wei (Stomach).
ST-13.clinicalNotes: As a local point, Qi Hu (ST-13) is indicated to treat disorders of the respiratory tract.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-14.locationClassical: On the chest, in the first intercostal space, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point on the vertical line through the nipple, at the middle of the first intercostal space.
ST-14.anatomy: Pectoralis major and minor muscles, intercostal muscles. Pectoral nerves.
ST-14.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space 0.5–0.8 cun.
ST-14.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of pneumothorax.
ST-14.etymology: Ku (庫), storehouse; Fang (房), room. Because the point lies near the breast, it stores fluids and nutrients that can be transformed into milk.
ST-14.clinicalNotes: Ku Fang (ST-14), as a local point, promotes the circulation of Qi to relieve thoracic stagnation and improve asthma.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-15.locationClassical: On the chest, in the second intercostal space, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point on the vertical line through the nipple, at the middle of the second intercostal space.
ST-15.anatomy: Pectoralis major and minor muscles, intercostal muscles. Pectoral nerves.
ST-15.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space 0.5–0.8 cun.
ST-15.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of pneumothorax.
tcmIndications: sensation of heaviness in the chest
ST-15.etymology: Wu (屋), room; Yi (翳), covering, secret. The point lies in the upper chest region, beside the breast, like a screen or roof.
ST-15.clinicalNotes:
1. As a local point, it is used to treat respiratory disorders and mastitis. In practice, combine with He Gu (LI-4).

2. The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, is the meridian with the most Qi and Xue, and is therefore indicated to treat dermatologic disorders by regulating Ying (essence) and Wei (Stomach).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-16.locationClassical: On the chest, in the third intercostal space, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point on the vertical line through the nipple, at the middle of the third intercostal space.
ST-16.anatomy: Pectoralis major muscle, intercostal muscles. Pectoral nerves.
ST-16.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space 0.5–0.8 cun.
ST-16.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of pneumothorax.
ST-16.etymology: Ying (膺), chest; Chuang (窗), window. The point is like a window of the chest.
ST-16.clinicalNotes:
1. The point may be used to treat disorders of the respiratory tract.

2. The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, belongs to the Wei (Stomach) and is indicated to treat gastrointestinal disorders.

3. By its location, it is used in the treatment of mastitis combined with He Gu (LI-4).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-17.locationClassical: On the chest, in the fourth intercostal space, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline, directly at the center of the nipple.
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point in the middle of the fourth intercostal space, at the center of the nipple (in males).
ST-17.needling: CONTRAINDICATED. Neither needling nor moxibustion is applied at this point. It serves strictly as an anatomic reference for measurement.
actions: Opens the channel and alleviates pain
ST-17.etymology: Ru (乳), breast; Zhong (中), center. The point lies at the center of the nipple.
ST-17.clinicalNotes: This point serves as an anatomic reference in the thoracic region. Classically, neither acupuncture nor moxibustion is performed at this point. This convention is currently debated, as the point is indicated in the treatment of certain conditions.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-18.locationClassical: On the chest, in the fifth intercostal space, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline, directly below the nipple.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point on the vertical line through the nipple, at the middle of the fifth intercostal space.
ST-18.anatomy: Inferior margin of the pectoralis major muscle.
ST-18.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space 0.5–0.8 cun.
ST-18.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of pneumothorax.
ST-18.etymology: Ru (乳), breast; Gen (根), root or base. The point lies at the base of the breast.
ST-18.clinicalNotes: This point is used to treat mastitis, combined with the needling of He Gu (LI-4).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-19.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 6 cun above the umbilicus (level of CV-14).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 6 cun above the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-19.safetyWarning: Deep needling can perforate the peritoneum or the underlying organs.
ST-19.etymology: Bu (不), not; Rong (容), to contain. The point lies in the upper abdomen, and treats abdominal distension when the Wei (Stomach) can no longer receive food and water.
ST-19.clinicalNotes: Patients with precordial pain often have associated epigastric pain. The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, passes over the Xin (Heart); for this reason the point is indicated in the treatment of associated precordial pain and epigastric pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-20.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 5 cun above the umbilicus (level of CV-13).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 5 cun above the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-20.safetyWarning: Deep needling can perforate the peritoneum or the underlying organs.
actions: Regulates Qi of the Middle Jiao and the Stomach
ST-20.etymology: Cheng (承), to receive; Man (满), full. The name of this point reflects the function of the Wei (Stomach).
ST-20.clinicalNotes:
1. Because the point lies near the Wei (Stomach), it is used to treat digestive disorders. Phlegm retention and generalized edema are caused by deficiency of Pi (Spleen) in transforming and transporting nutrients and fluids.

2. The point may be used to treat asthma due to inversion of the flow of Stomach Qi. By regulating Qi flow and calming the Wei (Stomach), it can relieve the discomfort caused by asthma.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-21.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 4 cun above the umbilicus (level of CV-12).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 4 cun above the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-21.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle and its sheath. Innervated by the 7th and 8th intercostal nerves. Superior epigastric artery and vein.
ST-21.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can perforate the peritoneal cavity.
ST-21.etymology: Liang (梁), grain or food; Men (门), gate. The point lies in the upper epigastric region, which is the gate for the passage of food into the Wei (Stomach).
ST-21.clinicalNotes:
Located in the epigastric region, it is used principally to treat digestive disorders.

The Yang Ming Meridian contains abundant Qi and Xue (Blood). Abdominal masses can be treated by activating and promoting the flow of Qi and Xue in the meridian and its collaterals, eliminating the stagnation of Qi and Xue.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.
