ST-22.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 3 cun above the umbilicus (level of CV-11).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 3 cun above the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-22.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle. Innervated by the 8th intercostal nerve.
ST-22.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can perforate the peritoneal cavity.
actions: Regulates the intestines and the Stomach
ST-22.etymology: Guan (关), passage; Men (门), gate. The point lies in the lower region of the Wei (Stomach), corresponding to the transition between the Wei (Stomach) and the Chang (Intestine).
ST-22.clinicalNotes:
As a local point, it is used to treat digestive disorders.

Ascites and generalized edema can be treated by regulating the function of Pi (Spleen) in the transport and transformation of nutrients.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-23.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 2 cun above the umbilicus (level of CV-10).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 2 cun above the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-23.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle. Innervated by the 8th and 9th intercostal nerves.
ST-23.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can perforate the peritoneal cavity.
actions: Transforms Phlegm and calms the Shen
ST-23.etymology: Tai (太), great; Yi (乙), part of an ancient Chinese system of ordinal numbers.
ST-23.clinicalNotes:
By its location, this point treats digestive disorders. Deficiency of Pi (Spleen) leads to phlegm retention in the body. The point is indicated to strengthen Pi (Spleen), eliminate dampness, and resolve phlegm.

By promoting the flow of Qi and eliminating the accumulated Heat in the Yang Ming Meridian, the point is indicated to treat neuropsychiatric disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-24.locationClassical: On the abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 1 cun above the umbilicus (level of CV-9).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 1 cun above the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-24.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle. Innervated by the 9th intercostal nerve.
ST-24.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can perforate the peritoneal cavity.
ST-24.etymology: Hua (滑), slippery; Rou (肉), flesh; Men (滑肉门), gate. Like a gate through which the soft tissues pass. Hua Rou may be translated as fat.
ST-24.clinicalNotes: Hua Rou Men (ST-24) is a local point of the Stomach Meridian on the upper abdomen, used primarily to harmonize the Stomach, transform Phlegm, and calm the Shen when a Phlegm component obstructs the Middle Jiao (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 166–167). Classically, the Jia Yi Jing records the point for rigid tongue, hematemesis, and manic delirium — patterns in which Phlegm clouds the Heart and disturbs the Shen. In contemporary practice it is typically combined with Tian Shu (ST-25) for abdominal pain and Middle-Jiao distension, and with Shen Men (HT-7) or Feng Long (ST-40) when Phlegm is associated with restlessness or insomnia (Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). It is less used than its neighbor Tian Shu (ST-25), the Front-Mu of the Large Intestine, which concentrates most of the intestinal indications; for this reason many texts refer the reader directly to Tai Yi (ST-23) and Tian Shu (ST-25) for technique details. Caution: deep needling may reach the peritoneal cavity — keep perpendicular insertion at 0.8–1.0 cun.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-25.category: Front-Mu Point of the Large Intestine
ST-25.locationClassical: On the abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the umbilicus.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 2 cun lateral to the umbilicus.
ST-25.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle. Innervated by the 10th intercostal nerve. Branches of the inferior epigastric artery and vein.
ST-25.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can perforate the peritoneal cavity. Contraindicated in advanced pregnancy.
ST-25.etymology: Tian (天), heaven; Shu (枢), pivot. The region above the umbilicus is considered Heaven, belonging to Yang; the region below the umbilicus is Earth, belonging to Yin. The point lies at the level of the umbilicus, like a pivot between Heaven and Earth.
ST-25.clinicalNotes:
1. Tian Shu (ST-25), being the Front Mu point of the Da Chang (Large Intestine), is used principally to treat local disorders such as diarrhea, dysentery, constipation, paralytic ileus, periumbilical pain, and abdominal distension.

2. The point lies near the Wei (Stomach) and belongs to the Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot; it is indicated to treat epigastric pain and vomiting.

3. Disorders such as jaundice, vertigo, and consumptive diseases can be treated by regulating the function of the Wei (Stomach) and Chang (Intestine), promoting the flow of Qi, and removing dampness.

4. The point lies on the abdomen, where the genitourinary system is located. The Nan Jing states that a collateral branch of the Chong Mai originates at Qi Chong (ST-30) and runs together with the Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot. The Chong Mai originates in the uterus, has an internal relationship with the reproductive system, and ascends together with the Kidney Meridian, Shao Yin of the Foot. Because the Shen (Kidney) governs the waterways, disorders of the reproductive and urinary systems can be treated by needling Tian Shu (ST-25).

5. The point is indicated to relieve low back pain located at the same level as the point. According to the principle of point correspondence, this method is termed "anterior-posterior point combination."

6. The point is needled to treat neuropsychiatric disorders caused by Heat-dryness in the Wei (Stomach) and Chang (Intestine).

combinations.indication: Diarrhea, dysentery, intestinal disorders

ST-26.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 1 cun below the umbilicus (level of CV-7).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 1 cun below the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-26.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle. Innervated by the 10th intercostal nerve.
ST-26.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can perforate the peritoneal cavity.
ST-26.etymology: Wai (外), outer; Ling (陵), mound. The local prominence of the point resembles a mound.
ST-26.clinicalNotes: The point lies near the genital region and the Chang (Intestine), and is indicated in the treatment of disorders of these organs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-27.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 2 cun below the umbilicus (level of CV-5).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 2 cun below the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-27.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle. Innervated by the 11th intercostal nerve.
ST-27.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can perforate the peritoneal cavity.
ST-27.etymology: Da (大), great; Ju (巨), huge. The point lies at the largest prominence of the abdominal wall.
ST-27.clinicalNotes:
Owing to its proximity to the genitourinary organs, this point is indicated to treat their pathologies.

Insomnia with palpitations and fear arising from these disorders can be treated with this point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-28.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 3 cun below the umbilicus (level of CV-4).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 3 cun below the umbilicus and 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
ST-28.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle. Innervated by the 12th intercostal nerve (subcostal nerve).
ST-28.safetyWarning: Deep needling can perforate a full bladder. The patient should void before treatment.
ST-28.etymology: Shui (水), water; Dao (道), way. The deep region of this point corresponds to the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine) and lies near the Pang Guang (Bladder). It is located in the Lower Jiao, where the waterways pass.
ST-28.clinicalNotes:
As a local point, it is used to treat urogenital disorders and constipation.

By the technique of anterior-posterior point combination, it can treat pain and stiffness in the spine and hip.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-29.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 4 cun below the umbilicus (level of CV-3).
howToFind: Supine, first locate Qu Gu (CV-2), in the depression on the upper aspect of the pubic bone. Locate Gui Lai (ST-29) 2 cun lateral and 1 cun superior to Qu Gu (CV-2).
ST-29.anatomy: Rectus abdominis muscle, lateral border of the rectus sheath. Innervated by the iliohypogastric nerve.
ST-29.etymology: Gui (归), return; Lai (来), to arrive, to come. This point is indicated to treat symptoms of inguinal hernia and "uterine prolapse," by returning the organs to their original place.
ST-29.clinicalNotes: Gui Lai (ST-29) is an important point of the Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, in the lower abdomen. The Wei (Stomach) is the reservoir of food and the source of the essence of nutrients after birth. The Chong Mai originates at Qi Chong (ST-30) and ascends together with the Kidney Meridian, Shao Yin of the Foot. The Chong Mai is the Sea of Xue (Blood), belongs to the Yang Ming system, and has a close relationship with reproductive disorders; for this reason it is commonly used to treat disorders of the genitourinary and reproductive systems.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-30.category: Meeting Point of the Stomach channel with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
ST-30.locationClassical: In the groin, 5 cun below the umbilicus, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline (level of CV-2 and the upper border of the pubic symphysis).
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 2 cun lateral to Qu Gu (CV-2), which lies in the depression on the upper aspect of the pubis.
ST-30.anatomy: Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle. Ilioinguinal nerve. The femoral artery and vein lie slightly lateral to this point.
ST-30.safetyWarning: Avoid the femoral artery. Empty the bladder.
actions: Regulates Qi in the Lower Jiao
ST-30.etymology: Qi (气), meridian Qi; Chong (冲), to surge. The point lies on the path of Qi (near the femoral artery). It corresponds to the origin of the Chong Mai, and on palpation the pulsation of Qi (the femoral artery) can be felt.
ST-30.clinicalNotes: Qi Chong (ST-30) is the meeting point of the Stomach Meridian with the Penetrating Vessel (Chong Mai) and a point of the Sea of Water and Grain, as described in Su Wen chapter 33 ("the Sea of Water and Grain has Qi Chong above and Zu San Li below"). Its central clinical function is to regulate Qi in the Lower Jiao, regulate the Chong Mai, and subdue running-piglet ascending Qi (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 179–181). It is indicated for menstrual irregularity, dysmenorrhea, anovulatory infertility, inguinal hernia, genital pain, and the sudden ascending sensation from the lower abdomen to the chest. Common combinations: Qi Chong (ST-30) + San Yin Jiao (SP-6) + Guan Yuan (CV-4) for Chong/Ren Deficiency patterns with irregular menstruation; with Gui Lai (ST-29) and Zhong Ji (CV-3) for pelvic pain and infertility; and as an adjunct in opening the Chong Mai alongside Gong Sun (SP-4), per Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015. The point is underused in modern practice for two anatomical reasons: the femoral artery lies immediately lateral to it and a distended bladder can be punctured — empty the bladder and palpate the femoral pulse before needling, keeping perpendicular insertion at 0.5–1.0 cun. See also Gui Lai (ST-29) for related gynecological and lower-abdominal complaints.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-31.locationClassical: On the anterior aspect of the thigh, directly below the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), in the depression lateral to the sartorius muscle when the thigh is flexed.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point below the anterior superior iliac spine, at the level of the inferior border of the pubis.
ST-31.anatomy: Rectus femoris and tensor fasciae latae muscles. Innervated by the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and the femoral nerve.
tcmIndications: motor impairment of the lower limb
ST-31.etymology: Bi (髀), thigh; Guan (关), joint. The point lies at the coxofemoral joint.
ST-31.clinicalNotes: The indications follow the location of the point and the course of the meridian.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-32.locationClassical: On the anterior aspect of the thigh, on the line connecting the ASIS to the lateral border of the patella, 6 cun above the upper border of the patella.
howToFind: With the patient seated and the knee flexed, the examiner faces the patient. Locate the midpoint of the upper border of the patella. There the examiner places the midpoint of the first transverse crease of the palm, fingers directed cranially. Locate the point Fu Tu (ST-32) at the level of the tip of the middle finger.
ST-32.anatomy: Rectus femoris and vastus lateralis muscles. Innervated by the anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve.
tcmIndications: Cold and pain in the lower limb
westernIndications: myofascial pain in the anterior thigh
ST-32.etymology: Fu (付), crouching; Tu (兔), rabbit. The prominence of the muscle where the point is located resembles a crouching rabbit.
ST-32.clinicalNotes: This point is used principally to treat disorders of the lower limbs. It tonifies the Shen (Kidney) and the legs, regulating the flow of Qi and Xue.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-33.locationClassical: On the anterior aspect of the thigh, 3 cun above the superolateral border of the patella, in a depression between the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis muscles.
howToFind: Seated, with the knee flexed, locate the point 3 cun above the superolateral border of the patella.
ST-33.anatomy: Tendon of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis. Innervated by the femoral nerve.
tcmIndications: pain and motor impairment of the leg and knee
ST-33.etymology: Yin (阴), genital region; Shi (市), garment that covers the genital area. The point lies at the inferior border of this ancient undergarment.
ST-33.clinicalNotes: Yin Shi (ST-33) is a local point of the Stomach Meridian on the anterior thigh, with clinical action centered on expelling Wind-Damp and warming the channels (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 183). Its classical indications, recorded in the Jia Yi Jing, include numbness and weakness of the lower limb, pain and motor restriction of the knee, and "cold hernia" — patterns of cold lower-abdominal pain radiating to the genitals that respond well to moxibustion over the point. In contemporary practice it is used mainly as a local point for patellofemoral pain syndrome, quadriceps weakness, and iliotibial band friction syndrome, typically in combination with Liang Qiu (ST-34) and He Ding (Extra) for anterior knee pain, or with Fu Tu (ST-32) for global quadriceps weakness (Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, Foreign Languages Press, Beijing). It is less used than its neighbors Fu Tu (ST-32), higher on the thigh and traditionally preferred for quadriceps weakness, and Liang Qiu (ST-34), the Xi-Cleft point of the meridian and the primary option for acute knee and stomach disorders — which is why most texts refer the reader to those two points. Perpendicular insertion of 1.0–1.5 cun, with no specific vascular caution; the patella is the standard bony landmark for palpation.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-34.locationClassical: On the anterior aspect of the thigh, 2 cun above the superolateral border of the patella.
howToFind: Seated, with the knee flexed, locate the point 2 cun above the superolateral border of the patella.
ST-34.anatomy: Tendon of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis. Innervated by the femoral nerve. Descending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery.
actions: Activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: motor impairment of the lower limb
ST-34.etymology: Liang (梁), ridge; Qiu (丘), mound. The prominent muscle above the knee where the point lies resembles the ridge of a mound.
ST-34.clinicalNotes:
1. This point is used to treat disorders along the course of the meridian, hence its indication for diseases of the lower limbs and for mastitis.

2. The Tendinomuscular Meridian of the Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, passes through the intercostal region and enters the Shen (Kidney). For this reason this point combined with Yin Shi (ST-33) treats low back pain.

3. Liang Qiu (ST-34) is a Xi (Cleft) point. It is used principally to treat sudden pain. In clinical practice, it is commonly used to treat epigastric pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-35.locationClassical: At the knee, in the cavity formed when the knee is flexed, immediately below the patella and lateral to the patellar ligament. (Also known as the lateral Xiyan point.)
howToFind: Seated, with the knee flexed, locate the point in the depression lateral to the patellar tendon, between the patella and the tibia.
ST-35.anatomy: Patellar ligament, lateral meniscus, knee joint capsule. Innervated by articular branches of the femoral and common fibular nerves.
ST-35.needling: Oblique insertion directed slightly medially and superiorly (behind the patellar ligament) 1.0–1.5 cun.
ST-35.safetyWarning: Strict aseptic technique must be observed, as the needle penetrates the joint space.
tcmIndications: swelling and stiffness of the knee
ST-35.etymology: Du (犊), calf; Bi (鼻), nose. The depressions below the patella are likened to a calf's nostrils. The point lies in the lateral foramen.
ST-35.clinicalNotes: Du Bi (ST-35) is frequently used to treat pain in the knee joint.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-36.locationClassical: On the anterior surface of the leg, 3 cun below ST-35, one finger-breadth (middle finger) lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia
howToFind: With the patient seated and the knee flexed, locate the point 3 cun directly below the lateral foramen of the knee, 1 cun lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia.
With the patient seated and the knee flexed, locate the point 1 cun below the inferior margin of the tibial tuberosity and 1 cun lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia.

With the patient seated and the knee flexed, have the patient place their own palm over the patella so that the index finger touches the anterior crest of the tibia. Zu San Li (ST-36) lies at the level of the tip of the middle finger.
ST-36.anatomy: Tibialis anterior muscle. Innervated by the deep fibular nerve. The anterior tibial artery and vein lie deep to this point
ST-36.safetyWarning: Avoid the anterior tibial artery when needling deeply
actions: harmonizes and strengthens the Spleen and Stomach
tcmIndications: pain and weakness of the knee and leg
ST-36.etymology: Zu (足), lower limb; San (三), three; Li (里), a unit of distance (equivalent to approximately 500 meters today). The point is located 3 cun below the knee.
ST-36.clinicalNotes:
1. Zu San Li (ST-36) is an important point for treating disorders of the lower extremities, particularly flaccidity. The Nei Jing states: "The Meridians of the Lung and Large Intestine are used to treat diseases located above the waist; the Meridians of the Stomach and Spleen-Pancreas can be used to treat diseases below the waist." The Yang Ming Meridian — sea of the five Zang and six Fu — nourishes the tendons and muscles and is used to treat Wei Syndrome (flaccidity). The tendons and muscles govern osteoarticular movement. The Chong Mai is the sea of the Meridians and connects with the Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, in the urogenital region. The Yang Ming of the Foot, together with the Dai Mai, connects with the Du Mai through the collaterals. Deficiency of the Yang Ming of the Foot therefore produces flaccidity of the lower limbs.

2. Zu San Li (ST-36) is the Inferior He point of the Yang Ming of the Foot meridian. The six Inferior He points treat the six Fu. For disorders of Pi (spleen) and Wei (stomach), ST-36 is therefore a primary point. It is indicated for epigastric pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, as well as disorders of the respiratory, digestive, circulatory, and reproductive systems, and for asthenia due to Deficiency Syndrome.

3. Pi (spleen) governs transportation and transformation. Deficiency of Pi (spleen) and Wei (stomach) can generate dampness and phlegm and give rise to neuropsychiatric disorders. Zu San Li (ST-36) is indicated for treating these conditions.

combinations.indication: Digestive disorders, fatigue, immune support, gynecological conditions
Nausea, vomiting, digestive disorders
Fever, skin disorders, immune regulation

ST-37.locationClassical: On the anterior surface of the leg, 6 cun below ST-35, one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia.
howToFind: Seated, with the knee flexed, locate the point 6 cun directly below Du Bi (ST-35), 1 cun lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia.
ST-37.anatomy: Tibialis anterior muscle. Extensor digitorum longus muscle. Innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
ST-37.etymology: Shang (上), upper; Ju (巨), great; Xu (虚), void. Between the tibia and the fibula, a great space is formed.
ST-37.clinicalNotes:
1. Inferior He point of the Da Chang (Large Intestine). It is commonly combined with Zu San Li (ST-36) to treat disorders of the Chang (Intestine).

2. The Stomach Collateral Meridian runs along the hypochondrium, ascends to the spine, and spreads over the chest. Symptoms of belching or fullness in the chest and hypochondrium caused by adverse ascent of Stomach Qi can therefore be treated with Shang Ju Xu (ST-37).

combinations.indication: Diarrhea, dysentery, intestinal disorders

ST-38.locationClassical: On the anterior surface of the leg, 8 cun below ST-35, one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia (midpoint between ST-35 and ST-41).
howToFind: Seated, with the knee flexed, locate the point 5 cun below Zu San Li (ST-36), at the midpoint of the line connecting Wai Xi Yan (EX-LE-5) and the tip of the lateral malleolus.
ST-38.anatomy: Tibialis anterior muscle, extensor digitorum longus muscle. Innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: pain and tenderness of the knee and leg
westernIndications: Adhesive capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) — highly effective when stimulated actively while the patient mobilizes the shoulder. Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome)
ST-38.etymology: Tiao (条), strip; Kou (口), mouth. The point lies in the depression between the fibula and the tibia, like the opening of a mouth.
ST-38.clinicalNotes: Currently, this point is used to treat pain in the shoulders and arms or pain with paresthesia of the lower extremity. The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, does not ascend to the shoulders, but the Large Intestine Meridian, Yang Ming of the Hand, does. Tiao Kou (ST-38) is indicated for shoulder pain according to the principle of treatment using points of the coupled meridians. In clinical practice, transfixion from Tiao Kou (ST-38) toward Cheng Shan (BL-57) is indicated for periarthritis of the shoulder.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-39.locationClassical: On the anterior surface of the leg, 9 cun below ST-35, one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia.
howToFind: Seated, with the knee flexed, locate the point 6 cun directly below Zu San Li (ST-36).
ST-39.anatomy: Tibialis anterior muscle, extensor digitorum longus muscle. Innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: low back pain radiating to the testicles
ST-39.etymology: Xia (下), lower; Ju (巨), great; Xu (虚), void. A large space is formed between the tibia and the fibula. The point lies at the lower part of this space.
ST-39.clinicalNotes:
1. Inferior He point of the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine). It is used to treat digestive disorders, diarrhea, and dysentery.

2. Zu San Li (ST-36) is the Inferior He point of the Stomach, Shang Ju Xu (ST-37) is the Inferior He point of the Large Intestine, and Xia Ju Xu (ST-39) is the Inferior He point of the Small Intestine; for this reason the three points are always combined to treat digestive disorders.

3. See Zu San Li (ST-36) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-40.locationClassical: On the anterolateral surface of the leg, 8 cun above the lateral malleolus, two finger-breadths lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia (lateral to ST-38).
howToFind: Seated, with the knee flexed, locate the point 8 cun above the lateral malleolus, at the same level as Tiao Kou (ST-38),
5 cun lateral to the anterior crest of the tibia.
ST-40.anatomy: Extensor digitorum longus and fibularis brevis muscles. Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve.
actions: Transforms Phlegm and Dampness (the principal point for all types of Phlegm)
clears Phlegm from the Lung and Heart
ST-40.etymology: Feng (丰), abundant; Long (隆), bulge. The point lies where the muscular mass is abundant.
ST-40.clinicalNotes:
1. The Pi (Spleen) governs the transport and transformation of nutrients. Feng Long (ST-40) belongs to the Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, which is coupled with the Spleen Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot. Deficiency of Pi (Spleen) can promote water retention, leading to phlegm accumulation. Accumulation of phlegm and dampness in the Fei (Lung) can produce cough with expectoration. Many disorders — precordial pain, pain in the chest and hypochondrium, mental illness, dementia, epilepsy, insomnia, and amnesia — can be caused by stagnation of phlegm and dampness within the Xin (Heart). Headache and vertigo can be caused by retention of phlegm and dampness in the upper meridians and collaterals. Flaccidity and arthralgia can be caused by retention of phlegm and dampness in the lower meridians and collaterals. This point is widely used to treat phlegm and all of the disorders mentioned above.

2. The collaterals of the Stomach Meridian ascend to the head, connect with the Qi of other meridians, and descend to the throat. The Divergent Meridian of the Stomach ascends to the Xin (Heart). For this reason Feng Long (ST-40) treats disorders of the head, sense organs, and circulatory system.

3. This point may be used to treat constipation.

4. Periarthritis of the shoulder can be treated by transfixing Feng Long (ST-40) toward Cheng Shan (BL-57). See Tiao Kou (ST-38) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-41.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the ankle, at the level of the prominence of the lateral malleolus, in the depression between the tendons of the extensor hallucis longus and the extensor digitorum longus.
howToFind: Supine or seated, locate the point on the transverse crease of the ankle joint, between the tendons of the extensor hallucis longus and the extensor digitorum longus muscles, at the level of the lateral malleolus.
ST-41.anatomy: Ankle joint capsule, cruciate crural ligament. Innervated by the superficial and deep fibular nerves. Branches of the anterior tibial artery.
ST-41.safetyWarning: Avoid the anterior tibial artery and vein.
actions: Clears Heat from the channel and the Stomach fu
activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: Pain and swelling of the ankle
redness of the face and eyes
ST-41.etymology: Jie (解), space in the joint; Xi (溪), stream, depression. Xi refers to a small depression between the tendons, like a brook. The point lies in the anterior depression of the ankle joint.
ST-41.clinicalNotes:
1. The indications follow the location of the point and the course of the meridian. This point is used frequently to treat symptoms of the lower extremities, especially flaccidity of the feet.

2. This point eliminates Stomach Fire and removes phlegm. It is commonly used to treat disorders of the head and sense organs and mental disorders caused by stagnation of phlegm-fire.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-42.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, in the depression formed by the junction of the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones with the cuneiform bones, 1.5 cun distal to ST-41, where the dorsalis pedis artery pulsates.
howToFind: Supine or seated, locate the point on the dorsum of the foot, 3 cun from Xian Gu (ST-43), where the pulse of the dorsalis pedis artery is palpable.
ST-42.anatomy: Extensor digitorum brevis muscle. Innervated by the deep fibular nerve. Dorsalis pedis artery.
ST-42.safetyWarning: Avoid puncturing the dorsalis pedis artery.
tcmIndications: swelling of the dorsum of the foot
westernIndications: evaluation of peripheral vascular disease (pulse palpation)
ST-42.etymology: Chong (冲), surging; Yang (阳), the Yang of Yin-Yang. The point lies where the dorsalis pedis artery is most prominent.
ST-42.clinicalNotes: Chong Yang (ST-42) is the Yuan-Source point of the Stomach Meridian, as classified in Ling Shu chapter 1. By Yuan-point theory it is the classical choice for treating chronic Stomach Deficiency patterns and a key point in Yuan-Luo pairings, needled together with Gong Sun (SP-4), the Luo point of the paired meridian, in the host-guest combination for chronic Stomach–Spleen disorders (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 196–197; Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). Its main functions are to clear Stomach Heat, harmonize the Stomach, and calm the Shen, with indications for chronic gastric pain, functional dyspepsia, facial palsy, and upper-jaw toothache — the latter following the meridian trajectory across the face. Useful combinations: Chong Yang (ST-42) + Zu San Li (ST-36) for chronic Stomach tonification; with Jia Che (ST-6) and He Gu (LI-4) for Bell palsy and upper toothache. It is clearly underused: despite being the Yuan-Source point, it is eclipsed by Zu San Li (ST-36), the He-Sea Earth point, which has dominated Stomach tonification in modern practice. Critical caution: the dorsalis pedis artery pulsates directly beneath the point — palpate the pulse, deflect the insertion, and limit needling to 0.3–0.5 cun perpendicular, avoiding arterial puncture. See also Jie Xi (ST-41) for related ankle complaints.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-43.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, between the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones, in a depression proximal to the metatarsophalangeal joints.
howToFind: Supine or seated, locate the point in the depression anterior to the junction of the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones.
ST-43.anatomy: Second dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: swelling and pain on the dorsum of the foot
ST-43.etymology: Xian (陷), depression; Gu (谷), valley. Gu denotes a depression on the body surface. The point lies in the depression between the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones.
ST-43.clinicalNotes:
Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach) have an interior-exterior relationship, and Pi (Spleen) nourishes the muscles.

See Jie Xi (ST-41) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-44.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, between the 2nd and 3rd toes, 0.5 cun proximal to the margin of the interdigital web.
howToFind: Supine or seated, locate the point at the junction between the 2nd and 3rd metatarsal bones.
ST-44.anatomy: Dorsal interosseous muscle, lumbricals. Innervated by the proper plantar digital nerve and the dorsal digital nerve.
ST-44.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion in a proximal direction 0.3–0.5 cun.
actions: Clears Heat from the Stomach channel
ST-44.etymology: Nei (内), inner; Ting (庭), courtyard. This point lies near Li Dui (ST-45).
ST-44.clinicalNotes:
1. The indications follow the location of the point and the course of the meridian. The point is indicated to treat the digestive system.

2. The Stomach Meridian, Yang Ming of the Foot, and the Large Intestine Meridian, Yang Ming of the Hand, traverse the head and the face. Collaterals of the Stomach Meridian connect with the vertex, meet with the Qi of the meridians, and descend to the throat. For this reason this point, together with the auxiliary point He Gu (LI-4), is commonly used to treat disorders of the head and face.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

ST-45.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the 2nd toe, 0.1 cun from the lateral (fibular) corner of the nail.
howToFind: Supine or seated, locate the point at the intersection of the line along the lateral aspect with the basal line of the lateral nail angle of the 2nd toe.
ST-45.anatomy: Nail bed. Innervated by the dorsal digital nerve from the deep fibular nerve.
ST-45.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion in a proximal direction 0.1–0.2 cun, or prick to bleed.
ST-45.etymology: Li (厉), top; Dui (兑), point. This point lies on the distal phalanx of the 2nd toe, like a gate of the Stomach Meridian.
ST-45.clinicalNotes:
1. As a Jing (Well) point, it has the function of resuscitating, restoring consciousness, lowering fever, and relieving convulsions. Thus this point is frequently used to treat neuropsychiatric disorders, such as clonic convulsions caused by fever.

2. This point is used to treat disorders of the head and face, based on the theory of distal-proximal point combination.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-1.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the distal phalanx of the great toe, at the junction of lines drawn along the medial border and the base of the nail, approximately 0.1 cun from the corner of the nail.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or supine, locate the point on the great toe, at the intersection of the lines passing along the medial margin and the base of the nail.
SP-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, dorsal digital nerve and vein of the medial side of the great toe, crural fascia, dorsal digital branches of the superficial fibular nerve, dorsal digital artery, and the distal phalanx of the great toe.
SP-1.needling: Perpendicular or proximally directed oblique insertion 0.1–0.2 cun, or prick to bleed with a needle, lancet, or three-edged needle.
actions: calms the Heart and the spirit
calms the shen (Heart and spirit) and revives consciousness.
tcmIndications: blood in the stool or urine
children easily frightened by strangers or falling ill because of strangers
SP-1.etymology: Yin (隐), hidden; Bai (白), white. The point lies on the great toe, at the transition between light and dark skin, as if hidden.
SP-1.clinicalNotes:
Yin Bai (SP-1) is indicated to restore consciousness and to treat lower-limb paralysis as a sequela of stroke.

The point belongs to the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot. Pi (Spleen), in addition to its role in the formation of Xue (Blood), governs Xue (Blood) by keeping it within the vessels and preventing hemorrhage. It can therefore be used in the treatment of hematemesis, hematochezia, epistaxis, hematuria, metrorrhagia, and metrostaxis. Direct moxibustion can produce positive results in metrorrhagia and metrostaxis (dysfunctional).

Pi (Spleen) is responsible for digestion and the transport of fluids. For this reason, the point may be used to treat disorders of the digestive system, such as abdominal distension and diarrhea.

Jing (Well) points have the therapeutic property of restoring consciousness and are indicated to awaken the mind. Yin Bai (SP-1) may therefore be used in the treatment of fainting and other psychiatric disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-2.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the great toe, along the border between the reddish and white skin, in the depression distal and inferior to the first metatarsophalangeal joint (in front of the joint at the base).
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or supine, locate the point on the medial aspect of the great toe, in the depression distal and anteroinferior to the first metatarsophalangeal joint, at the transition between light and dark skin.
SP-2.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, dorsal digital nerve and vein of the medial side of the great toe, crural fascia, dorsal digital branches of the superficial fibular nerve, dorsal digital artery, and proximal phalanx of the great toe.
SP-2.needling: 0.2–0.5 cun perpendicular or oblique (inferior insertion), just below the inferior border of the bone.
SP-2.safetyWarning: No standard precaution. Caution: needling this point may be painful.
actions: harmonizes the Middle and Lower Jiao and clears Heat.
tcmIndications: sensation of heaviness in the body
Sudden swelling of the four limbs
heaviness of the body with bone pain
agitation when hungry and dizziness when sated
disorders of the great toe and sensation of heat in the soles of the feet.
westernIndications: Gout (specifically of the first metatarsophalangeal joint)
SP-2.etymology: Da (大), great; Du (都), capital. The point lies on the great toe, at the transition between light and dark skin.
SP-2.clinicalNotes: Da Du (SP-2) is used principally to strengthen Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach), eliminate Heat, and relieve pain. It can therefore be used to treat disorders of the digestive system such as abdominal distension and epigastric pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-3.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the foot/great toe, in the depression behind/proximal to the metatarsophalangeal joint (head of the first metatarsal), along the border between the reddish and white skin (lateral aspect of the foot and sole).
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or supine, locate the point on the medial aspect of the foot, in the depression proximal and posteroinferior to the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
SP-3.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, dorsal digital nerve and vein of the medial side of the great toe, crural fascia, digital branches of the medial plantar nerve and artery, medial crural cutaneous branches of the saphenous nerve, dorsal digital branches of the superficial fibular nerve, medial head of the flexor hallucis brevis and abductor hallucis, and the first metatarsal.
SP-3.needling: 0.5–1 cun perpendicular or oblique from the medial to the lateral aspect (or 3 to 6 mm perpendicular).
SP-3.safetyWarning: No standard precaution. Caution: needling this point tends to be painful.
actions: eliminates Dampness and Damp-Heat and regulates Qi locally.
tcmIndications: sensation of fullness and tension in the chest and epigastric region
westernIndications: pain in the bunion (support for hallux valgus)
SP-3.etymology: Tai (太), great; Bai (白), white. Tai Bai means Golden Star, which in English corresponds to the Morning Star (planet Venus).
SP-3.clinicalNotes:
Tai Bai (SP-3) is the Yuan (Source) point of the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian. It is therefore generally used in the treatment of disorders of the digestive system.

The point may be used to treat cardiovascular disorders, since the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot, has a connection with the heart.

The Spleen-Pancreas Meridian and its tendinomuscular meridian distribute along the medial aspect of the leg. Pi (Spleen) has the function of removing phlegm and nourishing Xue (Blood) and the tendons. The point may therefore be used to treat low back pain, arthralgia with sensation of heaviness in the body, and Wei Syndrome (flaccidity).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-4.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the foot, 1 cun behind the joint at the base of the great toe, in the depression distal and inferior to the base of the first metatarsal, on the border between the reddish and white skin.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or supine, locate the point in the region anteroinferior to the base of the first metatarsal bone, 1 cun posterior to Tai Bai (SP-3).
SP-4.anatomy: Abductor hallucis muscle. Innervated by the saphenous nerve and the medial plantar nerve.
actions: Strengthens the Spleen and harmonizes the middle jiao
benefits the Heart and the chest
regulates Qi and resolves Dampness and regulates the Penetrating Vessel and menstruation.
tcmIndications: distension or upper and lower abdominal pain from Qi stagnation
blood stasis or obstruction by dampness
westernIndications: pain in the medial arch of the foot
indigestion with loose stools and diarrhea.
SP-4.etymology: Gong (公), nobleman; Sun (孙), grandson. The site where the branching of the collateral begins.
SP-4.clinicalNotes:
Gong Sun (SP-4) is the Luo (Connecting) point of the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot. It connects with the Wei (Stomach). Thus this point regulates the functions of the Wei (Stomach) and Pi (Spleen) and is indicated in the treatment of various diseases and symptoms of these organs.

Pi (Spleen) controls the circulation of Xue (Blood) within the vessels. It can therefore be used to treat gynecologic disorders, such as menstrual irregularity and leukorrhea.

It is responsible for the transport of fluids. Thus Gong Sun (SP-4) can treat edema, jaundice, and somnolence resulting from accumulated phlegm in the body, secondary to deficiency of Pi (Spleen) in transporting fluids.

The Qi of the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot, ascends to the center of the Xin (Heart). Gong Sun (SP-4) tonifies Pi (Spleen), nourishes Xue (Blood), calms the mind, and removes dampness and phlegm. For this reason it may be indicated in the treatment of psychiatric disorders.

Gong Sun (SP-4) is a Confluent point. It connects with the Chong Mai. When used together with Nei Guan (PC-6), the action can be enhanced for the disorders mentioned above.

combinations.indication: Chest and heart disorders, stomach pain, gynecological conditions

SP-5.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the ankle, in the depression inferior and slightly anterior to the medial malleolus, at the junction of straight lines drawn along the anterior and inferior borders of the medial malleolus (midway between the medial malleolus and the navicular tuberosity).
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or supine, locate the point at the intersection of the lines passing along the anterior and inferior margins of the medial malleolus.
SP-5.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, medial dorsal cutaneous nerve from the superficial fibular nerve, branches of the great saphenous vein, crural fascia, medial crural cutaneous branches of the saphenous nerve, inferior extensor retinaculum, between the tendons of the tibialis anterior and the extensor hallucis longus, medial anterior malleolar artery, branches of the deep fibular nerve, and the talus.
SP-5.needling: 0.3–0.6 cun perpendicular, oblique, or transverse (subcutaneous) deep to the tendons toward ST-41.
actions: Strengthens the Spleen and resolves Dampness
moves Qi locally and calms the spirit (shen).
tcmIndications: pain in the foot and ankle
stiffness and pain at the root of the tongue
pain and contraction of the tendons
pain on the medial aspect of the thigh
SP-5.etymology: Shang (商), one of the five notes of the ancient five-tone musical scale, represented by Metal; Qiu (丘), mound. The point lies below the medial malleolus, in a place that resembles a mound, and belongs to the Metal element.
SP-5.clinicalNotes: Shang Qiu (SP-5) is the Jing-River and Metal point of the Spleen Meridian (Foot Tai Yin), classified in Ling Shu chapter 1. As Metal on an Earth meridian it is the classical sedation (child) point of the Spleen, used to drain Heat and Damp-Heat from the meridian in excess patterns; as a Jing-River it is indicated for joint pain along the meridian trajectory and cough with chills (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 197–198; Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). Its central modern clinical indications are medial ankle sprain, posterior tibial tendinopathy, pain and tension in pes planus, and Damp-natured painful obstruction. The Jia Yi Jing adds stiffness and pain at the root of the tongue and excessive thinking, tied to the Foot Tai Yin’s connection with the tongue base. Common combinations: Shang Qiu (SP-5) + Jie Xi (ST-41) + Kun Lun (BL-60) for sprain and diffuse ankle pain; with San Yin Jiao (SP-6) and Tai Bai (SP-3) to drain Damp from the lower limb; and with Lian Quan (CV-23) for altered tongue motility and post-stroke dysphagia (Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, Foreign Languages Press, Beijing). It is underused next to San Yin Jiao (SP-6), the crossing point of the three foot Yin meridians, which has dominated lower-abdominal Yin tonification in modern practice. Perpendicular insertion of 0.3–0.5 cun; the direct bony landmark is the medial malleolus. Frequently paired with Da Du (SP-2), Tai Bai (SP-3), and Gong Sun (SP-4) for related complaints; see details under those points.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-6.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the leg, 3 cun above the most prominent point of the medial malleolus, in a depression near the posterior border of the medial crest of the tibia.
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point on the posterior margin of the tibia, 3 cun above the apex of the medial malleolus.
SP-6.anatomy: Flexor digitorum longus, soleus, and tibialis posterior muscles. Innervated by the saphenous nerve and the tibial nerve. The posterior tibial artery and vein run deep.
SP-6.needling: Perpendicular or proximally directed oblique insertion, 1 to 2 cun.
SP-6.safetyWarning: CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY (strongly induces labor). Caution: contraindicated in pregnancy (especially in the early and late stages of gestation).
actions: harmonizes the Liver and tonifies the Kidneys
tcmIndications: painful urinary dysfunction and turbid urine.
westernIndications: Principal point for gynecologic disorders (dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, pelvic inflammatory disease)
chronic pelvic pain syndrome. Crucial intersection for trigger points of the soleus and flexor digitorum longus (medial tibial stress syndrome, shin splints)
cutaneous disorders (eczema, urticaria) and gastrointestinal disorders.
SP-6.etymology: San Yin (三阴), three Yin meridians; Jiao (交), crossing. This is the intersection point of the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot, the Liver Meridian, Jue Yin of the Foot, and the Kidney Meridian, Shao Yin of the Foot.
SP-6.clinicalNotes:
1. San Yin Jiao (SP-6), in addition to belonging to the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, is the meeting point of the three Yin Meridians of the Foot (Spleen-Pancreas, Tai Yin of the Foot; Liver, Jue Yin of the Foot; and Kidney, Shao Yin of the Foot), which cross with the Ren Mai at Guan Yuan (CV-4). The point can therefore treat the disorders or symptoms related to dysfunctions of Pi (Spleen), Gan (Liver), and Shen (Kidney) and of the Ren Mai itself.

2. Dysfunction of Pi (Spleen) in transport and the inability of Gan (Liver) to drain are the most frequent causes of disorders of Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach). This point tonifies Pi (Spleen) and improves the drainage of Gan (Liver). It can therefore be indicated to treat diseases and symptoms of the digestive system.

3. Pi (Spleen) is responsible for fluid metabolism, Gan (Liver) for drainage, and Shen (Kidney) for the waterways. Diseases related to difficulty in eliminating these fluids are generally related to dysfunction of these three Zang. For this reason, this point is important to treat enuresis, strangury, and other disorders of the genitourinary system.

4. Pi (Spleen) is responsible for acquired Jing (essence) and the production of Xue (Blood), while Shen (Kidney) is responsible for innate Jing (essence) and is related to reproduction. Gan (Liver) stores Xue (Blood) and is responsible for drainage. Dysfunctions of these three Zang are related to physiopathologic disorders of male and female reproduction. The point is therefore indicated in the treatment of all diseases of the reproductive system.

5. The Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot, runs along the throat bilaterally, reaches the root of the tongue, and distributes along its inferior surface. The Kidney Meridian, Shao Yin of the Foot, passes around the root of the tongue, and the Liver Meridian, Jue Yin of the Foot, circulates behind the throat, passing along the posterior aspect of the larynx. Thus San Yin Jiao (SP-6) may be used to treat oropharyngeal pain, dysphasia as a sequela of stroke, and chronic pharyngitis.

combinations.indication: Digestive disorders, fatigue, immune support, gynecological conditions
Kidney and Spleen deficiency, menstrual disorders, insomnia
Gynecological disorders, menstrual irregularities, Liver Qi stagnation

SP-7.category: Point of the Spleen primary channel.
SP-7.locationClassical: 6 cun proximal to the most prominent point of the medial malleolus, on the posterior border of the medial crest of the tibia (3 cun above SP-6).
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point 3 cun directly above San Yin Jiao (SP-6), on the posterior margin of the tibia.
SP-7.anatomy: Soleus and flexor digitorum longus muscles. Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
actions: Strengthens the Spleen and resolves Dampness
opens the channel and promotes urination.
tcmIndications: coldness and numbness in the knee and leg
Paralysis and numbness in the knees and legs
edema and pain in the legs and ankles
abdominal pain and normal intake without growth of muscle or flesh.
SP-7.etymology: Lou (漏), leak; Gu (谷), valley. The point lies in the depression posterior to the medial border of the tibia, like a valley. It has a diuretic function.
SP-7.clinicalNotes: See the points Da Du (SP-2), Tai Bai (SP-3), and Yin Ling Quan (SP-9) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-8.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the calf, 5 cun below the knee (or 3 cun below Yinlingquan SP-9), in the depression along the posterior border of the tibia.
howToFind: Seated or supine, locate the point on the posterior margin of the tibia, 3 cun directly below Yin Ling Quan (SP-9).
SP-8.anatomy: Soleus muscle. Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
actions: harmonizes the Spleen and resolves Dampness
tcmIndications: edema and leukorrhea (especially when accompanied by menstrual disorders).
westernIndications: pain from uterine fibroids. Direct access to trigger points of the medial soleus with referred pain to the heel and calf
SP-8.etymology: Di (地), earth; Ji (机), pivot. The body is divided into three parts. From the feet to the umbilicus is the Earth part. The point Di Ji (SP-8) lies strategically at the center of the Earth part, important for the movement of the knee.
SP-8.clinicalNotes: Needling this point can have an excellent effect in the treatment of dysmenorrhea and digestive system disorders. See Da Du (SP-2) and Tai Bai (SP-3) for further detail.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-9.locationClassical: In the depression distal to the medial condyle of the tibia, at the transition from the medial condyle to the body of the tibia, in front of the belly of the gastrocnemius muscle (at the same level as GB-34).
howToFind: Seated with the knees flexed, or supine, locate the point in the posteroinferior depression of the medial condyle of the tibia, at the level of the inferior margin of the tibial tuberosity.
SP-9.anatomy: Medial head of the gastrocnemius, insertion of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles (pes anserinus). Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
actions: Regulates the Spleen and resolves Dampness (the principal point for systemic dampness)
transforms Dampness and benefits the lower jiao.
tcmIndications: Principal point for eliminating accumulations of water and dampness (especially in the lower part of the body). Abdominal distension
cold and pain in the abdomen
low back pain and pain in the knee.
westernIndications: osteoarthritis of the medial compartment of the knee
gonalgia and arthritis of the knees.
SP-9.etymology: Yin (阴), medial aspect; Ling (陵), mound; Quan (泉), spring, fountain. The interior is Yin. The point lies in the depression at the inferior margin of the medial condyle of the tibia, like a spring at the base of a mound.
SP-9.clinicalNotes:
Yin Ling Quan (SP-9) strengthens Pi (Spleen). Consequently, it promotes the formation of Qi and stimulates diuresis, removing pathogenic dampness. It can therefore be indicated to treat edema, dysuria, and other symptoms caused by deficiency of Pi (Spleen).

Compared with San Yin Jiao (SP-6), which is indicated principally to treat psychiatric disorders and disorders of the genitourinary system, Yin Ling Quan (SP-9) is more often used in the treatment of abdominal distension, diarrhea, jaundice, and edema.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-10.category: Important point for regulating the Blood
SP-10.locationClassical: With the knee flexed, 2 cun proximal to the medial cranial pole (upper border) of the patella, over the vastus medialis muscle, in a depression that is often clearly palpable.
howToFind: Seated with the knees flexed, locate the point 2 cun above the superomedial border of the patella, exactly at the center of the prominence of the vastus medialis muscle.
Seated with the knees flexed, the physician places the center of the right palm on the patient's left patella; the point lies at the tip of the thumb.
SP-10.anatomy: Vastus medialis muscle. Innervated by anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve.
actions: Regulates Blood and removes Blood Stasis, cools Blood and stops bleeding.
tcmIndications: Disharmony of Blood and skin diseases.
westernIndications: urticaria. Essential in orthopedics for patellofemoral pain syndrome and myofascial trigger points of the vastus medialis
SP-10.etymology: Xue (血), blood; Hai (海), sea. The point is indicated in hematologic disorders.
SP-10.clinicalNotes: Gynecologic disorders are caused mainly by dysfunction of the Chong Mai and Ren Mai and by the imbalance between Qi and Xue (Blood). Dermatitis usually results from accumulation of Damp-Heat in the Xue (Blood). Xue Hai (SP-10) regulates abnormalities of Xue (Blood) and menstruation, eliminates Wind (formed by stagnation of Qi or Heat), and removes dampness. It is therefore an important point, commonly indicated to treat gynecopathies and dermatoses.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-11.category: Point of the Spleen primary channel.
SP-11.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the thigh, 6 cun proximal to SP-10, on a line connecting SP-10 to SP-12 (on the lateral border of the sartorius muscle).
howToFind: Seated with the knees flexed and both legs slightly abducted, locate the point on the medial aspect of the sartorius muscle, 6 cun above Xue Hai (SP-10).
SP-11.anatomy: Sartorius muscle. The femoral artery and vein lie deep and slightly lateral. Innervated by the femoral nerve.
SP-11.safetyWarning: Avoid the femoral artery. Caution: femoral artery and vein.
actions: Regulates the Lower Jiao and urination
tcmIndications: pain and swelling in the groin
westernIndications: trigger points in the sartorius muscle
SP-11.etymology: Ji (箕), winnower (dustpan); Men (门), gate. Seated with the knees apart, like a winnower, the point lies on the medial aspect of the thigh and receives this name precisely because of the position the patient assumes for its localization.
SP-11.clinicalNotes: Ji Men (SP-11) strengthens Pi (Spleen), removes dampness, regulates Xue (Blood), and promotes diuresis. It may be effective in dermatoses and genitourinary disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-12.category: Meeting Point of the Spleen and Liver channels with the Yin Linking (Yin Wei) vessel
SP-12.locationClassical: In the inguinal region, 3.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of the upper border of the pubic symphysis (CV-2), lateral to the femoral artery.
howToFind: 1. Palpate the anatomical landmarks for SP-12 along the Spleen meridian.
2. Feel for the characteristic depression or inter-muscular groove at the specified Cun measurement.
3. Verify patient sensation (De Qi — soreness, numbness, distention, or heaviness upon palpation).
SP-12.anatomy: Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle. Innervated by the femoral nerve.
SP-12.safetyWarning: Strictly avoid the femoral artery and vein. Caution: medially directed insertion can puncture the femoral artery; laterally directed insertion can injure the femoral nerve.
actions: Regulates Qi and Blood in the Lower Jiao
SP-12.etymology: Chong (冲), pulse; Men (门), gate. At this point the pulsation of the femoral artery can be palpated. Here, the Qi of the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot, reaches the abdomen, as if passing through a gate.
SP-12.clinicalNotes:
The arterial pulse can be felt at Chong Men (SP-12), where the Qi of the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot, ascends into the abdomen. Thus Chong Men (SP-12) is indicated in the treatment of disorders of Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach). For example, abdominal distension and morning sickness in pregnancy can be treated by digital pressure at this point.

Pi (Spleen) governs the transport of fluids and controls the circulation of Xue (Blood). For this reason Chong Men (SP-12) may be used to treat gynecologic disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-13.category: Meeting Point of the Spleen and Liver channels with the Yin Linking (Yin Wei) vessel
SP-13.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 0.7 cun above and 0.5 cun lateral to SP-12, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: 1. Palpate the anatomical landmarks for SP-13 along the Spleen meridian.
2. Feel for the characteristic depression or inter-muscular groove at the specified Cun measurement.
3. Verify patient sensation (De Qi — soreness, numbness, distention, or heaviness upon palpation).
SP-13.anatomy: External and internal oblique muscles. Innervated by the ilioinguinal nerve.
SP-13.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can penetrate the peritoneal cavity. Caution: peritoneum.
tcmIndications: pain in the lateral costal region
sudden turbidity disorder and pain in the thigh.
SP-13.etymology: Fu (府), the six Fu of Zang Fu; She (舍), abode. The point lies in the abdominal cavity, the abode of the six Fu.
SP-13.clinicalNotes: Local effect to regulate intestinal Qi.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-14.category: Point of the Spleen primary channel.
SP-14.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 1.3 cun below Daheng SP-15, and 4 cun lateral to the abdominal midline.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline,
3 cun directly below Da Heng (SP-15) or 3 cun directly above Fu She (SP-13).
SP-14.anatomy: External and internal oblique muscles, rectus abdominis. Innervated by the 11th intercostal nerve.
SP-14.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can penetrate the peritoneal cavity. Caution: in lean patients, deep needling can penetrate the peritoneal cavity.
actions: warms the middle (lower jiao) and disperses
regulates the Lower Jiao and descends counterflow Qi and regulates Qi and relieves pain.
tcmIndications: agitated Heart and cold diarrhea and dysenteric disorder.
SP-14.etymology: Fu (腹), abdomen; Jie (结), union, knot. This point is indicated in stagnation of Qi in the abdomen.
SP-14.clinicalNotes: Owing to its location, this point is used principally to treat intestinal disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-15.category: Meeting Point of the Spleen channel with the Yin Linking (Yin Wei) vessel
SP-15.locationClassical: On the abdomen, in the depression at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, 4 cun lateral to the center of the umbilicus.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Shen Que (CV-8).
SP-15.anatomy: External and internal oblique muscles, transversus abdominis. Innervated by the 10th intercostal nerve.
SP-15.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can penetrate the peritoneal cavity. Caution: in lean patients, deep needling can penetrate the peritoneal cavity; deep needling at this point can penetrate a substantially enlarged spleen or liver.
actions: Moves Qi and regulates the intestines.
tcmIndications: cold and pain in the lower abdomen
sensation of heat in the hypogastrium with sighing
inability to lift and move the four limbs and profuse sweating.
westernIndications: Provides access to trigger points of the abdominal obliques.
SP-15.etymology: Da (大), great; Heng (横), horizontal. This point lies on the abdomen, at the level of the umbilicus.
SP-15.clinicalNotes: Da Heng (SP-15) may be indicated to treat disorders of the digestive system such as diarrhea, chronic constipation, abdominal pain, and dyspepsia. It may also be used to treat the common cold, cramps in the four limbs, and sweating accompanied by digestive system disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-16.category: Meeting Point of the Spleen channel with the Yin Linking (Yin Wei) vessel
SP-16.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 3 cun above the center of the umbilicus, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline, on the mammillary line (lateral border of the rectus abdominis).
howToFind: 1. Palpate the anatomical landmarks for SP-16 along the Spleen meridian.
2. Feel for the characteristic depression or inter-muscular groove at the specified Cun measurement.
3. Verify patient sensation (De Qi — soreness, numbness, distention, or heaviness upon palpation).
SP-16.anatomy: External oblique, rectus abdominis. Innervated by the 8th intercostal nerve.
SP-16.needling: Perpendicular 0.5–1 cun, or perpendicular insertion 0.5 to 1 cun.
SP-16.safetyWarning: Deep insertion can penetrate the peritoneal cavity. Caution: peritoneum, pregnancy. Depending on the shape of the chest, the point may lie over the costal cartilage (needle subcutaneously or choose an alternative). Deep needling can penetrate an enlarged spleen.
actions: drains Dampness and regulates the intestines.
tcmIndications: stools with pus and blood and constipation.
SP-16.etymology: Fu (腹), abdomen; Ai (哀), intestinal sound. This point treats abdominal disorders.
SP-16.clinicalNotes: According to its location, this point may be indicated to treat disorders of the stomach and large intestine.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-17.category: Point of the Spleen primary channel.
SP-17.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the chest, in the fifth intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the chest midline.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point in the fifth intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
SP-17.anatomy: Serratus anterior muscle and external intercostal muscles. Innervated by the 5th intercostal nerve.
SP-17.needling: 0.5–0.8 cun obliquely or transversely (subcutaneously), parallel to the intercostal space.
SP-17.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a high risk of pneumothorax. Caution: pneumothorax.
actions: harmonizes the Stomach and eliminates stagnation and drains Dampness.
tcmIndications: Fullness in the chest and hypochondrium
pus and blood with defecation and urination
pain in the lateral costal region and distension and pain of the abdomen and diaphragm with belching
vomiting, and undigested food in the stool (food stagnation).
SP-17.etymology: Shi (食), food; Dou (窦), cavity. The point promotes the absorption of nutrients from food.
SP-17.clinicalNotes:
This point lies near the stomach and the lung. It may therefore be used to treat disorders of Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach), such as abdominal distension and borborygmus, in addition to dyspnea.

The right-side Shi Dou (SP-17) may be used to treat disorders of the Gan (Liver) and Dan (Gallbladder), such as distension and pain in the hypochondrium.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-18.category: Point of the Spleen primary channel.
SP-18.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the chest, in the fourth intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point in the fourth intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline, 2 cun lateral to Ru Zhong (ST-17).
SP-18.anatomy: Pectoralis major and serratus anterior muscles. Innervated by the 4th intercostal nerve.
SP-18.needling: 0.5–0.8 cun obliquely or transversely (subcutaneously), parallel to the intercostal space.
SP-18.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a high risk of pneumothorax. Caution: pneumothorax.
actions: descends Qi and benefits the breasts.
tcmIndications: Fullness and pain in the chest
SP-18.etymology: Tian (天), heaven, upper, divine; Xi (溪), stream. Tian Xi refers to lactation.
SP-18.clinicalNotes: Owing to its location, this point is used principally to treat pulmonary and breast disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-19.category: Point of the Spleen primary channel.
SP-19.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the chest, in the third intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point in the third intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
SP-19.anatomy: Pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles. Innervated by the 3rd intercostal nerve.
SP-19.needling: 0.5–0.8 cun obliquely or transversely (subcutaneously), parallel to the intercostal space.
SP-19.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a high risk of pneumothorax. Caution: pneumothorax.
actions: Disperses and descends Lung Qi and opens the chest.
tcmIndications: pain in the chest and back
westernIndications: Trigger points in the pectoralis minor muscle (often simulating cardiac pain)
SP-19.etymology: Xiong (胸), chest; Xiang (乡), dwelling. The point lies on the lateral aspect of the chest.
SP-19.clinicalNotes: Owing to its location, this point is used principally to treat pulmonary and breast disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-20.category: Point of the Spleen primary channel.
SP-20.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the chest, in the second intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Supine, locate the point in the second intercostal space, 6 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
SP-20.anatomy: Pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles. Innervated by the 2nd intercostal nerve.
SP-20.needling: 0.5–0.8 cun obliquely or transversely (subcutaneously), parallel to the intercostal space.
SP-20.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a high risk of pneumothorax. Caution: pneumothorax.
actions: opens the chest and regulates Lung Qi.
westernIndications: pain of the upper chest wall
tags: pain of the upper chest wall
SP-20.etymology: Zhou (周), distribution; Rong (荣), nutrition. This point harmonizes the nutritive Qi and nourishes the entire body.
SP-20.clinicalNotes: Owing to its location, this point is used to treat pulmonary disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SP-21.category: Great Luo-Connecting point of the Spleen
SP-21.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the chest on the midaxillary line, 6 cun below the axilla, in the seventh (or sixth) intercostal space.
howToFind: In lateral decubitus, with the arm raised over the head, locate the point in the sixth intercostal space, on the midaxillary line, 6 cun below the axillary fossa.
SP-21.anatomy: Serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles. Innervated by the long thoracic nerve and the 6th intercostal nerve.
SP-21.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space, 0.5 to 1 cun.
SP-21.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a high risk of pneumothorax. Caution: perpendicular insertion, especially in lean patients, carries substantial risk of inducing pneumothorax.
actions: Regulates Qi and Blood of all the channels
governs and contains all the luo-connecting vessels of the body
opens the chest and benefits the lateral costal region and firms the tendons and joints.
tcmIndications: Pain in the chest and hypochondrium
generalized pain and weakness throughout the body
fatigue and flaccidity of the four limbs and the hundred joints
pain in the chest and lateral costal region with breathing and distension and fullness of the lateral costal region.
westernIndications: Fibromyalgia (principal point for systemic muscular pain)
SP-21.etymology: Da (大), great, encompassing; Bao (包), content. The point belongs to the Great Luo (connection) of the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Tai Yin of the Foot, and governs the Yin and Yang Meridians. Pi (Spleen) nourishes the five Zang Fu and the four limbs.
SP-21.clinicalNotes:
Located near the lung, Da Bao (SP-21) may be indicated to treat disorders of the respiratory system.

It is one of the Luo (Connecting) points, the Great Luo of Pi (Spleen). It connects all the meridians and their collaterals. It is responsible for limb activity, both for muscular trophism and for tone. By applying moxibustion to Da Bao (SP-21), Bi Syndromes (arthralgia) and Wei Syndromes (flaccidity) can be treated, as well as intercostal pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-1.category: Point of the Heart primary channel.
HT-1.locationClassical: In the center of the axilla, in the depression on the medial side of the axillary artery. Locate with the arm abducted.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed and the arm abducted, locate the point in the center of the axillary fossa.
HT-1.anatomy: Inferior border of the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi muscles, coracobrachialis muscle. Innervated by the ulnar nerve, median nerve, and medial cutaneous nerve of the arm. The axillary artery and vein lie directly adjacent.
HT-1.safetyWarning: Avoid puncturing the axillary artery. Medial insertion toward the chest wall carries a high risk of pneumothorax.
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and arm
HT-1.etymology: Ji (極), extreme; Quan (泉), spring. The point lies in the deepest part of the axillary depression.
HT-1.clinicalNotes: This point promotes the flow of Qi in the meridians, and is therefore used to treat upper-limb paralysis.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-2.category: Point of the Heart primary channel.
HT-2.locationClassical: 3 cun proximal to the cubital crease, on the medial border of the biceps brachii muscle. With the elbow flexed, measure 3 cun from the ulnar end of the cubital crease (HT-3) toward the axilla. Located in a groove on the medial border of the biceps brachii.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed, select Shao Hai (HT-3). Locate Qing Ling (HT-2) 3 cun above Shao Hai (HT-3).
HT-2.anatomy: Medial border of the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles. Innervated by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the ulnar nerve. The basilic vein runs superficially.
HT-2.safetyWarning: Avoid the basilic vein and the brachial artery.
actions: Activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and arm
HT-2.etymology: Qing (青), pain treatment; Ling (靈), efficacy. An analgesic point, indicated for the treatment of upper-limb pain and headache.
HT-2.clinicalNotes: The point promotes the flow of Qi in the meridians, and is therefore indicated in the treatment of headache, pain and difficulty moving the shoulder and upper limbs, and axillary pain and edema.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-3.locationClassical: With the elbow flexed, at the medial end of the transverse cubital crease, midway between the medial epicondyle of the humerus and the tendon of the biceps brachii muscle.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed and the arm abducted, support the head with the hand. Locate the point on the medial border, at the end of the cubital crease.
HT-3.anatomy: Origins of the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis muscles. Innervated by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm. The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle.
tcmIndications: mental agitation due to Heart Fire
westernIndications: cubital tunnel syndrome — ulnar nerve entrapment
HT-3.etymology: Shao (少), of Shao Yin; Hai (海), He point. Shao refers to the Hand Shao Yin Meridian and Hai to the He (Sea) point of the Heart Meridian. The Qi of the meridian circulates at this point like water flowing into the sea.
HT-3.clinicalNotes: The Xin (Heart) is the organ that controls blood circulation, houses the mind, corresponds to Fire among the Five Elements, and manifests in the tongue. Deficiency of Xin (Heart) Qi and stagnation in the Collateral may cause precordial pain and palpitations. Deficiency of Xin (Heart) Qi may cause bipolar disorder, epilepsy, and memory deficit. The tongue is the organ of voice. The divergent meridian of the Hand Shao Yin "connects with the root of the tongue." When Xin (Heart) Qi is deficient, dysphonia may occur. Headache and toothache may be caused by the rising of Xin (Heart) Fire. Boils result from stagnation of the Xin (Heart). This point has the function of calming the mind, promoting the flow of Qi in the meridians, and eliminating Heat. Hence its importance in the disorders mentioned.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-4.locationClassical: On the palmar aspect of the forearm, on the radial border of the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle, 1.5 cun proximal to the wrist crease (HT-7).
howToFind: With the palm facing up, locate the point on the radial side of the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle,
5 cun above the wrist crease.
HT-4.anatomy: Flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles. Innervated by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the ulnar nerve. The ulnar artery lies adjacent.
HT-4.needling: 0.3–1 cun perpendicularly or obliquely in a proximal or distal direction.
HT-4.safetyWarning: Avoid the ulnar artery and the ulnar nerve.
tcmIndications: spasmodic pain in the elbow and arm
HT-4.etymology: Ling (靈), function of Xin (Heart); Dao (道), pathway. The Xin (Heart) governs the mind. The point lies in the depression on the radial side of the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle, like a pathway for the mind.
HT-4.clinicalNotes: See Shao Hai (HT-3) and Shen Men (HT-7) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-5.locationClassical: On the palmar aspect of the forearm, on the radial border of the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle, 1 cun proximal to the wrist crease (HT-7).
howToFind: With the palm facing up, locate the point on the radial side of the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle, 1 cun proximal to the wrist crease.
HT-5.anatomy: Radial to the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle. The collateral diverges and connects to the base of the root of the tongue and to the eye connector.
HT-5.needling: Perpendicularly 0.3–0.5 cun, or obliquely 0.5–1 cun in a proximal or distal direction. Alternatively, up to 0.5 cun perpendicularly.
HT-5.safetyWarning: Avoid the ulnar artery and the ulnar nerve. Caution: needling may be painful.
actions: regulates and strengthens Heart Qi and the heart rhythm
benefits the Bladder via the Taiyang channel
opens the channel and the Luo vessels
tcmIndications: pain in the wrist and elbow
HT-5.etymology: Tong (通), conducted to; Li (里), meeting of Qi. Communication point with the Small Intestine Meridian.
HT-5.clinicalNotes: Luo (Connecting) point of the Heart Meridian. The tongue is traditionally related to the Xin (Heart), the organ of lingual function. For this reason, this point is used to treat dysphonia, alterations of motility, edema, and tenderness of the tongue. See Shao Hai (HT-3) and Shen Men (HT-7) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-6.locationClassical: 0.5 cun proximal to the palmar wrist crease, radial to the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris. On the posterior ulnar aspect of the palm, 5 fen above the transverse wrist crease and 5 fen below HT-5.
howToFind: With the palm facing up, locate the point on the border of the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle,
5 cun proximal to the wrist crease.
HT-6.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, median antebrachial vein, medial cutaneous branch of the forearm, palmar branch of the ulnar nerve, ulnar artery and nerve, radial border of the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris, and the ulna.
HT-6.safetyWarning: Avoid the ulnar artery and the ulnar nerve.
tcmIndications: hectic fever with night sweats (including profuse night sweating)
deficiency due to wasting or fatigue
westernIndications: pulmonary tuberculosis — adjuvant for night sweats
HT-6.etymology: Yin (陰), Yin of Yin Yang; Xi (郄), cleft.
HT-6.clinicalNotes: Compared with the other points of the Heart Meridian, Yin Xi (HT-6) is more efficient in the treatment of consumptive fever resulting from Yin deficiency and night sweats, by nourishing Xin (Heart) Yin and eliminating deficiency-type heat. See Shen Men (HT-7) and Shao Hai (HT-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-7.locationClassical: On the wrist flexion crease (palmar aspect of the wrist joint, distal wrist crease), radial to the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle. On the posterior ulnar aspect of the palm, in the depression at the end of the pointed bone (head of the ulna).
howToFind: With the palm facing up, locate the point on the radial border of the pisiform bone, on the wrist crease.
HT-7.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, median antebrachial vein, medial cutaneous branch of the forearm, palmar branch of the ulnar nerve, radial to the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle.
