HT-7.safetyWarning: Avoid the ulnar artery and the ulnar nerve. The flexion crease for locating this point lies between the radius and ulna on one side and the carpal bones on the other. Use the wrist flexion crease proximal to the pisiform bone.
actions: regulates and tonifies the Heart (Qi, Blood, Yin, and Yang)
absolute principal point for all emotional and mental disorders
westernIndications: local treatment for ulnar wrist pain
studied in clinical trials for improvement of cardiovagal modulation in mild depression and anxiety disorders
HT-7.etymology: Shen (神), mind; Men (門), gate. The Xin (Heart) houses the mind. This point is the gate to the mind.
HT-7.clinicalNotes: Yuan (Source) point, the most-used point of the Heart Meridian, Hand Shao Yin. 1. The Xin (Heart) controls blood circulation. Symptoms of cardiac diseases such as precordial pain, palpitations, irritability, and unconsciousness may be caused by deficiency of Xin (Heart) Qi. In these cases, Shen Men (HT-7) is considered the first choice in treatment. 2. The Xin (Heart) governs the mind. To regulate mental activity, in addition to treating the cause of the disease by activating Xin (Heart) Qi, it is necessary to treat the psychiatric disorders. 3. The Xin (Heart) controls blood circulation. All hemorrhagic disorders result from dysfunction of the Xin (Heart). For this reason, Shen Men (HT-7) is the first choice for treating gynecopathies, hematuria, and hematemesis.

combinations.indication: Insomnia, anxiety, palpitations, calming the mind

HT-8.locationClassical: Behind the base of the little finger, in the depression between the fourth and fifth metacarpal bones. When the fist is clenched, the point lies under the tip of the little finger on the palm.
howToFind: With the palm facing up and bending the fingers, the fingertips touch the palmar crease. Locate the point in the depression between the tips of the little and ring fingers, where the tip of the little finger touches when the hand is closed.
HT-8.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, palmar aponeurosis, median antebrachial vein, palmar branch of the median nerve, and part of the superficial branch.
HT-8.safetyWarning: Highly sensitive and painful point. Caution: needling of this point can be very painful.
actions: Clears Heat from the Heart and Small Intestine
tcmIndications: contracture of the hand with inability to extend
heat in the palms of the hands
deficiency of Heart and Gallbladder Qi
westernIndications: trigger finger affecting the 4th or 5th finger
HT-8.etymology: Shao (少), young; Fu (府), place. The point belongs to the Hand Shao Yin Meridian, where the Qi of the meridian is introduced.
HT-8.clinicalNotes: This point is indicated for eliminating Heat from the Xin (Heart). Clinically, Shao Fu (HT-8) may be used as the first option for symptoms related to Excess Heat Syndrome of the Xin (Heart), such as: pain and dryness of the throat, epistaxis, dryness of the nose, vulvar pruritus, and menstrual irregularity.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

HT-9.locationClassical: On the inner (dorsal) aspect of the little finger, at the junction of the lines drawn along the radial border of the nail and the base of the nail, approximately 0.1 cun from the corner of the nail.
howToFind: With the hand slightly closed, the palm facing up, and the little finger extended, locate the point at the intersection of the lines between the radial border of the nail of the little finger and its base.
HT-9.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, branches of the proper palmar digital nerve and distal branches of the proper palmar digital arteries, dorsal digital veins, distal phalanx.
HT-9.needling: 0.2–0.3 cun perpendicularly or obliquely in a proximal direction. For acute conditions (pain, inflammation), prick to bleed with a needle, lancet, or three-edged needle.
HT-9.safetyWarning: Extremely painful point. Caution: painful point.
actions: benefits the tongue and the eyes
clears Heat at the opposite end of the channel
regulates Qi in the chest and clears Heat in the Heart
tcmIndications: deficiency of Heart and Gallbladder Qi
HT-9.etymology: Shao (少), of Shao Yin; Chong (沖), surge. The point lies on the little finger of the Hand Shao Yin Meridian, where the Qi of the meridian originates and moves upward along the meridian.
HT-9.clinicalNotes: All Jing (Well) points have the function of eliminating heat, calming the mind, and inducing resuscitation. Shao Chong (HT-9) is efficient for mental disorders and disorders of the sense organs. It may be used with other Jing points alternately or in combination.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-1.locationClassical: On the outer (dorsal/ulnar) aspect of the little finger, in the depression 1 fen (approximately 0.1 cun) from the ulnar corner of the nail (at the junction of the lines drawn along the ulnar border and the base of the nail).
howToFind: With the palm facing down, locate the point at the intersection of the lines passing through the lateral border and the base of the nail of the little finger.
SI-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, dorsal digital nerve and vein, dorsal branches of the proper palmar digital branches of the ulnar nerve and proper palmar digital arteries, fifth distal phalanx.
SI-1.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion directed proximally 0.1 to 0.2 cun, or prick to bleed.
actions: Clears Heat and benefits the sensory orifices, promotes lactation and benefits the breasts.
tcmIndications: febrile diseases with agitation and fullness
heat in the mouth with dryness of the throat
contraction of the hand with inability to extend and pain in the elbow and wrist.
SI-1.etymology: Shao (少), little finger, small; Ze (澤), marsh. The point lies on the little finger where Qi and Xue (Blood) of the Meridian originate, like a small marsh.
SI-1.clinicalNotes:
1. The Small Intestine Meridian, Hand Tai Yang, distributes along the ulnar border of the little finger, the posterior region of the arm and shoulder, and the side of the nose, ear, throat, and infraorbital region. Therefore, Shao Ze (SI-1) is commonly used to treat disorders of the limbs, head, face, and sense organs.

2. It promotes lactation and may be used to treat mastalgia caused by milk stagnation, dissolving "masses." Milk production is related to the function of various Zang Fu and depends mainly on the proper functioning of the Small Intestine. This point is useful for treating agalactia.

3. The Small Intestine Meridian, Hand Tai Yang, and the Heart Meridian, Hand Shao Yin, are coupled. By regulating Xin (Heart) Qi and improving the flow of Xue (Blood), the point is used to treat precordial pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-2.locationClassical: On the ulnar border of the little finger, in a depression just distal to the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. Locate with the fist slightly closed, at the junction of the reddened and white skin.
howToFind: Bending the fingers slightly, locate the point at the dorsiventral border of the metacarpophalangeal transverse crease.
SI-2.anatomy: Tendon of the abductor digiti minimi muscle. Innervated by the dorsal digital nerve of the ulnar nerve.
SI-2.needling: Distal oblique insertion 0.2 to 0.3 cun, or perpendicular-oblique insertion toward the palm, 0.5 cun.
actions: ears, and throat, activates the channel and relieves pain.
tcmIndications: edema and pain in the neck
edema of the cheek radiating to the ear
sore throat that prevents swallowing. Superficial visual obstruction
febrile disease with absence of sweating
absence of postpartum lactation. Stiffness and pain in the neck and back
pain and inability to raise the arm
heat in the palms of the hands
heat and pain in the little finger, pruritus and numbness in the fingers.
SI-2.etymology: Qian (前), front; Gu (谷), valley. The depression in front of the fifth metacarpophalangeal joint is like a valley.
SI-2.clinicalNotes: See Shao Ze (SI-1) and Hou Xi (SI-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-3.locationClassical: On the ulnar border of the hand, with the fist slightly closed, proximal and dorsal to a skin fold at the ulnar end of the most distal palmar flexion crease. Located at the body-head transition of the fifth metacarpal.
howToFind: Bending the fingers of the hand slightly, locate the point at the dorsiventral division of the ulnar border at the end of the transverse palmar crease, of the fifth metacarpophalangeal joint.
SI-3.anatomy: Abductor digiti minimi muscle. Innervated by the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve.
SI-3.needling: Deep needling toward Sanjian LI-3 when all four fingers are affected. Exact depth/angle not specifically detailed.
actions: stiffness and contracture along the course of its related channels (occipital, neck, scapula, paravertebral regions), disperses febrile disease.
tcmIndications: pain in the neck and back
stiffness and pain in the neck
pain in the upper thoracic spine and scapula
acute lumbar sprain. Disorders of the finger joints (especially the little and ring fingers)
contracture of the arm, elbow and shoulder.
westernIndications: muscle spasms of the upper back
SI-3.etymology: Hou (后), behind; Xi (溪), stream. In the depression posterior to the fifth metacarpophalangeal joint, like a stream.
SI-3.clinicalNotes:
1. This point communicates with the Du Mai, which governs Yang Qi and the surface of the body. It can be used to eliminate heat in Excess Heat Syndrome, in symptoms of malaria, and in night sweats resulting from Yin deficiency.

2. Hou Xi (SI-3) treats low back pain because the point connects with the Du Mai. The Hand Tai Yang Small Intestine Meridian connects with the Foot Tai Yang Gallbladder Meridian. Needling He Gu (LI-4) directed toward Hou Xi (SI-3) is effective in treating acute low back pain.

3. Used to treat contractures, cramps, and to calm the mind.

4. Removing damp-heat from the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine) can treat jaundice, dysuria, and boils.

5. Confluence point, connecting with the Du Mai. Associated with Shen Mai (BL-62), it can treat ophthalmalgia and disorders of the meridians of the Small Intestine, Du Mai, Bladder, and Yang Qiao Mai, which cause cervical stiffness, torticollis, and pain in the cervical region and shoulder caused by meridian disorders.

combinations.indication: Neck and back pain, headache, epilepsy

SI-4.locationClassical: On the ulnar border of the hand, in the depression between the base of the fifth metacarpal and the triquetral bone.
howToFind: With the palm of the hand facing down, locate the point on the ulnar border of the hand, above Hou Xi (SI-3), in the depression between the base of the fifth metacarpal bone and the hamate bone.
SI-4.anatomy: Origin of the abductor digiti minimi muscle. Innervated by the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve.
actions: Activates the channel and relieves pain
clears Heat and reduces edema, clears Heat-Dampness and treats jaundice.
tcmIndications: febrile diseases with absence of sweating
Contracture of the five fingers with difficulty flexing and extending
weakness and pain in the wrist
contracture of the arm and elbow
stiffness and edema of the neck
coldness and pain in the shoulder and back
pain in the lateral costal region
low back pain radiating to the leg
clonic spasm. Pain and edema of the cheek radiating to the ear
loss of the sense of taste. Jaundice
febrile disease with absence of sweating
wasting and thirst disorder, agitation and fullness.
westernIndications: carpometacarpal osteoarthritis of the thumb (when used with the opposite point)
SI-4.etymology: Wan (腕), wrist; Gu (骨), bone. The point lies between the bones of the wrist.
SI-4.clinicalNotes: See Hou Xi (SI-3) and Shao Ze (SI-1) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-5.locationClassical: On the ulnar border of the wrist, in the depression between the head of the ulna and the triquetral bone (or between the styloid process of the ulna and the triquetral bone).
howToFind: With the palm of the hand facing down, locate the point on the ulnar border of the hand, above Wan Gu (SI-4), in the depression of the triquetral bone.
SI-5.anatomy: Tendon of the extensor carpi ulnaris muscle. Innervated by the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve.
actions: Clears Heart fire and calms the spirit.
tcmIndications: Edema of the neck and submandibular region
contracture and pain in the fingers and hemorrhoids.
westernIndications: Sprain of the ulnar collateral ligament
SI-5.etymology: Yang (阳), the dorsum of the wrist is Yang; Gu (谷), valley. The location of the point is like a valley.
SI-5.clinicalNotes: See Hou Xi (SI-3) and Shao Ze (SI-1) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-6.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the wrist. When the palm is facing the chest, the point lies in the bony cleft on the radial side of the styloid process of the ulna.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed and the palmar surface facing the chest, locate the point on the radial border of the styloid process of the ulna. (Fig.
SI-6.anatomy: Tendon of the extensor carpi ulnaris muscle. Innervated by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve.
SI-6.needling: Oblique insertion directed proximally toward the elbow, 0.5–0.8 cun.
actions: Benefits the eyes (especially ocular disorders due to deficiency).
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and back
shoulder pain as if fractured and pain in the lumbar region and knee.
westernIndications: Acute lumbar sprain (empirical point, tested with the patient standing and moving the spine)
SI-6.etymology: Yang (养), to sustain; Lao (老), the aged. This point is used to treat geriatric disorders such as blurred vision, hearing deficit, low back pain, and shoulder pain.
SI-6.clinicalNotes: The point is used to improve circulation of Xue (Blood), clear the mind, improve vision, relax muscles and tendons, and treat torticollis and low back pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-7.locationClassical: On a line connecting Yanggu SI-5 and Xiaohai SI-8, 5 cun proximal to Yanggu SI-5, in the groove between the anterior border of the ulna and the muscle belly of the flexor carpi ulnaris.
howToFind: With the elbow flexed and the palmar surface facing the chest, locate the point 5 cun above Yang Gu (SI-5), on the medial border of the ulna, on the line connecting Yang Gu (SI-5) and Xiao Hai (SI-8).
SI-7.anatomy: Flexor carpi ulnaris muscle. Innervated by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the ulnar nerve.
SI-7.needling: Perpendicular insertion 0.5 to 1 cun. The point should be needled with the patient supine, with the arm supinated or resting on the chest.
actions: Clears Heat and releases the exterior
activates the channel and relieves pain, benefits the finger joints.
tcmIndications: Febrile disease with pain in the neck and lumbar region
depression and constraint of all seven emotions
inability to grasp firmly and inability to close the fist.
westernIndications: anxiety. Clinically famous for the treatment of viral warts (verrucae)
SI-7.etymology:
Zhi (支), divergence; Zheng (正), Regular Meridian. The Collateral of the Hand Tai Yang Small Intestine Meridian leaves this point for the Hand Shao Yin Heart Meridian.

[Classified] Luo (Connecting) point of the Hand Tai Yang Small Intestine Meridian.
SI-7.clinicalNotes:
1. Luo (Connecting) point of the Hand Tai Yang Small Intestine Meridian, connects to the Hand Shao Yang Heart Meridian, therefore is used to treat psychiatric disorders.

2. Boil is caused by damp heat of the Small Intestine. This point has the function of eliminating fire from the Xin (Heart) and regulating the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine), and may thus be used to treat boils.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-8.locationClassical: At the elbow, in the depression between the olecranon of the ulna and the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Locate with the elbow flexed.
howToFind: With the elbow slightly flexed, locate the point at the olecranon, at the level of the transverse crease of the cubital fossa and of the medial epicondyle (Fig.
22). This point produces the sensation of a shock that radiates to the little finger when the region around it is percussed.
SI-8.anatomy: In the ulnar groove. The ulnar nerve passes directly through this space. Innervated by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
SI-8.needling: Distal or proximal oblique insertion 0.5 to 1 cun; or perpendicular insertion 0.3 to 0.5 cun.
SI-8.safetyWarning: Caution: the ulnar nerve lies directly beneath. Avoid direct puncture of the nerve (which causes a sharp electric sensation down to the little finger). Caution: the ulnar nerve is deep to this point.
actions: Clears Heat and dissipates edema, activates the channel and relieves pain.
tcmIndications: scrofula of the neck or axilla
pain in the scapula and posterolateral aspect of the shoulder
protrusion of the tongue, crazy walking and Heart agitation.
SI-8.etymology: Xiao (小), small; Hai (海), sea. Xiao refers to the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine) Meridian, and this is its He (Sea) point. The arrival of Qi and Xue (Blood) at this point is like river water flowing into the sea.
SI-8.clinicalNotes:
1. The Xiao Chang (Small Intestine) has the function of separating the clear (light) from the turbid (heavy). When there is fire in the Xin, pathogenic mucosity may circulate in the meridians and collaterals, forming boils and scrofula. The point eliminates fire, clears the Xin, and removes mucosity.

2. The Xin (Heart) controls the mind. If phlegm and fire affect the function of the Xin (Heart) or flow along the course of the meridian, disorders of the head, face, and sense organs and psychiatric disorders may arise. It may be used to remove phlegm and eliminate fire from the Xin (Heart).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-9.locationClassical: With the arm adducted, 1 cun superior to the posterior axillary crease, on the inferior border of the deltoid muscle.
howToFind: Seated, with the arm relaxed and the upper limb abducted, locate the point 1 cun immediately superior to the end of the posterior axillary crease.
SI-9.anatomy: Deltoid muscle, teres major and teres minor muscles. Innervated by the axillary nerve and radial nerve. Circumflex scapular artery.
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and arm
Sensation of heat in the shoulder with inability to turn the head and deafness.
westernIndications: myofascial pain of the posterior deltoid
SI-9.etymology: Jian (肩), shoulder; Zhen (貞), true. This is the first point where the Hand Tai Yang Small Intestine Meridian meets the shoulder.
SI-9.clinicalNotes: Generally used to treat diseases of the upper limbs along the course of the meridian or local diseases.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-10.category: Meeting Point of the Small Intestine channel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) and Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessels
SI-10.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the shoulder, in the depression inferior to the spine of the scapula, directly superior to the posterior axillary crease when the arm hangs in the adducted position.
howToFind: Seated, with the shoulder relaxed and the upper limb abducted, locate the point immediately superior to Jian Zhen (SI-9), at the end of the posterior axillary crease, on the inferior border of the spine of the scapula.
SI-10.anatomy: Posterior deltoid, infraspinatus muscle. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve and axillary nerve.
actions: relieves pain, activates the channel and relieves pain.
tcmIndications: Pain and weakness of the shoulder and arm
Pain and edema of the shoulder radiating to the scapula
weakness and pain of the arm and shoulder
SI-10.etymology: Nao (臑), arm; Shu (俞), point. Means that the point lies on the arm.
SI-10.clinicalNotes: This point may be used to drain the meridian and the collaterals, removing stagnation.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-11.locationClassical: On the scapula, in a depression over the infraspinatus muscle, one third of the distance from the midpoint of the spine of the scapula to the inferior angle of the scapula.
howToFind: Seated or in the prone position, the point is located:
At the junction of the upper third with the middle third of the distance between the inferior border of the spine of the scapula and the inferior angle of the scapula.

On the line connecting the inferior border of the spine of the scapula with the inferior angle of the scapula, at the same level as the lower part of the fourth thoracic spinous process, forming a triangle with Jian Zhen (SI-9) and Nao Shu (SI-10).
SI-11.anatomy: Infraspinatus muscle. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve. Circumflex scapular artery.
SI-11.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion 0.5 to 1.5 cun.
SI-11.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the bone; angle carefully.
actions: Activates the channel and relieves pain
moves Qi and opens the chest and the lateral costal region
tcmIndications: pain on the lateral-posterior aspect of the elbow and arm
Heaviness and pain in the shoulder
pain and inability to raise the elbow and arm
edema of the cheek and submandibular region. Fullness in the chest and lateral costal region
pain and edema of the breast
SI-11.etymology: Tian (天), heaven, upper part; Zong (宗), center. Tian Zong represents an important point in the upper part of the body.
SI-11.clinicalNotes:
1. Used principally to treat diseases in the scapular region and in the upper limbs.

2. Tian Zong (SI-11) and other neighboring points may be used to treat mastalgia.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-12.category: Meeting Point of the Small Intestine
SI-12.locationClassical: In the center of the suprascapular fossa, directly above Tianzong SI-11, in a depression formed when the arm is raised.
howToFind: Seated or in the prone position, locate the point 1 cun above the central point of the upper border of the spine of the scapula, that is, in the suprascapular fossa. The point forms a triangle with Nao Shu (SI-10) and Tian Zong (SI-11).
SI-12.anatomy: Trapezius and supraspinatus muscles. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve and accessory nerve. Suprascapular artery.
SI-12.needling: Medial oblique insertion toward the spine 0.5 to 1 cun.
SI-12.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of pneumothorax in lean patients. Caution: deep perpendicular insertion, especially in lean patients, carries substantial risk of inducing pneumothorax.
actions: benefits the shoulder and the scapula
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and the scapula
numbness and pain in the upper limb
Pain in the shoulder with inability to raise the arm.
westernIndications: myofascial pain of the upper trapezius
SI-12.etymology: Bing (秉), to grasp; Feng (风), pathogenic wind. The point treats wind syndromes.
SI-12.clinicalNotes: Generally used to treat diseases of the shoulder and the scapular region.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-13.locationClassical: In the tender depression superior to the medial end of the spine of the scapula, midway between Naoshu SI-10 and the spinous process of T2.
howToFind: Seated, with the upper limb relaxed, locate it at the midpoint of the line connecting Nao Shu (SI-10) and the spinous process of the second thoracic vertebra.
SI-13.anatomy: Trapezius and supraspinatus muscles. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve and accessory nerve.
SI-13.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of pneumothorax. Caution: perpendicular insertion, especially in lean patients, carries substantial risk of inducing pneumothorax.
actions: Benefits the shoulder and the scapula
Activates the channel and relieves pain
expels Wind and Cold and benefits the shoulder and the scapula.
tcmIndications: Pain and stiffness in the scapular region
Pain in the shoulder and scapula with a sensation of cold extending to the elbow
chills and fever accompanied by cervical stiffness and inability to turn the head and generalized painful obstruction.
westernIndications: Muscle tension of the levator scapulae and trapezius
SI-13.etymology: Qu (曲), curved; Yuan (垣), wall. The point lies on the spine of the scapula, which resembles a curved wall.
SI-13.clinicalNotes: See Bing Feng (SI-12) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-14.locationClassical: On the back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the first thoracic vertebra (T1).
howToFind: Seated or in the prone position, locate the point at the intersection of the vertical line of the vertebral margin of the scapula with the horizontal line of Tao Dao (GV-13).
SI-14.anatomy: Trapezius, levator scapulae, and rhomboid minor muscles. Innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve and accessory nerve. Transverse cervical artery.
SI-14.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Do not needle perpendicularly or deeply.
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and back
westernIndications: Trigger points in the rhomboid minor
SI-14.etymology: Jian (肩), shoulder; Wai (外), lateral aspect; Shu (俞), point. The point lies near the shoulder, lateral to the point Jian Zhong Shu (SI-15).
SI-14.clinicalNotes: See Bing Feng (SI-12) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-15.locationClassical: On the back, 2 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the seventh cervical vertebra (C7).
howToFind: Seated or in the prone position, first locate Da Zhui (GV-14). Locate the point Jian Zhong Shu (SI-15) 2 cun lateral to Da Zhui (GV-14), at the end of the transverse process of the first thoracic vertebra.
SI-15.anatomy: Trapezius and levator scapulae muscles. Innervated by the accessory nerve and dorsal scapular nerve. Transverse cervical artery.
SI-15.needling: 0.5–1 cun perpendicularly or obliquely in a medial direction.
SI-15.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Do not needle perpendicularly or deeply (the apex of the lung lies directly beneath). Caution: pneumothorax.
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and back
SI-15.etymology:
Jian (肩), shoulder; Zhong (中), central or medial; Shu (俞), point. The point lies near the midline of the spine.

[location] On the back, below the spinous process of the seventh cervical vertebra, 2 cun lateral to the posterior median line. (Fig. 9.23)
SI-15.clinicalNotes: Located in the region of the lung, it is effective in the treatment of pulmonary disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-16.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the neck, posterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle (SCM), at the level of the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple).
howToFind: Seated, locate the point on the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the level of Lian Quan (CV-23), which is between the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone.
SI-16.anatomy: Posterior border of the SCM, levator scapulae. Innervated by the cervical plexus and accessory nerve.
SI-16.safetyWarning: Avoid the external jugular vein. Deep insertion may perforate the carotid artery or jugular vein.
SI-16.etymology: Tian (天), heaven, upper; Chuang (窗), opening, window. The point lies on the neck and is indicated for otologic disorders. It treats hearing deficit, analogously to "opening a window."
SI-16.clinicalNotes:
1. The point is located beside the throat and is used to treat pain and edema in the throat and dysphonia.

2. With deep needling, it treats paresthesias of the upper limbs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-17.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the neck, posterior to the angle of the mandible, in a depression on the anterior border of the SCM muscle.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point at the same level as the angle of the mandible, on the anterior margin of the end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, on the inferior border of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle.
SI-17.anatomy: Anterior border of the SCM, posterior belly of the digastric muscle. Innervated by the facial nerve, great auricular nerve, and accessory nerve. External carotid artery and external jugular vein nearby.
SI-17.needling: Perpendicular insertion directed toward the root of the tongue, 0.5–1.0 cun.
SI-17.safetyWarning: Avoid the external carotid artery and the external jugular vein.
tcmIndications: sensation of a foreign body in the throat (plum-pit Qi)
Great rebellion of yang Qi ascending to fill the chest causing congestion

dyspnea and wheezing with inability to sit or lie down. Aversion to dust and smoke causing respiratory difficulty as if the throat were blocked. Also used for shoulder pain with inability to raise the arm.
SI-17.etymology: Tian (天), heaven, upper; Rong (容), appearance, face. The point lies on the head and treats tinnitus and hearing deficit.
SI-17.clinicalNotes: Generally used to treat diseases of the throat and the ear.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-18.category: Meeting Point of the Small Intestine and Triple Burner channels
SI-18.locationClassical: On the face, directly below the outer canthus of the eye, in the depression on the inferior border of the zygomatic bone.
howToFind: Seated, with the head erect, locate the point at the intersection of the horizontal line of the inferior margin of the zygomatic bone with the vertical line of the lateral commissure of the eyelid, approximately at the same level as Ying Xiang (LI-20).
SI-18.anatomy: Zygomaticus major muscle. Innervated by branches of the facial nerve and the infraorbital nerve (trigeminal).
SI-18.needling: Transverse insertion connecting to points such as Dicang ST-4, Xiaguan ST-7, Yingxiang LI-20, Jiache ST-6; or perpendicular insertion 0.5 to 0.7 cun.
SI-18.safetyWarning: Avoid facial vessels to prevent hematoma. According to some texts, this point is contraindicated for moxibustion.
tcmIndications: pain and deviation of the mouth
inability to chew and red and yellow eyes.
SI-18.etymology: Quan (顴), zygoma; Liao (髎), foramen. The point lies in the inferior depression of the zygomatic bone.
SI-18.clinicalNotes: In the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia, direct the needle toward the medial commissure of the contralateral eyelid. Insert the needle deeply, producing the sensation of a shock in the teeth and upper lip.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

SI-19.category: Meeting Point of the Small Intestine
SI-19.locationClassical: On the face, anterior to the tragus and posterior to the condyloid process of the mandible. Locate with the mouth open.
howToFind: 1. Palpate the anatomical landmarks for SI-19 along the Small Intestine meridian.
2. Feel for the characteristic depression or inter-muscular groove at the specified Cun measurement.
3. Verify patient sensation (De Qi — soreness, numbness, distention, or heaviness upon palpation).
SI-19.anatomy: Articular capsule of the temporomandibular joint. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve and branches of the facial nerve. Superficial temporal artery and vein.
SI-19.needling: With the patient's mouth slightly open, perpendicular insertion 0.5–1.0 cun.
SI-19.safetyWarning: Avoid the superficial temporal artery and vein. Ensure that the patient does not close the mouth firmly while the needle is inserted.
tcmIndications: fullness of the Heart and abdomen and toothache.
westernIndications: sudden deafness. Direct access to the TMJ capsule and insertions of the lateral pterygoid
SI-19.etymology: Ting (聽), hearing; Gong (宮), important place. Ting Gong refers to the ear. The point lies in front of the ear, indicated for otologic diseases.
SI-19.clinicalNotes:
Crossing point of the Hand and Foot Shao Yang Meridians and the Hand Tai Yang Meridian. The Foot Shao Yang Meridian penetrates posterior to the ear, emerges, and passes to its anterior region. A branch of the Hand Tai Yang Meridian also "penetrates the ear." Hearing deficit is one of the diseases of the Small Intestine Meridian.

Also indicated for hearing deficit caused by otitis media.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-1.locationClassical: 0.1 cun superior and medial to the inner canthus of the eye, in a depression where the temple of a pair of glasses tends to rest.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point
1 cun medial and
1 cun above the medial commissure of the eye, near the medial margin of the orbit.
BL-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, trigeminal nerve (infratrochlear and supratrochlear branches), branches of the facial nerve, supraorbital artery and vein, supratrochlear artery and vein, nasofrontal vein, dorsal nasal artery and vein, and orbicularis oculi muscle.
BL-1.needling: Perpendicular insertion of 0.2–0.3 cun. Alternatively, push the eyeball downward and outward (or laterally) and insert perpendicularly 0.5–1 cun. Do not lift, thrust, or rotate the needle.
BL-1.safetyWarning: HIGH RISK. Lifting, thrusting, or rotation are absolutely prohibited. After withdrawal, press firmly with a sterile cotton ball for 1–2 minutes to prevent severe hematoma ("black eye"). Moxibustion is strictly contraindicated. Caution: angular artery and vein, eyeball, periosteum. Should only be needled by experienced practitioners. Press firmly with cotton for approximately one minute on withdrawal to avoid hematoma. No needle stimulation. Moxibustion contraindicated.
actions: controls the musculature of the lower limbs and the opening and closing of the eyes (via the qiao vessels)
tcmIndications: Redness, swelling, and pain in the eyes
swelling and pain of the eyes
BL-1.etymology: Jing (腈), eye; Ming (明), brightness. The point lies near the eyes and its function is to treat ocular disorders.
BL-1.clinicalNotes:
1. This point lies near the eyes and may therefore be used to treat local disorders.

2. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, passes through the lumbar region, so it can be indicated in the treatment of low back pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-2.locationClassical: On the face, in the depression at the medial end of the eyebrow, directly above the inner canthus of the eye.
howToFind: With the head at rest or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point approximately
1 cun lateral to the medial end of the eyebrow.
BL-2.anatomy: Corrugator supercilii and frontalis muscles. Innervated by the frontal nerve (ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal) and the supratrochlear nerve.
BL-2.needling: 0.3–0.5 cun obliquely from lateral to medial, or transversely (subcutaneous); transverse-oblique insertion inferiorly toward BL-1; or prick to bleed in Heat disorders.
BL-2.safetyWarning: No standard contraindications, but it is a vascular area (prone to hematoma). Caution: branches of the frontal nerve, the facial nerve, and blood vessels. Moxibustion is contraindicated according to most texts.
actions: expels external pathogenic factors such as Wind
clears Heat from the head (especially eyes and nose)
moves Qi in the divergent channel of the Bladder
tcmIndications: redness and itching of the eyes
westernIndications: direct access to trigger points in the corrugator supercilii muscle
BL-2.etymology: Zan (攒), to gather; Zhu (竹), bamboo. The point lies at the medial end of the eyebrow, a location that resembles a lush bamboo grove.
BL-2.clinicalNotes:
1. The point lies in the supraorbital region and is therefore indicated in the treatment of disorders of the face and eyes.

2. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, connects with the brain through its collaterals and may therefore be used to treat neuropsychiatric disorders.

3. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, circulates in the lower limbs, where pain of sciatic origin frequently occurs. Needling this point may relieve leg pain and improve its movement.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-3.locationClassical: 0.5 cun within the anterior hairline, superior to the medial canthus of the eye (directly above BL-1/BL-2).
howToFind: Seated with the head supported or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point at the intersection of the horizontal line passing through Shen Ting (GV-24) and the vertical line passing through Cuan Zhu (BL-2).
BL-3.anatomy: Frontalis muscle. Innervated by the frontal nerve.
BL-3.needling: 0.5–1 cun obliquely in a dorsal direction, or transversely (subcutaneous).
BL-3.safetyWarning: No standard contraindications. Moxibustion is contraindicated according to some classical texts.
BL-3.etymology: Mei (眉), eyebrow; Chong (冲), above. The point lies on the anterior hairline, directly above the eyebrow.
BL-3.clinicalNotes: The point lies on the head. The meridian originates at the medial commissure of the eyelid and its tendinomuscular meridian connects to the nose. Based on the principle that a point treats disorders along the course of its own meridian, this point may be used in the treatment of disorders of the head and face.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-4.locationClassical: On the head, 0.5 cun within the anterior hairline, 1.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (GV-24), approximately one third of the distance between the midline and ST-8.
howToFind: Seated with the head supported, locate the point at the junction of the medial third and the middle third of the arched line connecting Shen Ting (GV-24) and Tou Wei (ST-8).
BL-4.anatomy: Frontalis muscle. Innervated by the frontal nerve.
tcmIndications: agitation and fullness of the Heart
agitation and Heat in the body
BL-4.etymology: Qu (曲), curved, bent; Chai (差), deviation. This meridian changes direction at Mei Chong (BL-3), making a curve at Qu Chai (BL-4).
BL-4.clinicalNotes: See Mei Chong (BL-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-5.locationClassical: 1 cun superior to the anterior hairline and 1.5 cun lateral to the midline (directly above BL-4, at the level of GV-23).
howToFind: Seated with the head supported, first locate Qu Chai (BL-4). Locate Wu Chu (BL-5)
5 cun directly above it.
BL-5.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the supraorbital nerve.
BL-5.safetyWarning: No standard contraindications. Moxibustion is contraindicated according to some texts.
BL-5.etymology: Wu (五), five; Chu (处), place or stop. The point lies 5 fen (each fen equals 0.1 cun) from Qu Chai (BL-4).
BL-5.clinicalNotes: See Mei Chong (BL-3) and Cuan Zhu (BL-2) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-6.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the midline and 2.5 cun superior to the anterior hairline (1.5 cun posterior to BL-5).
howToFind: Seated with the head supported, first locate Qu Chai (BL-4). Locate Cheng Guang (BL-6) 2 cun directly above it.
BL-6.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the supraorbital nerve.
BL-6.safetyWarning: No standard contraindications. Moxibustion only after careful diagnosis.
actions: clears Heat from the head (especially eyes and nose)
BL-6.etymology: Cheng (承), to receive; Guang (光), brightness. The point treats various ocular disorders.
BL-6.clinicalNotes: See Mei Chong (BL-3) and Tian Zhu (BL-10) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-7.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the midline and 4 cun superior to the anterior hairline, or 1 cun anterior to GV-20 (1.5 cun posterior to BL-6).
howToFind: Seated with the head supported, locate Qu Chai (BL-4). Locate Tong Tian (BL-7)
5 cun directly above it.
Seated with the head supported, locate Bai Hui (GV-20). Locate Tong Tian (BL-7)
5 cun lateral and 1 cun anterior to it.
BL-7.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the supraorbital nerve.
tcmIndications: sensation of heaviness in the head
loss of the sense of smell
an important point for treating nasal disorders
westernIndications: Primary distal point for all nasal disorders
BL-7.etymology: Tong (通), to reach; Tian (天), heaven. The point lies on the head and connects with the Du Mai.
BL-7.clinicalNotes: The Tendinomuscular Meridian of the Bladder Meridian connects above with the face and skull and below with the zygomatic arch, so this and other points of the meridian may be indicated to treat facial paralysis.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-8.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the midline and 5.5 cun superior to the anterior hairline, or 0.5 cun posterior to GV-20 (1.5 cun posterior to BL-7).
howToFind: Seated with the head supported, first locate Bai Hui (GV-20). Luo Que (BL-8) lies
5 cun lateral and
5 cun posterior to it.
BL-8.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve.
BL-8.etymology: Luo (络), connection; Que (却), return. The Bladder Connecting (Luo) Meridian, after connecting with the brain, returns to the surface of the body from this point.
BL-8.clinicalNotes:
The Bladder Connecting Meridian originates at the vertex of the head and ends at the upper part of the ear. The Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, is the coupled meridian of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, and its somatic opening is in the ears. This point may therefore be used to treat ear disorders.

Since it is at this point that the Bladder Connecting Meridian connects with the brain, this point, as well as many others on this meridian, are indicated to treat neuropsychiatric disorders such as bipolar disorder and epilepsy. For other conditions, use Cuan Zhu (BL-2) and Mei Chong (BL-3).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-9.locationClassical: On the nape, 1.3 cun lateral to the posterior midline, directly at the level of GV-17 (which is located in the depression superior to the external occipital protuberance).
howToFind: Seated with the head erect or with the neck flexed, first locate Nao Hu (GV-17). Locate Yu Zhen (BL-9)
3 cun lateral to it.
BL-9.anatomy: Occipital muscle. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve. Occipital artery.
actions: opens the channel and the Luo vessels
tcmIndications: plays an important role as one of the three gates (san guan) in Qigong practice
BL-9.etymology: Yu (玉), jade; Zhen (枕), pillow. The ancient name of the occipital bone was Yu Zhen Gu (jade pillow bone). The point lies over the occipital bone.
BL-9.clinicalNotes: See Mei Chong (BL-3) and Tian Zhu (BL-10).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-10.locationClassical: 1.3 cun lateral to the posterior midline, above the first palpable spinous process of the cervical spine (C2, the axis), in the trapezius muscle where its belly begins to descend, near the exit of the greater occipital nerve (0.5 cun cranial to the dorsal hairline).
howToFind: Seated with the neck slightly flexed, first locate Ya Men (GV-15). Locate Tian Zhu (BL-10)
3 cun lateral to it, at the lateral margin of the trapezius muscle.
BL-10.anatomy: Trapezius and splenius capitis muscles. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve. Occipital artery and vein.
BL-10.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5–0.8 cun.
BL-10.safetyWarning: Deep or upward perpendicular insertion may enter the foramen magnum. Caution: do not needle in a superior direction.
actions: calms Wind (especially internal Wind) and the Shen
benefits the head and the sensory orifices
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and back
westernIndications: access to trigger points in the splenius capitis and semispinalis capitis muscles
BL-10.etymology: Tian (天), heaven; Zhu (注), pillar. In ancient times, the vertex was considered heaven and the cervical spine, Zhu Gu, the pillar of bone. The point lies lateral to the cervical spine.
BL-10.clinicalNotes:
1. The occipital region is where the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, branches and descends along the back. The Bladder Meridian therefore treats musculoskeletal disorders of the dorsal region, such as occipital headache, neck pain and rigidity, torticollis, dorsalgia, and low back pain. It may also be used to eliminate pathogenic Wind from the body surface and improve the flow of Qi in the meridians and collaterals.

2. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, is considered the protector of the body surface. It is frequently the first meridian to be affected by external factors. This point may be indicated in cases of headache and sore throat in exogenous diseases. Perpendicular needling at a depth of 1 cun for 20 to 30 minutes yields good results in tonsillitis and acute pharyngitis.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-11.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the first thoracic vertebra (T1), at the highest point of the paravertebral musculature.
howToFind: Seated with the neck flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the first thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to Tao Dao (GV-13).
BL-11.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, medial cutaneous branch of the thoracic nerve, branch of the accessory nerve, dorsal scapular nerve, dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries, transverse cervical artery and vein, trapezius, rhomboids, serratus posterior superior, and erector spinae muscles.
BL-11.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5 to 1 cun, or transverse-oblique insertion of 1 to 1.5 cun.
BL-11.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Caution: perpendicular needling carries a substantial risk of causing pneumothorax. When needling in an oblique medial direction, guide the needle tip slightly in a caudal direction.
actions: expels pathogenic factors and secures the exterior
regulates Lung Qi and relieves cough
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and back
rigidity and pain of the nape, spine, and lumbar region
painful bone obstruction (Wind, Cold, Damp, or Heat penetrating deeply into bones and joints)
contracture of the tendons (including with manic behavior)
BL-11.etymology: Da (大), great; Zhu (杼), first thoracic vertebra.
BL-11.clinicalNotes: See Tian Zhu (BL-10) and Luo Que (BL-8) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-12.category: Meeting Point of the Bladder channel with the Governing Vessel (Du Mai)
BL-12.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the second thoracic vertebra (T2), at the highest point of the paravertebral musculature.
howToFind: Seated with the neck flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the second thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-12.anatomy: Trapezius, rhomboid minor, and erector spinae muscles.
BL-12.needling: 0.5–1 cun obliquely toward the spine. Frequently needled transversely (subcutaneously) toward the spine to allow recumbent position during retention.
BL-12.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Caution: pneumothorax.
actions: releases the exterior (main point for Wind-Cold and Wind-Heat)
BL-12.etymology: Feng (风), pathogenic wind; Men (门), gate. The point lies in a location easily invaded by pathogenic wind. This point is considered the gate of pathogenic wind.
BL-12.clinicalNotes:
1. This point is also called Re Fu, meaning "gate to pathogenic wind." It is indicated to treat aversion to cold, fever, headache, cough, and asthma resulting from invasion of exogenous factors, as well as Bi syndrome (arthralgia) and urticaria caused by pathogenic wind.

2. Pathogenic wind is the principal cause of various disorders, among them stroke and epilepsy. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, connects with the brain, the organ responsible for neuropsychiatric functions. The function of this point is to eliminate wind, so it may be used in the treatment of stroke sequelae and epilepsy.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-13.locationClassical: On the upper back, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra (T3).
howToFind: Seated with the neck flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to Shen Zhu (GV-12).
BL-13.anatomy: Trapezius, rhomboid major, and erector spinae muscles.
BL-13.needling: 0.5 cun, perpendicularly or in an oblique medial-caudal direction.
actions: drains Heat from the five zang
BL-13.etymology: Fei (肺), lung; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Fei (Lung) reaches the back.
BL-13.clinicalNotes:
1. This point lies in the area of the lung, where the Qi of the Fei (Lung) converges. It is therefore indicated to treat pulmonary problems caused by internal or external disorders. As the Lung is responsible for the skin, this point is used to treat various dermatological disorders.

2. The Lung Meridian, Hand Tai Yin, originates in the gastric region, in the Middle Jiao, so this point may be indicated to treat disorders of the digestive system, especially those related to pulmonary disorders.

3. Diabetes is classified into three types involving the Upper, Middle, and Lower Jiao. The type involving the Upper Jiao is caused by Yin deficiency of the Fei (Lung), so this point is indicated in its treatment.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-14.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the fourth thoracic vertebra (T4), at the highest point of the paravertebral musculature.
howToFind: Seated with the neck flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the fourth thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-14.anatomy: Trapezius, rhomboid major, and erector spinae muscles.
BL-14.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5–0.8 cun.
actions: unblocks the chest by stimulating Qi circulation
tcmIndications: pain in the chest and diaphragm from Qi accumulation
BL-14.etymology: Jue Yin (厥阴), here referring to the Xin Bao (Pericardium); Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Xin Bao (Pericardium) reaches the back.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-15.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the fifth thoracic vertebra (T5), at the highest point of the paravertebral musculature.
howToFind: Seated with the neck flexed or in prone position, locate the point below the spinous process of the fifth thoracic vertebra (T5),
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, level with Shen Dao (GV-11) (WHO 2008, §BL-15).
BL-15.anatomy: Trapezius, rhomboid major, and erector spinae muscles.
BL-15.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5–0.8 cun.
actions: regulates and tonifies the Heart at the deepest level (tonifies Blood, Yin, Qi, and Yang)
Heart Fire and obstruction by Phlegm
drains Heat from the five zang
BL-15.etymology: Xin (心), Heart; Shu (俞), transport point. The place where the Qi of the Xin (Heart) reaches the back and emerges on the Bladder Meridian, designating the Back-Shu (Bei Shu) point of the Heart (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 282).
BL-15.clinicalNotes: As this point lies in the area of the Xin (Heart) and the Fei (Lung) and near the epigastrium, it may be indicated in the treatment of disorders of the Xin (Heart), the Fei (Lung), the Pi (Spleen), and the Wei (Stomach).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-16.category: Back-shu point of the du mai
BL-16.locationClassical: On the upper back, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the sixth thoracic vertebra (T6).
howToFind: Seated with the neck flexed or in prone position, locate the point below the spinous process of the sixth thoracic vertebra (T6),
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, level with Ling Tai (GV-10) (WHO 2008, §BL-16).
BL-16.anatomy: Trapezius, rhomboid major, and erector spinae muscles.
BL-16.needling: 0.5–1 cun obliquely toward the spine or transversely (subcutaneous).
actions: Regulates Qi in the chest and abdomen
regulates the movement of Qi in the chest and abdomen
BL-16.etymology: Du (督), of the Du Mai (Governing Vessel); Shu (俞), transport point. The place where the Qi of the Du Mai reaches the back and emerges on the Bladder Meridian, designating the Back-Shu (Bei Shu) point of the Governing Vessel (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 300).
BL-16.clinicalNotes: Du Shu (BL-16) is the Back-Shu (Bei Shu) point of the Governing Vessel (Du Mai), where the Qi of the Du Mai reaches the back and emerges on the Bladder Meridian (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 300). Its earliest recorded mention is in the Wai Tai Mi Yao, compiled by Wang Tao in 752 CE; it is therefore one of the later points in the Back-Shu series and, for that reason, less represented in earlier classical texts. Its central clinical function is to regulate Qi in the chest and abdomen — an action that reflects the topographical relationship of the Du Mai to the thoraco-abdominal axis — with indications for cardiogastric pain, abdominal pain, borborygmus, and chest fullness. As the Back-Shu point of a vessel rather than of a Zang-Fu organ, it is used less as an isolated tonification; it enters more often as a complement in combinations that need to reinforce the Du Mai axis. Common combinations: Du Shu (BL-16) + Xin Shu (BL-15) and Jue Yin Shu (BL-14) for anginal cardiac pain from Upper-Jiao Stagnation; with Ge Shu (BL-17) and Gan Shu (BL-18) for chest pain and intercostal neuralgia; with Da Zhui (GV-14) and Ling Tai (GV-10) to reinforce the Du Mai trajectory (Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). Caution: high risk of pneumothorax — restrict to oblique medial insertion toward the spine or subcutaneous transverse insertion, depth 0.5–1.0 cun (WHO 2008, §BL-16).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-17.locationClassical: On the back, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the seventh thoracic vertebra (T7). At the level of the inferior angle of the scapula.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the seventh thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to Zhi Yang (GV-9), at the level of the infrascapular margin.
BL-17.anatomy: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, and erector spinae muscles.
BL-17.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5–0.8 cun.
actions: Invigorates the Blood and disperses stasis
unblocks the chest and the diaphragm
BL-17.etymology: Ge (膈), diaphragm; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Ge (diaphragm) reaches the back.
BL-17.clinicalNotes:
1. As the Influential Point of the Xue (Blood), it is indicated in the treatment of various blood disorders, such as anemia and leukopenia. There is a saying in Traditional Chinese Medicine: "Wind syndrome should be treated through the Xue (Blood), for with the normalization of the Xue (Blood), pathogenic wind will be eliminated." It is a point commonly used to treat urticaria and other skin diseases.

2. This point is located at the diaphragm, between the Xin (Heart) and the Fei (Lung) in the Upper Jiao, and the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach) in the Middle Jiao. It is therefore indicated in the treatment of hiccup and disorders of the Xin (Heart), the Fei (Lung), the Pi (Spleen), and the Wei (Stomach).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-18.locationClassical: On the back, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the ninth thoracic vertebra (T9). (Note: there is no standard back-shu point at T8.)
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the ninth thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to Jin Suo (GV-8).
BL-18.anatomy: Latissimus dorsi and erector spinae muscles.
BL-18.needling: 0.5 cun, perpendicularly or in an oblique medial-caudal direction.
BL-18.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Risk of pneumothorax (inferred from depth notes of associated thoracic points).
actions: benefits the eyes and the tendons
drains Heat from the five zang
tcmIndications: tension in the epigastric and hypochondriac region
BL-18.etymology: Gan (肝), Liver; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Gan (Liver) reaches the back.
BL-18.clinicalNotes:
This is one of the back-shu points, directly related to the Gan (Liver). It is the place to which the Qi of the Gan (Liver) converges. It may be used to treat symptoms of chronic hepatitis and cholecystitis.

The Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, distributes through the hypochondrium, and the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, descends along the lumbar spine. This point may therefore be indicated to treat pain in the hypochondrium and the vertebral column.

The opening of the Gan (Liver) is in the eye, and the Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, ascends toward the vertex. Disorders of the face, head, and sense organs may be treated through this point.

Stroke is generally caused by hyperactivity of Yang and deficiency of Yin, so this point may be used to treat stroke sequelae.

The Gan (Liver) and the Dan (Gallbladder) are directly related to the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach). Stagnation of Gan (Liver) Qi is the principal cause of disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach). This point may therefore be used to calm the Gan (Liver) and regulate the flow of Qi in disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach) caused by imbalance of the Gan (Liver) and the Dan (Gallbladder).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-19.category: Back-Shu Point of the Gall Bladder
BL-19.locationClassical: On the back, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the tenth thoracic vertebra (T10).
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the tenth thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to Zhong Shu (GV-7).
BL-19.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, posterior cutaneous branches of the medial branches of the dorsal rami of the thoracic nerve, dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries, latissimus dorsi and erector spinae muscles.
BL-19.needling: 0.5 cun, perpendicularly or in an oblique medial-caudal direction.
actions: Clears Damp-Heat from the Liver and Gallbladder
tcmIndications: bitter taste in the mouth with dryness
distension and fullness in the Heart and abdomen
distension and pain in the chest and lateral costal region with inability to turn
BL-19.etymology: Dan (胆), Gallbladder; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Dan (gallbladder) reaches the back.
BL-19.clinicalNotes:
The Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, passes along the costal region and the hypochondrium. Disharmony between the Gan (Liver) and the Dan (Gallbladder) frequently causes disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach). This point may therefore be indicated in the treatment of cholecystitis, cholelithiasis, jaundice, hypochondriac pain, and disorders of the digestive system.

The function of this point is to eliminate heat and normalize the function of the Dan (Gallbladder). Ascension of heat from the Dan (Gallbladder) may result in headache and sore throat, which may be treated with this point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-20.locationClassical: On the back, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the eleventh thoracic vertebra (T11).
howToFind: In prone or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the eleventh thoracic vertebra (T11),
5 cun lateral to Ji Zhong (GV-6).
BL-20.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, posterior cutaneous branches of the medial branches of the dorsal rami of the thoracic nerve, dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae, and serratus posterior inferior muscles.
BL-20.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5 to 1 cun, or transverse-oblique insertion of 1 to 1.5 cun.
BL-20.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Caution: perpendicular or oblique needling away from the spine carries a substantial risk of causing pneumothorax.
actions: regulates and harmonizes the Qi of the middle jiao
drains Heat from the five zang
tcmIndications: continuous weakness and emaciation despite increased intake
heaviness in the body with painful joints
loss of use of the limbs
Spleen deficiency with undigested food in the stools
BL-20.etymology: Pi (脾), Spleen; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Pi (Spleen) reaches the back.
BL-20.clinicalNotes:
Back-Shu point of the Pi (Spleen), the place to which the Qi of the Pi (Spleen) converges. The Pi (Spleen) has the function of transporting and transforming nutrients, nourishing the muscles and the four limbs. This point is indicated to treat various disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach).

Dysfunction of the Pi (Spleen) in transformation and transport may cause retention of water in the body, abundant expectoration, and edema. In these cases, this point is used to strengthen the Pi (Spleen).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-21.locationClassical: 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the twelfth thoracic vertebra (T12), at the highest point of the paravertebral musculature.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the twelfth thoracic vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-21.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, posterior cutaneous branches of the medial branches of the dorsal rami of the thoracic nerve, dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae, and serratus posterior inferior muscles.
BL-21.needling: 0.5 cun, perpendicularly or in an oblique medial-caudal direction.
BL-21.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion may puncture the kidney. High risk of pneumothorax.
actions: Regulates the Stomach and descends rebellious Qi
tcmIndications: lack of appetite combined with absence of muscular growth
BL-21.etymology: Wei (胃), Stomach; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Wei (Stomach) reaches the back.
BL-21.clinicalNotes: Back-Shu point of the Wei (Stomach), the place to which the Qi of the Wei (Stomach) converges. For this reason, it is indicated in the treatment of disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-22.category: Back-Shu Point of the Sanjiao (Triple Burner)
BL-22.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the first lumbar vertebra (L1).
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the first lumbar vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, lateral to Xuan Shu (GV-5).
BL-22.anatomy: Thoracolumbar fascia, latissimus dorsi, and erector spinae muscles. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the 10th–12th thoracic nerves and the first lumbar nerve.
BL-22.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5–1.0 cun.
BL-22.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of puncturing the kidney.
actions: Moves and regulates the water passages
tcmIndications: rigidity and pain in the lumbar region
BL-22.etymology: San (三), three; Jiao (焦), cavity, part; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the San Jiao reaches the back.
BL-22.clinicalNotes:
This point lies in the region of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach), in the Middle Jiao, and is therefore indicated in the treatment of disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach).

The San Jiao has the function of controlling the metabolism of fluids and draining the water passages. Edema, dysuria, and jaundice may therefore be treated with this point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-23.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the second lumbar vertebra (L2). At the level of the navel.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point
5 cun lateral to Ming Men (GV-4), which lies opposite the umbilical scar.
BL-23.anatomy: Thoracolumbar fascia, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae, and quadratus lumborum muscles. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the L1 and L2 lumbar nerves.
BL-23.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.5–1.0 cun.
BL-23.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a risk of puncturing the kidney.
actions: Tonifies the Kidneys and strengthens Yang
nourishes the eyes and the ears
westernIndications: Primary point for chronic low back pain
BL-23.etymology: Shen (肾), Kidney; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Shen (Kidney) reaches the back.
BL-23.clinicalNotes:
1. Back-Shu point of the Shen (Kidney), the place to which the Qi of the Shen (Kidney) converges. The Shen (Kidney) commands reproduction and controls the metabolism of water, so this is one of the principal points for treating disorders of the genitourinary system.

2. The Fei (Lung) is responsible for respiration and the Shen (Kidney) controls and promotes inhalation. This point is therefore indicated to treat pulmonary disorders caused by deficiency of the Shen (Kidney) in promoting inhalation.

3. The Shen (Kidney) lies in the lumbar region, and its deficiency may cause low back pain. In this case, Shen Shu (BL-23) is one of the points of first choice.

4. Deficiency of the Yang of the Shen (Kidney) hinders nourishment of the Pi (Spleen), causing insufficiency of the Yang of the Pi (Spleen). For this reason, this point is indicated in the treatment of disorders of the digestive system caused by deficiency of the Yang of the Pi (Spleen) and the Shen (Kidney).

combinations.indication: Kidney deficiency, low back pain, tinnitus, sexual dysfunction

BL-24.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the third lumbar vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of Qi Hai (CV-6).
BL-24.anatomy: Thoracolumbar fascia, erector spinae, and quadratus lumborum muscles.
BL-24.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.8–1.2 cun.
BL-24.etymology: Qi Hai (气海), Sea of Qi; Shu (俞), point. This point, on the side opposite Qi Hai (CV-6), is the place where the primordial Qi reaches the back.
BL-24.clinicalNotes:
1. This point lies at the level of Qi Hai (CV-6). Qi Hai (CV-6) is the place to which the primordial Qi converges. The primordial Qi originates in the Shen (Kidney), which is responsible for reproduction and the metabolism of water. This point lies in the region of the genitourinary system and is therefore important for treating disorders of this system.

2. In the treatment of disorders of the lower limbs, this point should be needled deeply so that the needling sensation reaches the affected part.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-25.category: Back-Shu Point of the Large Intestine
BL-25.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4). At the level of the iliac crest.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, first locate Yao Yang Guan (GV-3) at the level of the iliac crest. Locate Da Chang Chu (BL-25)
5 cun lateral to Yao Yang Guan (GV-3).
BL-25.anatomy: Thoracolumbar fascia, erector spinae, and quadratus lumborum muscles. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the lumbar nerves.
BL-25.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.8–1.2 cun.
actions: strengthens the lumbar region and the lower limbs
BL-25.etymology: Da Chang (大肠), Large Intestine; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Da Chang (Large Intestine) reaches the back.
BL-25.clinicalNotes:
1. Back-Shu point of the Da Chang (Large Intestine), to which the Qi of the Da Chang (Large Intestine) converges. It is indicated to treat diarrhea, abdominal pain, and other disorders of the large intestine.

2. This point is in the Lower Jiao, where the reproductive organs and the urinary system are located, and is therefore indicated in the treatment of disorders of the genitourinary system.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-26.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, 1.5 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5).
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point at the inferior margin of the spinous process of the fifth lumbar vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-26.anatomy: Thoracolumbar fascia, erector spinae muscle, and origin of the gluteus maximus.
BL-26.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.8–1.2 cun.
actions: regulates the lower jiao (urination and intestines)
BL-26.etymology: Guan (关), strategic; Yuan (元), primordial Qi; Shu (俞), point. The point lies on the side opposite Guan Yuan (CV-4), the place where the Qi of Primordial Yin and Yang penetrates the lumbar region.
BL-26.clinicalNotes:
This point lies in the Lower Jiao, where the Qi of the Da Chang (Large Intestine), the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine), the Pang Guang (Bladder), and the organs of the genitourinary system converge. It is therefore indicated in the treatment of disorders of the digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems.

This point connects with Guan Yuan (CV-4), pathway of the primordial Qi, and may therefore be indicated to treat symptoms of diabetes.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-27.category: Back-Shu Point of the Small Intestine
BL-27.locationClassical: On the sacrum, 1.5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of the first posterior sacral foramen.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the first sacral vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-27.anatomy: Gluteus maximus muscle and tendon of the erector spinae. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the S1 and S2 sacral nerves.
BL-27.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion, 0.8–1.2 cun.
actions: Separates the pure from the impure
regulates the intestines and the bladder
BL-27.etymology: Xiao Shang (小肠), Small Intestine; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine) reaches the back.
BL-27.clinicalNotes:
1. Back-Shu point of the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine), the place where the Qi of the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine) converges. It is therefore indicated in the treatment of disorders of the digestive system.

2. This point lies near the organs of the genitourinary system and is therefore indicated to treat disorders of this system.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-28.locationClassical: On the sacrum, 1.5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of the second posterior sacral foramen.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point below the second sacral vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-28.anatomy: Gluteus maximus muscle and tendon of the erector spinae.
BL-28.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion, 0.8–1.2 cun.
actions: clears Damp-Heat from the lower jiao
tcmIndications: rigidity and pain in the lumbar and sacral region
BL-28.etymology: Pang Guang (膀胱), Bladder; Shu (俞), point. Place where the Qi of the Pang Guang (Bladder) reaches the back.
BL-28.clinicalNotes: Back-Shu point of the Pang Guang (Bladder), the place where the Qi of the Pang Guang (Bladder) converges. It lies in a region near the Chang (Small and Large Intestines), as well as the reproductive system. It is therefore indicated in the treatment of disorders of these organs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-29.locationClassical: On the sacrum, 1.5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of the third posterior sacral foramen.
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point below the third sacral vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
tcmIndications: rigidity and pain in the lumbar region
BL-29.etymology: Zhong (中), center; Lu (膂), paravertebral muscles; Shu (俞), point. This point lies in the middle of the paravertebral muscles.
BL-29.clinicalNotes: This point lies in the sacral region, where the Qi of the Xiao Chang (Small Intestine) and the Da Chang (Large Intestine) converge. Disorders related to these organs may be treated with this point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-30.locationClassical: On the sacrum, 1.5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of the fourth posterior sacral foramen.
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point below the fourth sacral vertebra,
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
actions: benefits the lumbar region and the lower limbs
BL-30.etymology: Bai (白), white; Huan (环), ring; Shu (俞), point. White Ring point.
BL-30.clinicalNotes: Because of its proximity to the reproductive organs and the urinary system, this point may be used to treat genitourinary disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-31.category: Meeting Point of the Bladder and Gall Bladder channels
BL-31.locationClassical: On the sacrum, in the first posterior sacral foramen (midpoint between the posterior superior iliac spine and the posterior midline).
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, the examiner places the tip of the index finger at the midpoint between Xiao Chang Shu (BL-27) and the posterior midline, and the little finger on the ipsilateral sacral cornu (the sacral cornua are rounded processes resembling small soybeans and represent the posterior articular processes of the fifth sacral vertebra). Rest the middle and ring fingers equidistantly between the index and little fingers. In this manner, Shang Liao (BL-31) lies at the tip of the index finger, Ci Liao (BL-32) at the tip of the middle finger, Zhong Liao (BL-33) at the tip of the ring finger, and Xia Liao (BL-34) at the tip of the little finger.
BL-31.anatomy: Gluteus maximus and erector spinae muscles. The first sacral nerve root lies within the foramen.
BL-31.needling: Perpendicular insertion directly into the foramen, 0.5–1.0 cun.
BL-31.safetyWarning: High sensitivity when the nerve root is reached.
actions: Regulates the lower jiao and facilitates urination and defecation
BL-31.etymology: Shang (上), upper; Liao (髎), foramen. Located in the first sacral foramen.
BL-31.clinicalNotes: This point lies in the region of the genitourinary system and is therefore indicated to treat disorders of this system. It has the function of tonifying the Shen (Kidney), removing dampness, and promoting diuresis.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-32.category: Meeting Point of the Bladder and Gall Bladder channels
BL-32.locationClassical: On the sacrum, in the second posterior sacral foramen (slightly medial and inferior to the posterior superior iliac spine).
howToFind: See Shang Liao (BL-31) for further details.
BL-32.anatomy: Gluteus maximus and erector spinae muscles. Second sacral nerve root.
BL-32.needling: Perpendicular insertion directly into the foramen, 0.5–1.0 cun.
BL-32.safetyWarning: High sensitivity when the nerve root is reached.
actions: invigorates the Blood and regulates menstruation
strongly relieves pain (main point for pelvic and menstrual pain)
BL-32.etymology: Ci (次), second; Liao (髎), foramen. Located in the second sacral foramen.
BL-32.clinicalNotes:
The Chang (Large and Small Intestines) and the organs of the genitourinary system are near this point, so it may be used in disorders related to these organs.

Among the eight Liao points, this is the most used. It has the function of regulating the Lower Jiao, strengthening the lumbar region and the knees, and activating the Qi of the meridians.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-33.category: Meeting Point of the Bladder and Gall Bladder channels
BL-33.locationClassical: On the sacrum, in the third posterior sacral foramen.
howToFind: See Shang Liao (BL-31) for further details.
BL-33.anatomy: Gluteus maximus muscle. Third sacral nerve root.
BL-33.needling: Perpendicular insertion directly into the foramen, 0.5–1.0 cun.
BL-33.etymology: Zhong (中), center; Liao (髎), foramen. Located in the third sacral foramen.
BL-33.clinicalNotes: See Ci Liao (BL-32) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-34.category: Meeting Point of the Bladder and Gall Bladder channels
BL-34.locationClassical: On the sacrum, in the fourth posterior sacral foramen.
howToFind: See Shang Liao (BL-31) for further details.
BL-34.anatomy: Gluteus maximus muscle. Fourth sacral nerve root.
BL-34.needling: Perpendicular insertion directly into the foramen, 0.5–1.0 cun.
BL-34.etymology: Xia (下), low or lower; Liao (髎), foramen. Located in the fourth sacral foramen.
BL-34.clinicalNotes: See Ci Liao (BL-32) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-35.locationClassical: On the sacrum, 0.5 cun lateral to the tip of the coccyx.
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, the point lies
5 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of the inferior end of the coccyx.
BL-35.anatomy: Gluteus maximus muscle and ischiococcygeus muscle. Innervated by the coccygeal nerve.
actions: benefits the coccyx and the anus
BL-35.etymology: Hui (会), meeting; Yang (阳), of Yin-Yang. Meeting of the Qi of the Du Mai.
BL-35.clinicalNotes: See Ci Liao (BL-32) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.
