BL-36.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the thigh, at the midpoint of the transverse gluteal crease.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point at the intersection of the lines passing through the infragluteal sulcus and the midline of the posterior femoral region.
BL-36.anatomy: Inferior border of the gluteus maximus, origin of the hamstring muscles (biceps femoris and semitendinosus). The sciatic nerve passes deep below this point.
BL-36.safetyWarning: Avoid direct trauma to the sciatic nerve.
tcmIndications: pain in the lumbar and gluteal region
motor impairment of the lower limbs
BL-36.etymology: Cheng (承), to hold; Fu (扶), to support. This point lies at the root of the femur, in the center of the infragluteal sulcus. Its function was believed to be supporting the weight of the body.
BL-36.clinicalNotes: This point belongs to the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, and lies near the anus and the genital organs. It may therefore be indicated in the treatment of disorders related to these organs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-37.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the thigh, 6 cun inferior to BL-36, on the line connecting BL-36 and BL-40.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point 6 cun below Cheng Fu (BL-36), at the center of the posterior margin of the muscle.
BL-37.anatomy: Between the biceps femoris and semitendinosus muscles. Deep to the point lies the sciatic nerve.
BL-37.safetyWarning: Avoid direct trauma to the sciatic nerve.
tcmIndications: pain on the posterior aspect of the thigh
BL-37.etymology: Yin (殷), thickness or center; Men (门), gate. The point lies on the line between Cheng Fu (BL-36) and Wei Zhong (BL-40), where the muscle is thick.
BL-37.clinicalNotes: This point is commonly indicated in the treatment of flaccidity, numbness, pain, and loss of muscle strength of the lower limbs. It may be indicated to reduce muscle rigidity, activate the flow of Qi in the collaterals, and relieve numbness and pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-38.locationClassical: At the lateral end of the popliteal crease, 1 cun superior to BL-39, on the medial side of the tendon of the biceps femoris.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, first locate Wei Yang (BL-39). Locate Fu Xi (BL-38) 1 cun directly superior to Wei Yang (BL-39), medial to the tendon of the biceps femoris muscle.
BL-38.anatomy: Tendon of the biceps femoris, lateral head of the gastrocnemius. Innervated by the common fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: Numbness and pain in the popliteal fossa
BL-38.etymology: Fu (浮), above; Xi (郗), crevice. The point lies above the popliteal fossa when the knee is flexed.
BL-38.clinicalNotes: It has the function of relaxing muscles and activating the flow of Qi in the meridians and the collaterals.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-39.locationClassical: At the lateral end of the popliteal crease, on the medial border of the tendon of the biceps femoris.
howToFind: In ventral or lateral decubitus, locate the point 1 cun lateral to Wei Zhong (BL-40).
BL-39.anatomy: Tendon of the biceps femoris, lateral head of the gastrocnemius. Innervated by the common fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: Rigidity and pain in the lumbar region
distension and fullness in the lower abdomen
BL-39.etymology: Wei (委), referring to Wei Zhong (BL-40); Yang (阳), lateral. The point lies lateral to Wei Zhong (BL-40).
BL-39.clinicalNotes: Lower He-Sea point of the San Jiao. The San Jiao Meridian, Hand Shao Yang, commands the drainage of the water passages and controls the function of the organs in this region. This point is therefore indicated to treat dysuria and urinary retention.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-40.locationClassical: At the midpoint of the popliteal crease, between the tendons of the biceps femoris and semitendinosus.
howToFind: With the patient prone or in lateral decubitus, locate the point at the center of the popliteal fossa, between the tendons of the biceps femoris and semitendinosus muscles.
BL-40.anatomy: Popliteal fascia. Innervated by the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve and the tibial nerve. The popliteal artery and vein lie deep to the point.
BL-40.needling: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.0 cun; or prick to bleed in acute conditions.
BL-40.safetyWarning: HIGH-RISK VASCULAR AREA. Deep insertion risks puncturing the popliteal artery or vein. Do not use aggressive lift-and-thrust technique. Avoid injury to the tibial nerve.
actions: Benefits the lumbar region and knees
activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: Acute and chronic low back pain (primary point)
motor impairment of the hip joint
BL-40.etymology: Wei (委), bend of the knee; Zhong (中), center. The point sits at the center of the popliteal fossa.
BL-40.clinicalNotes:
1. This point is widely used to treat spinal stiffness and pain, and hemiplegia.

2. It is also known as Xue Xi (blood cleft). Bloodletting at this site restores consciousness, clears heat, relaxes muscles and tendons, and activates the flow of Xue (blood). It is frequently indicated for stroke sequelae, coma, heatstroke, acute vomiting, pharyngitis, and skin eruptions and diseases.

3. As a point of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, it may be used to treat dysuria.

combinations.indication: Acute low back pain, emergency resuscitation

BL-41.category: Meeting Point of the Bladder and Small Intestine channels. (Note: This point begins the outer line of the Bladder channel on the back)
BL-41.locationClassical: On the upper back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the second thoracic vertebra (T2), at the level of BL-12.
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the second thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-41.anatomy: Trapezius, levator scapulae, and rhomboid muscles.
BL-41.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-41.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Do not needle perpendicularly or deeply.
tcmIndications: Stiffness and pain in the shoulder, back, and nape
numbness of the elbow and arm
westernIndications: trigger points of the levator scapulae and rhomboids
BL-41.etymology: Fu (附), lateral; Fen (分), separation. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, descends bilaterally from the neck. This point, joined to the first line, is the starting point of the second line of the meridian.
BL-41.clinicalNotes: Promotes the flow of Qi and Xue (Blood) in the region of the point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-42.locationClassical: On the upper back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra (T3), at the level of BL-13 (Lung Shu point).
howToFind: Seated with the head flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Shen Zhu (GV-12).
BL-42.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-42.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Do not needle perpendicularly or deeply.
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and back
westernIndications: myofascial pain of the upper back
BL-42.etymology: Po (魄), soul; Hu (户), dwelling. The Fei (Lung) houses the soul. The point lies at the level of Fei Shu (BL-13), as a dwelling for the Qi of the Fei (Lung).
BL-42.clinicalNotes: This point lies beside Fei Shu (BL-13). See Fei Shu (BL-13) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-43.locationClassical: On the upper back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the fourth thoracic vertebra (T4), at the level of BL-14.
howToFind: Seated with the head flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the fourth thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-43.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-43.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Do not needle perpendicularly or deeply.
actions: Tonifies and nourishes the Lung, Heart, Kidney, Spleen, and Stomach
calms the spirit (traditionally considered highly effective for all types of severe deficiency and chronic disease)
BL-43.etymology: Gao (膏), fat; Huang (肓), membrane. Gao Huang refers to a terminal-stage patient with disease that is difficult to treat.
BL-43.clinicalNotes:
1. It was observed in antiquity that this point was effective in the treatment of consumptive disorders such as hemoptysis caused by pulmonary disease, hectic fever, night sweats, fatigue of the limbs, spontaneous sweating, memory deficit, insomnia, nocturnal emission, and emaciation from prolonged illness. Moxibustion is frequently used at this point.

2. The point lies in the scapular region. For this reason, it is commonly used to treat pain in the scapular region, particularly if the patient presents pain on digital pressure at this point.

3. Because this point is located on the side opposite the breasts, it has a corresponding therapeutic effect. Therefore, to treat breast abscess, local points are frequently used in association with points in the dorsal region.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-44.locationClassical: On the upper back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the fifth thoracic vertebra (T5), at the level of BL-15 (Heart Shu point).
howToFind: Seated with the head flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the fifth thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Shen Dao (GV-11).
BL-44.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-44.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Do not needle perpendicularly or deeply.
tcmIndications: stiffness and pain in the back
BL-44.etymology: Shen (神), mind; Tang (堂), hall. The Xin (Heart) houses the mind. The point lies at the level of Xin Shu (BL-15), as a hall where the mind dwells.
BL-44.clinicalNotes: This point lies beside Xin Shu (BL-15). See Xin Shu (BL-15) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-45.locationClassical: On the upper back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the sixth thoracic vertebra (T6), at the level of BL-16.
howToFind: Seated with the head flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the sixth thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Ling Tai (GV-10).
BL-45.anatomy: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, and rhomboid major muscles.
BL-45.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-45.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Do not needle perpendicularly or deeply.
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and back
BL-45.etymology: Yi Xi (譩譆), the sound of a sigh. At the moment of inserting the needle at this point, in antiquity the patient was asked to pronounce the sound Yi Xi — hence "the sound of a sigh."
BL-45.clinicalNotes: This point lies in the dividing area between the heart and the lung and is used to treat cardiac and pulmonary disorders. The occurrence of fever and epistaxis is associated with loss of the diffusing capacity of the Wei Qi of the Fei (Lung). It also has the function of treating insomnia and anxiety.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-46.locationClassical: On the back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the seventh thoracic vertebra (T7), at the level of BL-17 (Diaphragm Shu point).
howToFind: Seated with the head flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the seventh thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Zhi Yang (GV-9), at the level of the inferior angle of the scapula.
BL-46.anatomy: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboid major, and iliocostalis thoracis muscles. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the T7 and T8 thoracic nerves.
BL-46.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
tcmIndications: pain and stiffness of the back
westernIndications: myofascial pain of the mid back
BL-46.etymology: Ge (膈), diaphragm; Guan (关), pass. The point lies at the level of Ge Shu (BL-17) and is the Dorsal Shu point of the Diaphragm.
BL-46.clinicalNotes:
This point lies near the Wei (Stomach), in the Middle Jiao. It is therefore generally used to treat disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach).

Because it lies beside Ge Shu (BL-17), it is also indicated in the treatment of various hemorrhagic disorders. See Ge Shu (BL-17) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-47.locationClassical: On the back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the ninth thoracic vertebra (T9), at the level of BL-18 (Liver Shu point).
howToFind: Seated with the head flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the ninth thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Jin Suo (GV-8).
BL-47.anatomy: Latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis thoracis muscles. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the thoracic nerves.
BL-47.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-47.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Deep insertion may puncture the liver on the right side.
tcmIndications: Fullness in the chest and hypochondrium
BL-47.etymology: Hun (魂), soul; Men (门), gate. The Gan (Liver) houses the soul. The point lies at the level of Gan Shu (BL-18), as a gate for the Qi of the Gan (Liver).
BL-47.clinicalNotes: This point lies beside Gan Shu (BL-18). See Gan Shu (BL-18) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-48.locationClassical: On the back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the tenth thoracic vertebra (T10), at the level of BL-19 (Gallbladder Shu point).
howToFind: Seated with the head flexed, locate the point below the spinous process of the tenth thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Zhong Shu (GV-7).
BL-48.anatomy: Latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis thoracis muscles.
BL-48.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-48.etymology: Yang (阳), six Fu; Gang (纲), commander. The Dan (Gallbladder) belongs to Yang. The point lies at the level of Dan Shu (BL-19), as commander of the Dorsal Shu points of the six Fu.
BL-48.clinicalNotes: The point lies beside Dan Shu (BL-19). See Dan Shu (BL-19) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-49.locationClassical: On the back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the eleventh thoracic vertebra (T11), at the level of BL-20 (Spleen Shu point).
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the eleventh thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Ji Zhong (GV-6).
BL-49.anatomy: Latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis thoracis muscles.
BL-49.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-49.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may puncture the kidney. High risk of pneumothorax (lower pleural cavity).
BL-49.etymology: Yi (意), idea or thought; She (舍), residence. The Pi (Spleen) stores thought. The point lies at the level of Pi Shu (BL-20), as a residence for the Qi of the Pi (Spleen).
BL-49.clinicalNotes: The Pi (Spleen) stores thought. This point lies beside Pi Shu (BL-20) and has similar functions. See Pi Shu (BL-20) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-50.locationClassical: On the back, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the twelfth thoracic vertebra (T12), at the level of BL-21 (Stomach Shu point).
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the twelfth thoracic vertebra, 3 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-50.anatomy: Latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis lumborum muscles.
BL-50.needling: Oblique insertion toward the spine, 0.3–0.5 cun.
BL-50.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may puncture the kidney.
BL-50.etymology: Wei (胃), stomach; Gang (仓), granary. The point lies at the level of Wei Shu (BL-21). The stomach receives food, functioning as a granary.
BL-50.clinicalNotes: This point lies beside Wei Shu (BL-21) and has similar functions. See Wei Shu (BL-21) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-51.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the first lumbar vertebra (L1), at the level of BL-22.
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point below the spinous process of the first lumbar vertebra, 3 cun lateral to Xuan Shu (GV-5).
BL-51.anatomy: Thoracolumbar fascia, latissimus dorsi, and quadratus lumborum muscles.
BL-51.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may puncture the kidney.
BL-51.etymology: Huang (肓), membrane; Men (门), gate. The point lies at the level of San Jiao Shu (BL-22) as a gate for the Qi of the San Jiao.
BL-51.clinicalNotes: This point lies beside San Jiao Shu (BL-22) and has similar functions. See San Jiao Shu (BL-22) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-52.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, 3 cun lateral to the inferior border of the spinous process of the second lumbar vertebra (L2), at the level of BL-23 (Kidney Shu point).
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point 3 cun lateral to Ming Men (GV-4), which lies on the side opposite the umbilicus.
BL-52.anatomy: Thoracolumbar fascia, latissimus dorsi, and quadratus lumborum muscles.
BL-52.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may puncture the kidney.
westernIndications: chronic low back pain (quadratus lumborum trigger-point zone)
BL-52.etymology: Zhi (志), will; Shi (室), chamber. The Shen (Kidney) stores the will.
BL-52.clinicalNotes: The Shen (Kidney) stores the will. This point lies beside Shen Shu (BL-23). Both are important for tonifying the Shen (Kidney). See Shen Shu (BL-23) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-53.locationClassical: In the gluteal region, 3 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of the second sacral foramen (at the level of BL-32).
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point below the second sacral vertebra, 3 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-53.anatomy: Gluteus maximus muscle. Innervated by the superior gluteal nerve.
BL-53.etymology: Bao (胞), bladder; Huang (肓), membrane that supports the bladder. The point lies at the level of Pang Guang Shu (BL-28).
BL-53.clinicalNotes: This point lies beside Pang Guang Shu (BL-28) and has similar functions. See Pang Guang Shu (BL-28) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-54.locationClassical: In the gluteal region, 3 cun lateral to the posterior midline, at the level of the fourth sacral foramen (at the level of BL-34).
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, locate the point at the level of the fourth posterior sacral foramen, 3 cun lateral to the posterior midline.
BL-54.anatomy: Gluteus maximus and piriformis muscles. The sciatic nerve passes deep to this point. Innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.
BL-54.safetyWarning: Avoid direct trauma to the sciatic nerve.
actions: Benefits the lumbar region and the buttocks
tcmIndications: muscle atrophy of the lower limbs
BL-54.etymology: Zhi (秩), in line, sequence; Bian (边), lateral. The Dorsal Shu points of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, are arranged in a sequence, and this is the most inferior of all of them.
BL-54.clinicalNotes:
1. According to the principle that a point can treat disorders manifested along the course of its own meridian, this point is indicated for the treatment of disorders of the spine and lower limbs.

2. Different depths and angles of needle insertion at this point treat different conditions. Vertical insertion can treat the lower limbs; oblique upward and deep insertion can treat anal and external genital disorders, prostatitis, and other urinary conditions.

3. When acupuncture is performed, the De Qi sensation from needling must reach the affected area. Thus, needling sensation directed to the lower limbs may enhance the efficacy of treatment of pain and tingling in the lower extremities; needling sensation directed to the external genitalia is recommended for treating genital and anal disorders; needling sensation directed to the lower abdomen is effective for treating prostatitis and gynecological disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-55.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the leg, 2 cun directly inferior to BL-40, between the medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius muscle.
howToFind: In ventral decubitus or seated with the foot in plantar flexion, locate the point 2 cun immediately below Wei Zhong (BL-40).
BL-55.anatomy: Gastrocnemius muscle. The tibial nerve and the popliteal artery and vein lie deep.
tcmIndications: pain and paralysis of the lower limbs
BL-55.etymology: He (合), confluence; Yang (阳), the Yang of Yin-Yang. The meridian, from the nape, descends and divides into two branches, reuniting at Wei Zhong (BL-40). He Yang (BL-55) lies below Wei Zhong (BL-40).
BL-55.clinicalNotes:
1. According to the principle that a point can treat disorders manifested along the course of its own meridian, this point is indicated for the treatment of disorders of the spine and lower limbs.

2. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, connects with the brain, the spine, the dorsal region, and the gluteal region through its collateral branches; the point may therefore be used to treat disorders of the head, epilepsy, and clonic convulsion.

3. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, and the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, are coupled meridians. The Shen (Kidney) controls reproduction, so the point may also be indicated for the treatment of disorders of the reproductive system.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-56.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the leg, midway between BL-55 and BL-57, at the center of the belly of the gastrocnemius muscle.
howToFind: Seated with the ankle in plantar flexion or in horizontal ventral decubitus, locate the point at the center of the bulge of the gastrocnemius muscle, between Wei Zhong (BL-40) and Cheng Shan (BL-57).
BL-56.anatomy: Gastrocnemius and soleus muscles. Innervated by the tibial nerve.
actions: benefits the heel and the foot
BL-56.etymology: Cheng (承), to support; Jin (筋), tendon. Cheng Jin refers to the gastrocnemius muscle. The point lies over this important muscle of the lower limb, which supports the weight of the body.
BL-56.clinicalNotes: The collateral branches of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, connect with the anus and have the function of regulating Qi and maintaining the activities of the Chang (intestines) in good working order. The point may be used to treat digestive disorders, particularly anal disorders. See Cheng Shan (BL-57) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-57.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the leg, in the depression formed below the bellies of the gastrocnemius muscle when the muscle is flexed (approximately 8 cun inferior to BL-40).
howToFind: In ventral decubitus, with the leg extended and the ankle in plantar flexion, locate the point below the apex of the inverted "V"-shaped depression formed by the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle.
Standing on tiptoe, locate the point below the apex of the inverted "V"-shaped depression formed by the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle.
BL-57.anatomy: Junction of the gastrocnemius with the Achilles tendon, overlying the soleus muscle. Innervated by the tibial nerve.
actions: benefits the calf and the heel
BL-57.etymology: Cheng (承), to support; Shan (山), mountain. The two bulges of the gastrocnemius muscle are like prominent mountains. This point lies below them, as the support of the mountains.
BL-57.clinicalNotes:
1. This point belongs to the Bladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, whose collaterals are distributed in the head, neck, dorsal region, and lower limbs. It is therefore indicated to treat disorders of the lower limbs, infantile convulsions, and epilepsy with muscular contractions.

2. The Tai Yang Meridians are the most superficial of the Yang meridians and have the function of protecting the body like a fence. They are frequently the first to be affected by external pathogenic factors. In this way, most of the points of the Tai Yang Meridians may be used to treat sore throat caused by invasion of external pathogenic factors and epistaxis caused by Heat resulting from aggression by external pathogenic factors.

3. The Tendinomuscular Meridian of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, connects with the nose. Nasal obstruction caused by Excess syndrome and epistaxis caused by Deficiency syndrome are symptoms of disorders of the collaterals of the Bladder Meridian. The Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, passes through the throat and is the coupled meridian of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang. Thus, points of the Bladder Meridian may be indicated in the treatment of pharyngitis and epistaxis.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-58.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the leg, 7 cun directly superior to BL-60, 1 cun inferior and lateral to BL-57.
howToFind: Seated with the ankle in plantar flexion, locate the point 1 cun obliquely and inferior to Cheng Shan (BL-57), immediately above Kun Lun (BL-60).
BL-58.anatomy: Gastrocnemius and soleus muscles. Innervated by the sural nerve.
actions: Harmonizes the upper and lower body
expels Wind from the Tai Yang channel
westernIndications: rheumatoid arthritis affecting the lower limbs
BL-58.etymology: Fei (飞), to fly; Yang (扬), to lift. It signifies that the collateral of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, emerges from this point toward the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin.
BL-58.clinicalNotes: See Cheng Shan (BL-57) and Cheng Jin (BL-56) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-59.category: Xi-Cleft Point of the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
BL-59.locationClassical: On the posterolateral aspect of the leg, 3 cun directly superior to BL-60.
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported, locate the point 3 cun immediately above Kun Lun (BL-60).
BL-59.anatomy: Peroneus brevis and soleus muscles. Innervated by the sural nerve.
actions: Benefits the lumbar region and the legs
tcmIndications: Sensation of heaviness in the head
paralysis and pain in the lower limbs
BL-59.etymology: Fu (跗), tarsus; Yang (阳), the Yang of Yin-Yang. The exterior and the upper are Yang. The point lies above the tarsus and on the lateral aspect of the leg.
BL-59.clinicalNotes:
1. This is the Xi (Cleft) point of the Yang Qiao Mai. The Xi (cleft) points are mainly used to treat acute pain. The Yang Qiao Mai is distributed along the lateral aspect of the lower limbs, shoulders, and head, where the meridians of the Bladder, Foot Tai Yang; the Gallbladder, Foot Shao Yang; the San Jiao, Hand Shao Yang; the Large Intestine, Hand Yang Ming; and the Stomach, Foot Yang Ming, converge. The Yin Qiao Mai and the Yang Qiao Mai are responsible for inertia and activity, respectively. The Yang Qiao Mai governs the Yang-Qi and the Yin Qiao Mai controls the Yin-Qi. Both have the function of controlling and regulating the Qi and Xue (Blood), harmonizing the Yin and the Yang in the meridians distributed on the lateral and medial aspects of the lower limbs, respectively. Thus, for acute shoulder pain, torticollis, hemiplegia, flaccidity, and numbness of the lower limbs, this point is frequently used.

2. The Yang Qiao Mai connects with several meridians that converge to the head. This point is generally indicated for the treatment of headache, sensation of heaviness in the head, and vertigo.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-60.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the ankle, in the depression midway between the prominence of the lateral malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
howToFind: Seated with the foot at rest or in dorsal decubitus, locate Kun Lun (BL-60) at the midpoint of the distance between the apex of the lateral malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
BL-60.anatomy: Anterior to the Achilles tendon. Innervated by the sural nerve. Small saphenous vein nearby.
actions: activates the entire Bladder channel and relieves pain
BL-60.etymology: Kun Lun (昆仑), the name of a mountain located in western China. The point lies near the lateral malleolus, the shape of which resembles that of a mountain.
BL-60.clinicalNotes:
1. This point is highly effective for treating occipital headache and cervicodorsal pain and is frequently used in association with Hou Xi (SI-3).

2. The Shen (Kidney) is responsible for reproductive function. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, and the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, are coupled meridians. Thus, points of the two meridians may treat disorders of the Zang Fu. This point may be used to treat placental retention.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-61.category: Meeting Point of the Bladder channel with the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
BL-61.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the foot, posterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus, directly below BL-60, lateral to the calcaneus.
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point 2 cun immediately below Kun Lun (BL-60), in the depression at the transition between light and dark skin.
BL-61.anatomy: Calcaneofibular ligament. Innervated by the sural nerve.
tcmIndications: Atrophy and muscular weakness of the lower limbs
BL-61.etymology: Pu (仆), servant, attendant; Shen (参), to assist, to attend. The point signifies a servant attending his master. Pu Shen is also written as Pu Can.
BL-61.clinicalNotes: This point is mainly used to treat heel pain and low back pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-62.category: Confluent Point of the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
BL-62.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the foot, in the depression directly inferior to the lateral malleolus.
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point
5 cun below the lateral malleolus, immediately below the apex.
BL-62.anatomy: Tendons of the peroneus longus and brevis muscles. Innervated by the sural nerve.
tcmIndications: pain in the lumbar region and leg
BL-62.etymology: Shen (申), to extend; Mai (脉), vessel. This point is important for treating leg spasms because it improves the flow of Xue (Blood) at the site, relaxing the muscle.
BL-62.clinicalNotes:
1. It is the Confluent point with the Yang Qiao Mai, the site where the Yang Qiao Mai originates. The Yin Qiao Mai and the Yang Qiao Mai are distributed in the lateral and medial regions of the lower limbs, ascending and ending at the medial commissure of the eye. The Qiao Mai has a regulatory function, keeping the Yin and Yang activities in balance. The signs of disorders of the Yang Qiao Mai are intense in Yang and mild in Yin, and those of the Yin Qiao Mai are intense in Yin and mild in Yang. Because this is the Confluent point with the Yang Qiao Mai, it is indicated in the treatment of equinus foot caused by paralysis of the lower limbs and of epilepsy with daytime seizures.

2. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, is distributed through the eyes, head, and neck and is therefore indicated to treat disorders of the face and head.

combinations.indication: Neck and back pain, headache, epilepsy

BL-63.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the foot, directly anterior and inferior to BL-62, in the depression posterior to the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal.
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point
5 cun anterior and inferior to Shen Mai (BL-62), in the depression of the inferior margin of the cuboid bone.
BL-63.anatomy: Tendon of the peroneus brevis muscle, abductor digiti minimi. Innervated by the lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve.
BL-63.etymology: Jin (金), gold; Men (门), gate. The starting point of the Yang Wei Mai, the site where Qi and Xue (Blood) are concentrated, with a value equivalent to gold.
BL-63.clinicalNotes: It is the Xi (Cleft) point of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, and is also the point of origin of the Yang Wei Mai. It may therefore be used to treat headache, acute low back pain, and cramps due to cholera.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-64.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the foot, below the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal, at the junction of the red and white skin.
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point on the lateral aspect of the foot, at the transition between light and dark skin, anterior and inferior to the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal.
BL-64.anatomy: Abductor digiti minimi muscle. Innervated by the lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve.
tcmIndications: pain in the lumbar region and thigh
westernIndications: pain at the base of the fifth metatarsal (rehabilitation of Jones fracture)
BL-64.etymology: Jing Gu (京骨), the ancient name of the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal. The point lies at the anteroinferior margin of this tuberosity.
BL-64.clinicalNotes: See Jin Men (BL-63) and Pu Shen (BL-61) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-65.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the foot, in the depression posterior and inferior to the head of the fifth metatarsal (proximal to the metatarsophalangeal joint).
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point on the lateral aspect of the foot, proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint, at the transition between light and dark skin.
BL-65.anatomy: Abductor digiti minimi muscle. Innervated by the lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve.
BL-65.etymology: Shu (束), bind; Gu (骨), bone. Shu Gu is the ancient name for the head of the fifth metatarsal.
BL-65.clinicalNotes: See Jin Men (BL-63) and Pu Shen (BL-61) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-66.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the foot, in the depression anterior and inferior to the head of the fifth metatarsal (distal to the metatarsophalangeal joint).
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported, locate the point on the lateral aspect of the foot, in the depression distal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint, at the transition between light and dark skin.
BL-66.anatomy: Tendon of the abductor digiti minimi muscle. Innervated by the lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve.
actions: descends the Qi of the Lung and Stomach
BL-66.etymology: Zu (足), foot; Tong (通), passage; Gu (谷), valley. The point lies in the depression of the foot, comparable to a valley, through which the Qi of the meridian flows.
BL-66.clinicalNotes: See Jin Men (BL-63) and Pu Shen (BL-61) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

BL-67.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the small toe, 0.1 cun from the lateral (fibular) corner of the nail.
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point at the intersection of the line passing along the lateral margin and the line passing along the base of the nail of the fifth toe.
BL-67.anatomy: Nail bed. Innervated by the proper plantar digital nerve and the lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve.
BL-67.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion directed proximally, 0.1–0.2 cun. Moxibustion is commonly used here.
BL-67.safetyWarning: CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY (unless one is actively attempting to turn a baby in breech presentation or to induce labor).
actions: Turns the fetus and facilitates labor
clears the head and the eyes
BL-67.etymology: Zhi (至), to reach; Yin (阴), the Yin of Yin Yang. Yin in this case refers to the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin. Zhi Yin (BL-67) is the last point of the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, the site where it reaches the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin.
BL-67.clinicalNotes:
1. The Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, begins at the medial commissure of the eyelid and is distributed over the head, neck, and the dorsal and lumbar regions. Its Tendinomuscular Meridian connects with the nose. The Bladder Meridian has the function of protecting the body. According to the principle that, to treat a disorder of the upper part of the body one should needle the lower part, and also according to clinical experience, this point may be used to treat disorders of the face and head, especially headache with difficulty opening the eyes (migraine with photophobia).

2. The Shen (Kidney) and the Pang Guang (Bladder) are directly related, and the Shen (Kidney) is responsible for reproductive function. Thus, Kun Lun (BL-60) and Zhi Yin (BL-67) have the function of correcting the position of the fetus, with Zhi Yin (BL-67) being used more frequently. Moxibustion or massage directly at this point may correct the fetal position and stimulate labor (Note from the updater: this is still a controversial subject and merits further and more systematic research).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-1.locationClassical: On the sole of the foot, between the second and third metatarsal bones, approximately one-third of the distance from the interdigital folds to the heel, in the depression formed when the foot is in plantar flexion.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, with the ankle in plantar flexion, locate the point in the depression at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of the distance between the heel and the base of the second and third toes, just posterior to the second and third metatarsophalangeal joints.
KI-1.anatomy: Plantar aponeurosis and flexor digitorum brevis muscle. Innervated by the medial and lateral plantar nerves. Plantar arterial arch.
KI-1.etymology: Yong (涌), to gush; Quan (泉), spring, source. The point lies in the plantar depression. The Qi of the meridian flows upward as if from a spring.
KI-1.clinicalNotes:
1. The Kidney Meridian travels through the throat and ends at the root of the tongue. According to the principles: "Points on the lower part of the body can be used to treat diseases that occur in the upper part of the body" and "the point can treat disorders of its own meridian," Yong Quan (KI-1) can be indicated to treat disorders of the head, face, and sense organs. It has therapeutic effect on headache and dizziness caused by hyperactivity of Liver Yang, sore throat, hysteria, and dysphasia resulting from Yin deficiency.

2. According to the principle: "Jing (Well) points are used for diseases of the Zang," Yong Quan (KI-1) is an important point for treating coma, fainting, sequelae of stroke, heatstroke, and infantile convulsions.

3. The Shen (Kidney) is the foundation of the innate constitution. It stores primordial Yin and Yang. It is the palace in which the Jing (essence) resides. It is connected to the uterus. Thus, the point can be indicated to treat all types of diseases of the Zang Fu, especially those of the genitourinary and reproductive systems.

combinations.indication: Hypertension, dizziness, loss of consciousness, calming the mind

KI-2.locationClassical: On the medial side of the foot, inferior to the tuberosity of the navicular bone, at the junction of the red and white skin.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point anterior to the medial malleolus, in the anteroinferior depression below the tuberosity of the navicular bone, at the transition between light and dark skin.
KI-2.anatomy: Abductor hallucis muscle. Innervated by the medial plantar nerve and the saphenous nerve.
westernIndications: pain in the medial arch of the foot
KI-2.etymology: Ran (然), tuberosity of the navicular bone; Gu (谷), valley. The point lies in the depression below the tuberosity of the navicular bone, at the transition between light and dark skin.
KI-2.clinicalNotes: See Yong Quan (KI-1) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-3.locationClassical: On the medial side of the ankle, in the depression equidistant between the prominence of the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point at the midpoint between the posterior border of the medial malleolus and the anterior border of the calcaneal tendon, at the level of the apex of the medial malleolus.
KI-3.anatomy: Anterior to the Achilles tendon. Innervated by the saphenous nerve and the tibial nerve. The posterior tibial artery and vein run deep and adjacent.
KI-3.needling: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.0 cun (may be directed toward BL-60).
KI-3.safetyWarning: Avoid the posterior tibial artery and vein.
actions: benefits the Lungs (principal point for tonifying the Kidneys)
KI-3.etymology: Tai (太), great; Xi (溪), ravine. The point lies in the depression between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon, like an immense ravine.
KI-3.clinicalNotes:
The Shen (Kidney) is the root of the innate constitution and stores the Jing (essence), the material basis of reproduction. Tai Xi (KI-3) is the Yuan (Source) point and has the function of replenishing the Jing (essence) and tonifying the Shen (Kidney). Therefore, the point can be indicated to treat diseases of the genitourinary system due to Shen (Kidney) deficiency.

Tai Xi (KI-3) is indicated to tonify Yin and suppress hyperactivity of Yang. Hence its use in headache, dizziness, tinnitus, and hearing deficit due to Liver Yin deficiency, Kidney Yin deficiency, and Liver Yang hyperactivity.

Needling or pressing with the thumb and index finger on the points Tai Xi (KI-3) and Kun Lun (BL-60) can have an immediate effect in relieving sore throat, toothache, and epistaxis caused by Kidney Yin deficiency.

The Shen (Kidney) stores the Jing (essence) and belongs to the Water element. The Xin (Heart) controls mental and emotional activities and belongs to the Fire element. The point can be indicated to treat neuropsychiatric disorders resulting from disharmony between the Xin (Heart) and Shen (Kidney).

The Shen (Kidney) is responsible for the storage of Jing (essence) and controls the distribution and excretion of fluids. Some cases of diabetes and constipation result from this dysfunction of the Shen (Kidney).

Tai Xi (KI-3) is an important point for strengthening Qi. Cholera and diarrhea easily consume Qi, so the point can be used to recover the patient from a state of Yang depletion.

combinations.indication: Kidney and Spleen deficiency, menstrual disorders, insomnia
Kidney deficiency, low back pain, tinnitus, sexual dysfunction

KI-4.locationClassical: On the medial side of the ankle, posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus, in the depression anterior to the medial insertion of the Achilles tendon.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point posteroinferior to the medial malleolus, at the anterior border of the calcaneal tendon,
5 cun below Tai Xi (KI-3).
KI-4.anatomy: Medial border of the Achilles tendon. Innervated by the medial calcaneal branches of the tibial nerve.
KI-4.etymology: Da (大), great; Zhong (钟), heel. The calcaneus is a very important bone, as it supports the body when standing.
KI-4.clinicalNotes:
1. The Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, runs along the vertebral column and connects with the Pang Guang (Bladder) through its collaterals. For this reason, Da Zhong (KI-4) can be indicated to treat stiffness and pain along the vertebral column and heel pain.

2. The Shen (Kidney) is responsible for reproduction, controls water metabolism, and connects with the Pang Guang (Bladder). Thus, it can be used to treat diseases of the genitourinary system.

3. See Yong Quan (KI-1) and Tai Xi (KI-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-5.locationClassical: On the medial side of the foot, 1 cun directly inferior to KI-3, in the depression anterior to the tuberosity of the calcaneus.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point 1 cun immediately below Tai Xi (KI-3), in the depression at the medial border of the tuberosity of the calcaneus.
KI-5.anatomy: Medial surface of the calcaneus, flexor retinaculum. Innervated by the medial calcaneal branches of the tibial nerve.
KI-5.etymology: Shui (水), water; Quan (泉), spring. The Shen (Kidney) governs the release of water. Shui Quan (KI-5) is the Xi (Cleft) point of the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, and is indicated for cases of dysuria.
KI-5.clinicalNotes: See Da Zhong (KI-4) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-6.category: Confluent Point of the Yin Motility (Yin Qiao) Vessel
KI-6.locationClassical: On the medial side of the ankle, in the depression 1 cun directly inferior to the prominence of the medial malleolus.
howToFind: Seated, locate the point in the depression inferior to the medial malleolus,

4 cun below the intersection of the vertical line passing through the apex of the medial malleolus with the transverse line passing through the base of the medial malleolus, at the transition between light and dark skin.
KI-6.anatomy: Tibialis posterior tendon, flexor digitorum longus muscle. Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
KI-6.etymology: Zhao (照), to shine; Hai (海), sea. Indicated for the treatment of eye disorders.
KI-6.clinicalNotes:
1. It is the opening point of the Yin Qiao Mai. Together with the Yang Qiao Mai, it regulates the physiological cycle of sleep and wakefulness. The symptoms of Yin Qiao Mai disorders are characterized by acute Yin and flaccidity of Yang. Therefore, Zhao Hai (KI-6) can be indicated to treat nocturnal epilepsy and flaccidity of the lower limbs with clubfoot.

2. The Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, penetrates the center of the Fei (Lung). Zhao Hai (KI-6) together with Lie Que (LU-7) form one of the four pairs of Confluent Points. It is indicated to treat thoracodiaphragmatic and laryngopharyngeal diseases. Zhao Hai (KI-6) can treat diseases of the respiratory system, such as cough, asthma, dyspnea, excessive mucus, hemoptysis, and sore throat.

3. See Tai Xi (KI-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Throat disorders, chest tightness, respiratory and urogenital conditions

KI-7.locationClassical: On the medial side of the leg, 2 cun directly superior to KI-3, on the anterior border of the Achilles tendon.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point 2 cun immediately above Tai Xi (KI-3), at the anterior border of the calcaneal tendon.
KI-7.anatomy: Soleus muscle, medial border of the Achilles tendon. Innervated by the medial sural cutaneous nerve and the tibial nerve.
actions: regulates sweating (both spontaneous and night sweats)
KI-7.etymology: Fu (复), return; Liu (溜), current, swift. The point lies above Tai Xi (KI-3). The Qi of the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, makes a turn around the medial malleolus before continuing on to Fu Liu (KI-7).
KI-7.clinicalNotes:
1. Fu Liu (KI-7) has the function of warming the Shen (Kidney) to promote diuresis. The Fei (Lung) is responsible for the skin and body hair and has the function of regulating Ying (nutrition) and Wei (defense). Both Fu Liu (KI-7) and the Fei (Lung) belong to the Metal element. Consequently, needling Fu Liu (KI-7) can treat profuse sweating, anhidrosis, cough, dyspnea, and sensation of cold-heat.

2. See Tai Xi (KI-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-8.category: Xi-Cleft Point of the Yin Motility (Yin Qiao) Vessel
KI-8.locationClassical: On the medial side of the leg, 2 cun superior to KI-3, 0.5 cun anterior to KI-7, posterior to the medial border of the tibia.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point 2 cun above Tai Xi (KI-3) and
5 cun anterior to Fu Liu (KI-7), or at the midpoint between Fu Liu (KI-7) and the posterior border of the tibia.
KI-8.anatomy: Flexor digitorum longus and tibialis posterior muscles. Innervated by the saphenous nerve and the tibial nerve.
actions: Regulates the Conception and Penetrating vessels
clears Heat from the Lower Jiao
tcmIndications: pain on the medial side of the leg
KI-8.etymology: Jiao (交), crossing; Xin (信), faith. Xin is one of the Five Moralities (benevolence, loyalty, courtesy, intelligence, and faith), belongs to Earth, and is connected to the Pi (Spleen). It is the Crossing point with the Spleen-Pancreas Meridian, Foot Tai Yin, at San Yin Jiao (SP-6).
KI-8.clinicalNotes: See Tai Xi (KI-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-9.category: Xi-Cleft Point of the Yin Linking (Yin Wei) Vessel
KI-9.locationClassical: On the medial side of the leg, 5 cun superior to KI-3, on the line connecting KI-3 to KI-10, at the inferior border of the medial belly of the gastrocnemius muscle.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point 5 cun immediately above Tai Xi (KI-3), at the anterior border of the calcaneal tendon.
KI-9.anatomy: Soleus and gastrocnemius muscles. Innervated by the medial sural cutaneous nerve and the tibial nerve.
tcmIndications: pain on the medial side of the leg
westernIndications: Detoxification (drug, alcohol, and heavy metal withdrawal)
KI-9.etymology: Zhu (筑), strong; Bin (宾), knee and leg. The point lies on the medial side of the leg. It has the function of strengthening the knee and leg.
KI-9.clinicalNotes: See Tai Xi (KI-3) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-10.locationClassical: At the medial end of the popliteal crease, between the tendons of the semitendinosus and semimembranosus. Locate with the knee flexed.
howToFind: Seated with the knee flexed, locate the point at the medial end of the transverse popliteal line, between the tendons of the semimembranosus and semitendinosus muscles. (Fig.
KI-10.anatomy: Between the tendons of the semitendinosus and semimembranosus. Innervated by the medial femoral cutaneous nerve.
actions: Clears Damp-Heat from the Lower Jiao
tcmIndications: pain on the medial side of the thigh
KI-10.etymology: Yin (阴), medial side; Gu (谷), valley. The interior is Yin. The point lies medial to the knee joint. The local depression resembles a valley.
KI-10.clinicalNotes:
1. The Shen (Kidney) is responsible for reproduction and controls water metabolism. Yin Gu (KI-10) is indicated to strengthen the Shen (Kidney), regulate menstruation, and relieve water retention. Thus, it is indicated to treat diseases of the genitourinary system caused by deficiency of Kidney Qi.

2. Because the Kidney Meridian ends at the root of the tongue, the point can be indicated to treat persistent protrusion of the tongue with sialorrhea.

3. Deficiency of Kidney Yang can lead to deficiency of Spleen Yang. Thus, gastrointestinal disorders caused by deficiency of both Pi (Spleen) and Shen (Kidney) can be treated with Yin Gu (KI-10).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-11.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-11.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 5 cun below the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-2).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of the upper border of the pubic symphysis or of Qu Gu (CV-2).
KI-11.safetyWarning: Empty the bladder before needling. Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
tcmIndications: Fullness and pain in the lower abdomen
KI-11.etymology: Heng (横) is the ancient name for the pubis; Gu (骨), bone. The point lies at the upper border of the pubis.
KI-11.clinicalNotes: This point lies where the organs of the genitourinary system meet. Based on the principle of local point treatment, this point can treat the diseases mentioned above.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-12.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-12.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 4 cun below the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-3).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 4 cun below the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Zhong Ji (CV-3).
KI-12.safetyWarning: Empty the bladder before needling. Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
actions: regulates the Penetrating and Conception vessels
KI-12.etymology: Da (大), great; He (赫), abundance. This is the Crossing point of the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, with the Chong Mai, the place where the Qi of the Lower Jiao is abundant.
KI-12.clinicalNotes: According to its location, this point is used to treat diseases of the genitourinary and digestive systems.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-13.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-13.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 3 cun below the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-4).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 3 cun below the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Guan Yuan (CV-4).
KI-13.safetyWarning: Empty the bladder before needling. Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
actions: Regulates the Penetrating and Conception vessels
KI-13.etymology: Qi (气), vital Qi; Xue (穴), opening, point. This point lies beside Guan Yuan (CV-4).
KI-13.clinicalNotes: See Da He (KI-12) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-14.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-14.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 2 cun below the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-5).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 2 cun below the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Shi Men (CV-5).
KI-14.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
actions: regulates the Penetrating and Conception vessels
westernIndications: trigger points in the rectus abdominis
KI-14.etymology: Si (四), four; Man (满), fullness. This is the fourth point of the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, located on the abdomen. Indicated in abdominal distension resulting from four causes: hernia, enlargement of the uterus, ascites, and intestinal disorders.
KI-14.clinicalNotes: See Da He (KI-12) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-15.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-15.locationClassical: On the lower abdomen, 1 cun below the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-7).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 1 cun below the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Yin Jiao (CV-7).
KI-15.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
KI-15.etymology: Zhong (中), middle; Zhu (注), to flow. Through this point, the Qi of the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, together with the Qi of the Chong Mai, flows to the uterus.
KI-15.clinicalNotes: See Da He (KI-12) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-16.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-16.locationClassical: On the abdomen, 0.5 cun lateral to the center of the umbilicus (at the level of CV-8).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point
5 cun lateral to the umbilicus, at the level of Shen Que (CV-8).
KI-16.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
tcmIndications: sensation of cold in the abdomen
KI-16.etymology: Huang (肓), peritoneum; Shu (俞), to transport. The Qi of the Shen (Kidney) is introduced into the peritoneum from this point.
KI-16.clinicalNotes: According to its location, this point can be used to treat intestinal diseases. Low back pain at the level of the umbilicus can be assessed with this point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-17.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-17.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 2 cun above the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-10).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 2 cun above the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Xia Wan (CV-10).
KI-17.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
KI-17.etymology: Shang (商), one of the five notes of the ancient five-tone musical scale; Qu (曲), bend. Shang is a musical note belonging to Metal, as is the Da Chang (Large Intestine). This point lies near the bends of the Chang (intestines).
KI-17.clinicalNotes: See Huang Shu (KI-16) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-18.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-18.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 3 cun above the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-11).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 3 cun above the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Jian Li (CV-11).
KI-18.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
KI-18.etymology: Shi (石), stone; Guan (关), obstruction. Shi means hard in consistency. This is an important point for the treatment of abdominal diseases of hardened consistency: constipation, stagnation of Xue (Blood), and infertility.
KI-18.clinicalNotes:
1. Due to its local action, Shi Guan (KI-18) can be used to treat diseases of the digestive system.

2. All points of the Kidney Meridian located on the abdomen connect with the Chong Mai, called the "Sea of Blood." Thus, most of these points can be used to treat gynecological diseases.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-19.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-19.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 4 cun above the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-12).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 4 cun above the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Zhong Wan (CV-12).
KI-19.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
KI-19.etymology: Yin (阴), Yin of Yin-Yang; Du (都), to gather. Yin is related to the abdomen and to the Yin meridians. The point lies on the abdomen, where the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, and the Chong Mai meet.
KI-19.clinicalNotes:
1. Yin Du (KI-19) lies in the epigastrium, so it can be indicated to treat diseases of the digestive system.

2. It strengthens the Shen (Kidney) and the Pi (Spleen) and removes mucus. Therefore, it can be used in the treatment of asthma.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-20.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-20.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 5 cun above the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-13).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 5 cun above the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Shang Wan (CV-13).
KI-20.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity.
KI-20.etymology: Fu (腹), abdomen; Tong (通), passage; Gu (谷), point of influence of the flesh. The point lies on the abdomen, where food passes.
KI-20.clinicalNotes:
1. The point Fu Tong Gu (KI-20) lies in the epigastric region, for which reason it can be used to treat diseases of the digestive system.

2. The Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, flows to the Fei (Lung) and from the Fei (Lung) connects with the Xin (Heart). There is a close relationship between the Shen (Kidney), Fei (Lung), and Xin (Heart). Hence the reason for the use of Fu Tong Gu (KI-20) in the treatment of the diseases mentioned.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-21.category: Meeting Point with the Penetrating (Chong) Vessel
KI-21.locationClassical: On the upper abdomen, 6 cun above the umbilicus, 0.5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (at the level of CV-14).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point 6 cun above the umbilicus,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of Ju Que (CV-14).
KI-21.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the peritoneal cavity (and the enlarged liver, on the right side).
KI-21.etymology: You (幽), pylorus; Men (门), gate. The point belongs to the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, and lies in the epigastric region, the location that corresponds to the pylorus.
KI-21.clinicalNotes:
This point lies in the epigastric region, so it is indicated to treat diseases of the Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach).

The Pi (Spleen) provides the material basis for the acquired constitution, benefits the formation of Qi and Xue (Blood), and removes dampness. Thus, the point can be indicated in the treatment of gynecological diseases and digestive system diseases caused by retention of mucus, secondary to deficiency of Qi of both the Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-22.locationClassical: On the chest, in the fifth intercostal space, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the fifth intercostal space, at the midpoint between the sternal and midclavicular lines, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
tcmIndications: fullness in the chest and hypochondrium
KI-22.etymology: Bu (步), lateral; Lang (廊), corridor. The Qi of the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin, ascends to the chest, one on each side, from this point.
KI-22.clinicalNotes: The point Bu Lang (KI-22) is located in the region of the lung and breasts, thus it can be indicated in the treatment of pulmonary and breast diseases.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-23.locationClassical: On the chest, in the fourth intercostal space, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the fourth intercostal space, at the midpoint between the sternal and midclavicular lines, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
actions: descends rebellious Lung and Stomach Qi
KI-23.etymology: Shen (神), heart; Feng (封), border. The point lies near the Xin (Heart), where the Shen (spirit) is stored.
KI-23.clinicalNotes: See Bu Lang (KI-22) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-24.locationClassical: On the chest, in the third intercostal space, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the third intercostal space, at the midpoint between the sternal and midclavicular lines, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
actions: descends rebellious Lung and Stomach Qi

KI-24.clinicalNotes: See Bu Lang (KI-22) for further details.

KI-25.locationClassical: On the chest, in the second intercostal space, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the second intercostal space, at the midpoint between the sternal and midclavicular lines, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
actions: descends rebellious Lung and Stomach Qi
KI-25.etymology: Shen (神), heart; Cang (藏), storehouse. The point lies near the heart.
KI-25.clinicalNotes: See Bu Lang (KI-22) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-26.locationClassical: On the chest, in the first intercostal space, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the first intercostal space, at the midpoint between the sternal and midclavicular lines, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
westernIndications: pain in the upper chest wall
tags: pain in the upper chest wall
KI-26.etymology: Yu (彧), exuberance; Zhong (中), middle. The point lies near the Fei (Lung), the place where the Qi of the Fei (Lung) is exuberant.
KI-26.clinicalNotes: See Bu Lang (KI-22) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

KI-27.locationClassical: On the chest, in the depression immediately below the inferior border of the clavicle, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the depression below the medial end of the clavicle, at the midpoint between the sternal and midclavicular lines, 2 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
KI-27.anatomy: Pectoralis major muscle, subclavius muscle. Supraclavicular nerves.
KI-27.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Avoid the subclavian vessels.
actions: descends rebellious Lung and Stomach Qi
KI-27.etymology: Shu (俞), point; Fu (府), meeting of Qi and Shen. The Qi of the Shen (Kidney) flows to the Fu organs from this point.
KI-27.clinicalNotes: See Bu Lang (KI-22) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-1.locationClassical: On the chest, in the fourth intercostal space, 5 cun lateral to the anterior midline (approximately 1 cun lateral to the nipple).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the intercostal space of the 4th rib, 1 cun lateral to the nipple.
PC-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, mammary and lymphatic tissues, lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal artery and nerve, pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles, internal thoracic nerve, long thoracic nerve, and lateral thoracic artery.
PC-1.needling: 0.5–0.8 cun obliquely or transversely (subcutaneous) along the path of the intercostal space, in the same direction as or against the channel pathway.
PC-1.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Deep perpendicular insertion is strictly contraindicated. Caution: risk of penetrating the Heart or causing pneumothorax.
tcmIndications: pain in the lateral costal region
pain of the upper limbs from Bi syndrome
rattling in the chest and throat
agitation of the chest and diaphragm
westernIndications: myofascial pain of the pectoralis major muscle
PC-1.etymology: Tian (天), high (heaven); Chi (池), pool (pond). The point lies lateral to the breast, as if the milk produced there originated from a celestial reservoir.
PC-1.clinicalNotes: The point is located on the chest, beside the breast, a region that corresponds to the heart and lung. According to the principle of treating the local point, it is indicated for diseases of the heart, lung, and breasts.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-2.category: Point of the Pericardium primary channel.
PC-2.locationClassical: On the anterior aspect of the arm, 2 cun below the anterior axillary fold, between the two heads of the biceps brachii muscle.
howToFind: With the arm extended and the palmar surface facing up, locate the point 2 cun below the anterior end of the axillary fold, in the biceps brachii muscle, or 7 cun above the cubital fold.
PC-2.anatomy: Biceps brachii muscle, coracobrachialis muscle. Innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve. The brachial artery and vein lie medially.
PC-2.needling: Oblique insertion distally or proximally along the channel line, 1 to 1.5 cun.
tcmIndications: pain in the chest, back, and anterior aspect of the arm
pain in the chest, shoulder, scapula, and arm
fullness of the chest and lateral costal region
pain on the medial aspect of the arm
westernIndications: coronary heart disease (indicated in clinical trials)
PC-2.etymology:
Tian (天), heaven; Quan (泉), spring. The Qi of the meridian originates at Tian Chi (PC-1), flowing downward like a spring of water from the sky.

FIGURE 8.7 – Tian Chi point
PC-2.clinicalNotes: The Pericardium Meridian, Hand Jue Yin, "originates in the chest, emerges, penetrates the pericardium, and communicates with San Jiao." The Fei (Lung) is located in the Upper Jiao, which is why this point is indicated for the treatment of diseases of the Xin (heart) and Fei (Lung). The Foot and Hand Jue Yin Meridians communicate with each other. The Gan (liver) is responsible for the function of the tendons, so the point can be used to treat difficulty walking in the lower limbs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-3.locationClassical: At the elbow, at the midpoint of the transverse cubital crease, on the ulnar border of the biceps brachii tendon, where the pulse of the brachial artery can be palpated.
howToFind: With the elbow slightly flexed and the palmar surface facing up, locate the point on the ulnar side of the biceps brachii tendon, in the middle of the cubital crease.
PC-3.anatomy: Bicipital aponeurosis, pronator teres muscle. The median nerve and brachial artery lie deep to this point. Innervated by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
PC-3.needling: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.0 cun, or pricking to bleed.
PC-3.safetyWarning: Avoid puncture of the brachial artery or direct trauma to the median nerve (which produces a radiating electric-shock sensation). Caution: the brachial artery and veins lie deep, immediately medial to this point.
actions: Clears Heat at the Qi, Ying, and Blood levels
activates the channel to relieve pain
tcmIndications: tremors of the hand and arm
fullness and pain in the chest and lateral costal region
pain in the scapulae, arms, back, and chest
PC-3.etymology: Qu (曲), bend; Ze (澤), marsh (pond). The Qi of the meridian enters the depression of the elbow, with water flowing into a marsh.
PC-3.clinicalNotes: Qu Ze (PC-3) is the He-Sea and Water point of the Pericardium Meridian (Hand Jue Yin), classified in Ling Shu chapter 1. As the He-Sea of a Yin meridian, its classical action is to clear Heat at the Qi, Ying, and Blood levels, cool the Blood, and harmonize the Stomach and intestines, with preferential indication in acute presentations with Heat: febrile disease with restlessness, abrupt vomiting with a sensation of internal heat, acute gastroenteritis, heatstroke, and palpitations with agitation from Heart Fire (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 372–374; Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). The Jia Yi Jing adds hand and arm tremor, cardiac pain, and chest fullness. Common combinations: Qu Ze (PC-3) + Wei Zhong (BL-40) bled in heatstroke and acute gastroenteritis — a classical Yin/Yang He-Sea pairing (Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, Foreign Languages Press, Beijing); with Nei Guan (PC-6) and Zu San Li (ST-36) for vomiting from Stomach Heat; and with Shen Men (HT-7) and Da Ling (PC-7) for palpitations with acute anxiety. It is underused because Nei Guan (PC-6), the Luo point and opening point of the Yin Wei Mai, has dominated the meridian’s cardiovascular and dyspeptic indications. Anatomical caution: the brachial artery pulsates immediately medial to the biceps tendon — palpate the pulse, deflect the insertion, and limit needling to 1.0 cun perpendicular, avoiding arterial puncture and the underlying median nerve. Frequently paired with Tian Quan (PC-2), Jian Shi (PC-5), and Nei Guan (PC-6); see details under those points.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-4.locationClassical: On the palmar aspect of the forearm, 5 cun proximal to the transverse crease of the wrist, on the line connecting PC-3 to PC-7, between the tendons of the palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis muscles.
howToFind: With the arm extended and the palmar surface facing up, locate the point 5 cun above the wrist crease, between the tendon of the palmaris longus and the radial side of the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis.
PC-4.anatomy: Located between the radius, the ulna, and two muscles. Detailed anatomy is not specified in the available sources.
PC-4.needling: Perpendicular insertion 0.5 to 1 cun, or proximal oblique insertion 1 to 1.5 cun.
PC-4.safetyWarning: Deep puncture directly stimulates the median nerve.
actions: principal point for acute painful Blood stasis in the chest and Heart
tcmIndications: heat in the palms of the hands
PC-4.etymology: Xi (郄), cleft; Men (門), gate. Gate through which the Qi of the meridian enters and exits.
PC-4.clinicalNotes: 1. The Xi (cleft) point is used to treat Xue syndromes such as: hematemesis, hemoptysis, epistaxis, and uterine hemorrhage. 2. The Xin Bao (pericardium) envelops the Xin (heart) and protects it from pathogenic factors. As the Pericardium Meridian communicates with the Xin (heart), the point can be used to treat cardiac diseases such as: precordial pain, palpitations, atrial fibrillation, among others. The Xin (heart) controls mental activity, for which reason this point is commonly used to treat mental disorders. 3. The Pericardium Meridian and the Tendinomuscular Meridian of the Hand Jue Yin distribute through the chest; thus, many of its points are used in the treatment of mastitis. 4. This point has the function of eliminating heat and can be used to treat boils.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-5.locationClassical: On the palmar aspect of the forearm, 3 cun proximal to the transverse crease of the wrist, between the tendons of the palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis muscles.
howToFind: With the arm extended and the palmar surface facing up, locate the point 3 cun above Da Ling (PC-7), or 3 cun above the first wrist crease.
PC-5.anatomy: Flexor digitorum superficialis muscle. The median nerve lies directly beneath the point.
PC-5.needling: Perpendicular insertion 0.5 to 1 cun, or proximal oblique insertion 1 to 1.5 cun.
PC-5.safetyWarning: Avoid direct trauma to the median nerve.
actions: transforms Phlegm in the Upper Jiao (predominantly in the Heart)
regulates Stomach function and promotes its descending function
tcmIndications: pain on the medial aspect of the elbow and arm
heat in the palms of the hands
acute collapse syndrome with vomiting and diarrhea
urethral pain or painful urinary dysfunction
westernIndications: angina pectoris (in combination with other points)
PC-5.etymology: Jian (間), space; Shi (使), minister of the monarch. The point lies in the space between the two tendons and has the function of transmitting Qi. It is so called because Xin Bao is the minister of the Xin (heart).
PC-5.clinicalNotes: Jian Shi (PC-5) is the Jing-River and Metal point of the Pericardium Meridian, classified in Ling Shu chapter 1. Its central classical function is to transform Phlegm at the Heart/Pericardium level, open the chest, and calm the Shen — the primary indication for Phlegm-misting-the-Mind patterns (epilepsy with a Phlegm component, manic-depressive disorders, presentations with a thick sticky tongue coating, confused agitation) (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 378–379). It also functions as a classical antimalarial point along the meridian and clears Heat from the Blood, indicated in febrile presentations with a Shen component. Common combinations: Jian Shi (PC-5) + Feng Long (ST-40) + Zhong Wan (CV-12) for Heart-Phlegm patterns; Jian Shi (PC-5) + Shen Men (HT-7) for anxious agitation with a Phlegm-Heat aspect; Jian Shi (PC-5) + Da Zhui (GV-14) as the classical historical antimalarial pairing. It is eclipsed by Nei Guan (PC-6), the Pericardium Luo and opening point of the Yin Wei Mai, for chest and gastric complaints (PC-6 dominates nausea, dyspepsia, cardiovascular palpitations); and by Qu Ze (PC-3), the He-Sea, for acute Heart Heat presentations — hence the restricted modern use of Jian Shi to the Phlegm-Mind-Heart indication. Perpendicular insertion of 0.5–1.0 cun, between the tendons of palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis; mind the underlying median nerve.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-6.locationClassical: On the palmar aspect of the forearm, 2 cun proximal to the transverse crease of the wrist, between the tendons of the palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis muscles.
howToFind: With the arm extended and the palmar surface facing up, locate the point 2 cun above Da Ling (PC-7) or 2 cun above the wrist crease.
PC-6.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm, palmar branch of the median nerve, median antebrachial vein, flexor digitorum superficialis muscle, tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus, and median nerve.
PC-6.needling: Perpendicularly 0.5 cun, or obliquely upward 0.1 cun.
PC-6.safetyWarning: Caution: the median nerve lies directly beneath this point. Insert slowly to avoid an electric-shock sensation.
actions: descends rebellious Qi (principal point for nausea and vomiting)
regulates the Qi and Blood of the Heart
descends rebellious Qi of the Lung and Stomach
tcmIndications: preeminent point for pain and disorders in the thoracic and epigastric regions
alterations in heart rate and rhythm
balancing effect on anxiety and agitation
westernIndications: Principal distal point for nausea (motion sickness, morning sickness, chemotherapy-induced nausea)
PC-6.etymology: Nei (內), Inner; Guan (關), strategy. The point lies on the anterior aspect of the forearm and "has the function of internal strategy."
PC-6.clinicalNotes: The Pericardium Meridian communicates with the San Jiao, and its collateral branch with the Xin (heart). The Xin (heart) and Fei (lung) are located in the Upper Jiao, the Pi (spleen) and Wei (stomach) in the Middle Jiao, and the Gan (liver) and Shen (kidney) in the Lower Jiao. Therefore, the point can be used to treat diseases of the Xin (heart) and Fei (lung) in the Upper Jiao, such as: precordial pain, palpitations, thoracic fullness, and dyspnea, with excellent therapeutic effect. It is the point of choice in the treatment of epigastric pain, epigastric distension, and vomiting, since the Pi (spleen) and Wei (stomach) are located in the Middle Jiao.
