Indicated in the treatment of menstrual irregularity, hyperemesis gravidarum, postpartum vertigo, and nocturnal emission, as it treats disorders in the Lower Jiao.

combinations.indication: Nausea, vomiting, digestive disorders
Insomnia, anxiety, palpitations, calming the mind
Chest and heart disorders, stomach pain, gynecological conditions

PC-7.locationClassical: At the wrist joint, in the depression at the center of the transverse wrist crease, between the tendons of the palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis muscles.
howToFind: With the arm extended and the palmar surface facing up, locate the point in the middle of the wrist crease, between the tendon of the palmaris longus and the ulnar side of the flexor carpi tendon.
PC-7.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm, palmar branch of the median nerve, median antebrachial vein, palmar carpal branches of the radial and ulnar arteries, palmar carpal ligament, pronator quadratus muscle, tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus, and median nerve.
PC-7.needling: Perpendicular insertion 0.3 to 0.5 cun. For carpal tunnel syndrome, distal oblique insertion along the tunnel, 0.5 to 1 cun.
PC-7.safetyWarning: High risk of injury to the median nerve with aggressive manipulation. Caution: the median nerve lies directly beneath this point. Puncture often produces an intense electrical sensation; once triggered, any further manipulation is inappropriate and may injure the nerve.
actions: clears Heart Fire and calms the Shen
reduces excess Heat or Fire of the Pericardium
unblocks the Qi of the chest
westernIndications: enthesopathy of the lower forearm region
PC-7.etymology: Da (大), great; Ling (陵), mound. The lunate bone is prominent, like a mound. The point lies in the depression proximal to the prominence of the wrist.
PC-7.clinicalNotes: With application similar to Nei Guan (PC-6), this point is frequently combined with Nei Guan (PC-6) or Jian Shi (PC-5). The choice of two or more points on the same meridian, with the same function, aims to enhance the curative effect.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-8.locationClassical: On the palm of the hand, in the depression between the second and third metacarpal bones. When the fist is clenched, the point lies where the tip of the middle finger touches the palm.
howToFind: With the hand closed and the fingers flexed, press the palmar crease with the tips of the middle and ring fingers. Locate the point between the second and third metacarpals, on the radial side of the third metacarpal.
PC-8.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, palmar branch of the median nerve, branches of the palmar vein, palmar aponeurosis, superficial and deep palmar arterial arches, median nerve, adductor pollicis muscle, and lumbrical muscles.
PC-8.safetyWarning: Highly sensitive and painful point. Use finer needles, as puncture of this point can be quite painful.
actions: Clears Heat of the Pericardium and Heart
clears Heart Fire and calms the Shen
clears the Ying-nutritive level and cools Blood
tcmIndications: sweating of the palms of the hands
pain in the chest and lateral costal region
spasms and pain in the elbows and arms
redness and pain of the eye
westernIndications: desquamation of the palm of the hand (palmar dermatopathies)
PC-8.etymology: Lao (勞), labor; Gong (宮), center. The hand is for labor and Lao refers to the hand. The point lies in the center of the palm of the hand.
PC-8.clinicalNotes: This point has the function of eliminating heat, inducing resuscitation, calming the mind, and relieving pain. It can be used to treat headache, trigeminal neuralgia, wind attack, fever, dyspnea, aphthae, and mental disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

PC-9.locationClassical: At the tip of the middle finger, in the center, approximately 0.1 cun from the free margin of the nail. Some texts locate the point at the radial border of the nail root.
howToFind: With the palmar surface facing up, locate the point at the tip of the middle finger,
1 cun above the upper border of the nail.
PC-9.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, proper palmar digital branch of the median nerve, and proper palmar digital arteries.
PC-9.needling: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun, or pricking to bleed.
PC-9.safetyWarning: Extremely painful point. Caution: puncture of this point is very painful.
actions: clears the Heart and benefits the tongue
clears Heat (especially of the Heart and Pericardium)
tcmIndications: rigidity and edema of the tongue
loss of consciousness with rigidity of the tongue
pain at the root of the tongue
PC-9.etymology: Zhong (中), middle; Chong (衝), gushing. The point lies at the tip of the middle finger, where the Qi of the meridian originates and gushes upward along the meridian.
PC-9.clinicalNotes: See Shao Shang (LU-11) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-1.locationClassical: On the ulnar side of the ring finger, a small distance from the corner of the nail. Specifically, 0.1 cun from the ulnar corner of the nail.
howToFind: With the palmar surface facing down, locate the point at the intersection of the lines passing through the ulnar border and the base of the nail of the ring finger.
TE-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, dorsal digital nerve and vein, dorsal branches of the proper palmar digital branches of the ulnar nerve and proper palmar digital arteries, and the fourth distal phalanx (distal phalanx of the ring finger).
TE-1.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion directed proximally, 0.1–0.2 cun, or pricking to bleed.
actions: Clears Heat of the Upper Jiao
tcmIndications: diseases on the side of the head and diseases of the eyes and ears (general indications of the channel).
TE-1.etymology: Guan (关), strategy; Chong (冲), gushing. Qi exits this point rapidly as if gushing. Strategic departure point of Qi for the three Yang meridians of the Hand.
TE-1.clinicalNotes:
Point used in emergency treatments. Indicated to treat fever, stroke, heatstroke, and coma or loss of consciousness, by promoting bleeding. It is used to treat numbness in the tips of the fingers.

Shao Shang (LU-11), Shang Yang (LI-1), Zhong Chong (PC-9), Guan Chong (TE-1), Shao Chong (HT-9), Shao Ze (SI-1) on both hands are called the Twelve Jing (Well) Points. They are used to awaken the patient from unconsciousness, sedate the meridians and collaterals, and eliminate perverse heat. Used to treat coma, loss of consciousness, numbness in the tips of the fingers, and fever. Clinically, each one has its own characteristics.

Shao Shang (LU-11) is used to improve Qi flow in the Fei (lung) and resolve Biao syndrome. Relieve sore throat and eliminate heat.

Shang Yang (LI-1) is used to eliminate accumulated heat in the Yang Ming, relieve sore throat, and exterior syndrome.

Zhong Chong (PC-9) is used to eliminate heat in the Xin (heart), to tranquilize the mind and eliminate heat stagnation in the Xin Bao (Pericardium) and to awaken the patient from the state of unconsciousness (its main function).

Guan Chong (TE-1) is used to eliminate heat in the Upper Jiao and heat stagnation in the Hand Shao Yang Meridian. It is effective in treating diseases of the ears and eyes.

Shao Chong (HT-9) is used to eliminate and remove fire from the Xin (heart), tranquilize the mind, eliminate stagnant heat, and stimulate the Qi of the Xin (heart).

Shao Ze (SI-1) is used to eliminate heat from the Xin (heart), improve irritability, and promote lactation.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-2.locationClassical: With the hand slightly clenched, in the depression between the metacarpophalangeal joints of the ring finger and little finger, proximal to the margin of the interdigital fold.
howToFind: With the fingers slightly flexed and the palmar surface facing down, locate the point in the cleft at the level of the intersection between the little and ring fingers, at the transition of light and dark skin.
TE-2.anatomy: Fourth dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the dorsal digital nerve from the ulnar nerve.
TE-2.needling: Vertical insertion up to 0.5 cun. Alternatively, proximal oblique insertion of 0.2 to 0.3 cun.
actions: Clears Heat of the Upper Jiao
benefits the ears and calms the shen and opens the channel and relieves pain.
tcmIndications: pain in the hand and arm
Psychoneurological disorders due to Heat and local channel problems. Deafness and otalgia.
TE-2.etymology: Ye (液), water; Men (門), gate. It has the function of regulating the passage of water, like a gate.
TE-2.clinicalNotes: This point is effective in diseases and symptoms of the head, face, and the five sense organs, because the distribution of the meridian is in the ears, eyes, and throat. Its tendinomuscular meridian penetrates connecting with the root of the tongue. See Wai Guan (TE-5) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-3.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the hand, in the depression just proximal to the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of the 4th and 5th fingers.
howToFind: With the palmar surface facing down, locate the point 1 cun below Ye Men (TE-2), in the depression posterior to the 4th and 5th metacarpals.
TE-3.anatomy: Fourth dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve.
actions: benefits the ears (principal distal point for ear disorders)
activates the channel and relieves pain
Reduces and clears excess Heat of the Triple Energizer channel in the upper part of the body.
tcmIndications: swelling and pain of the eyes
TE-3.etymology: Zhong (中), middle; Zhu (渚), small portion of land in the water. The point lies in the middle of the Five Shu Points and the Qi of the meridian flows like water along the banks.
TE-3.clinicalNotes:
Point used to treat pain in the spine, shoulder, and back. It can be employed to drain and activate the meridians and collaterals, eliminate wind, and promote analgesia. This point is used to treat pain in the dorsal region.

By the rule that indications follow the principle of the meridian pathway, the point can also be used to treat disorders of the head, face, and sense organs. The treatment of headache by points of the San Jiao Meridian refers, in particular, to migraine resulting from Qi stagnation. The San Jiao Meridian distributes in the parietal region and "is used for diseases consequent to Qi dysfunction."

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-4.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the wrist. In the depression of the transverse carpal crease, between the third and fourth metacarpals.
howToFind: With the palmar surface facing down, locate the point in the depression at the intersection between the proximal portion of the 3rd and 4th metacarpal bones and the dorsal carpal crease, or at the ulnocarpal joint, between the tendons of the extensor digitorum communis and the extensor proprius of the 5th finger.
TE-4.anatomy: Extensor retinaculum, tendon of the extensor digiti minimi muscle. Innervated by the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve and the posterior interosseous nerve.
actions: Relaxes the tendons and relieves pain
tcmIndications: redness and swelling of the eyes
TE-4.etymology: Yang (阳), Yang of Yin Yang; Chi (池), pool. The point lies in the depression posterior to the wrist: the Qi of the Meridian flows like water in a pool.
TE-4.clinicalNotes: Yuan (Source) point of the San Jiao Meridian. The Yuan (Source) Qi travels throughout the body via the San Jiao. This point has an intimate relationship with the Yuan Qi and is an important point to regulate it, and can be used to treat enuresis and pediatric diseases. See Wai Guan (TE-5) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-5.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the forearm, 2 cun proximal to the dorsal carpal crease (TE-4), between the radius and the ulna.
howToFind: With the arm extended and pronated, locate the point 2 cun immediately above the midpoint of the dorsal wrist crease, between the ulna and the radius, opposite Nei Guan (PC-6).
TE-5.anatomy: Motor point of the extensor pollicis longus muscle. Between the ulna and the radius. The dorsal antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the posterior interosseous nerve. The posterior interosseous artery and vein.
TE-5.needling: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.0 cun (often needled through to PC-6 Neiguan).
actions: Expels Wind and releases the exterior (principal point for Wind-Heat)
activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: fever and itching of the ear.
westernIndications: Carpal tunnel syndrome (when combined with PC-6).
TE-5.etymology: Wai (外), lateral; Guan (关), strategy. The point lies at a vital location on the lateral aspect of the humerus.
TE-5.clinicalNotes:
1. It is a Confluence point, communicating with the Yang Wei Mai. The Yang Wei Mai connects with Yang and transmits in a network throughout the body. It is one of the principal points for eliminating external pathogenic factors and eliminating heat in the treatment of the common cold, fever, and symptoms of malaria.

2. A point widely used to treat headache and ocular and auditory disorders, due to the fact that the Shao Yang Meridian distributes along the lateral aspect of the hand, eye, and ear.

3. Needling the point produces a perceptible effect in activating Qi to eliminate stagnation. It can be used for fullness and pain in the chest and hypochondrium, dysfunction of the gastrointestinal tract, depressive disorder, irritability, and susceptibility to anger.

combinations.indication: Temporal headache, ear disorders, hypochondriac pain

TE-6.locationClassical: 3 cun proximal to the dorsal carpal crease (Yangchi TE-4), in the depression between the radius and the ulna, on the radial side of the extensor digitorum communis muscle.
howToFind: With the arm extended and pronated, locate the point 3 cun immediately above the middle of the dorsal wrist crease, between the ulna and the radius, opposite Jian Shi (PC-5).
TE-6.anatomy: Motor point of the extensor pollicis longus muscle. Between the ulna and the radius. The dorsal antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the posterior interosseous nerve. The posterior interosseous artery and vein.
actions: Regulates the Qi of the Triple Energizer
clears Heat in the three Jiao
benefits the chest and lateral costal region

Clears and facilitates the Qi dynamic of the Triple Energizer. The most important point of the Triple Energizer channel for moving Qi and clearing Heat in the three Jiao (upper, middle and lower). Drains ministerial fire of the three Jiao and resolves stagnant Heat of the Liver and Gallbladder.
TE-6.etymology: Zhi (支), limb; Gou (沟), ditch. Zhi refers to the upper limb. The point lies between the radius and the ulna.
TE-6.clinicalNotes:
1. This is the most important point for Qi stimulation, used in the treatment of distension in the hypochondrium, irritability, gastrointestinal diseases, and gynecological diseases caused by Qi stagnation. It is a frequently chosen point for chronic constipation.

2. The point promotes the circulation of Qi, while Wai Guan (TE-5) is employed to stimulate Qi to improve depressive disorders and eliminate heat, eliminate stagnation, eliminate fever, and resolve Biao syndrome.

3. Both can be used to treat gastrointestinal diseases through stimulation of Qi and removal of stagnation.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-7.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the forearm, 3 cun proximal to the dorsal carpal crease, approximately one finger-width ulnar to TE-6, on the radial border of the ulna.
howToFind: With the arm extended and pronated, locate the point 3 cun above the dorsal transverse crease of the wrist, on the ulnar side of Zhi Gou (TE-6) and on the radial border of the ulna.
TE-7.anatomy: Extensor digiti minimi and extensor carpi ulnaris muscles. Innervated by the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the posterior interosseous nerve.
tcmIndications: pain in the arm and skin
Tinnitus (when used together with other points).
TE-7.etymology: Hui (会), meeting, confluence; Zong (宗), family, several. This point is indicated to treat hearing deficit because the ear is a place where various meridians and collaterals converge.
TE-7.clinicalNotes: See Wai Guan (TE-5) and Zhi Gou (TE-6) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-8.category: Meeting Point of the Three Yang Channels of the Arm (Sanjiao
TE-8.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the forearm, 4 cun proximal to the dorsal carpal crease, between the radius and the ulna.
howToFind: With the arm extended and pronated, locate the point 4 cun immediately above the midpoint of the dorsal wrist crease, between the ulna and the radius.
TE-8.anatomy: Extensor digitorum communis and abductor pollicis longus muscles. Innervated by the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the posterior interosseous nerve.
TE-8.needling: Vertical or oblique insertion up to 1.5 cun.
actions: activates the channel and relieves pain
opens the channel and the luo-connecting vessels and relieves pain.
tcmIndications: pain in the hand and arm
TE-8.etymology: San Yang (三阳), three Yang meridians of the hand; Luo (絡), connection. This point connects the three Yang meridians of the hand.
TE-8.clinicalNotes: See Wai Guan (TE-5) and Zhi Gou (TE-6) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-9.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the forearm, 5 cun distal to the olecranon, between the radius and the ulna.
howToFind: With the arm extended and pronated, locate the point 7 cun above the dorsal wrist crease, or 5 cun distal to the olecranon, between the ulna and the radius.
TE-9.anatomy: Extensor digitorum communis and extensor carpi ulnaris muscles. Innervated by the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the posterior interosseous nerve.
TE-9.etymology: Si (四), four; Du (瀆), river. The Yangtze, Yellow, Huai He, and Ji Shui rivers were called Si Du in ancient times. The point lies between the radius and the ulna, as if it were a river.
TE-9.clinicalNotes: See Wai Guan (TE-5) and Zhi Gou (TE-6) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-10.locationClassical: With the elbow flexed, in the depression 1 cun proximal to the olecranon.
howToFind: With the hand on the hip and the elbow flexed, locate the point in the depression 1 cun posterior and superior to the olecranon.
TE-10.anatomy: Tendon of the triceps brachii muscle. Innervated by the posterior brachial cutaneous nerve and the radial nerve.
actions: clears Heat of the Triple Energizer
tcmIndications: pain in the chest and hypochondrium
TE-10.etymology: Tian (天), heaven, upper part; Jing (井), well. The point lies 1 cun above the elbow (upper portion, Tian). At this location there is a small depression like a well.
TE-10.clinicalNotes: This point eliminates heat and tranquilizes the mind, activates the meridians, and removes "masses." Thus, it is used to treat cough and expectoration with blood and pus, inflammation of the throat, edema of the face, precordial pain, and hearing deficit caused by the fire of San Jiao.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-11.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the arm, 1 cun proximal to TE-10 (2 cun proximal to the olecranon).
howToFind: With the hand on the hip and the elbow flexed, locate the point 2 cun posterior and superior to the olecranon and 1 cun immediately above Tian Jing (TE-10).
TE-11.anatomy: Triceps brachii muscle. Innervated by the posterior brachial cutaneous nerve and the radial nerve.
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and arm
TE-11.etymology: Qing (清), cool; Leng (冷), deep, depression; Yuan (渊), deep water. This point is useful for treating headache and difficulty abducting the shoulder due to attack by pathological cold.
TE-11.clinicalNotes: The ancient physicians considered it useful to treat headache, common cold, and difficulty abducting the shoulder due to attack by pathogenic wind.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-12.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the arm, midway between TE-11 and TE-13, on the line connecting the olecranon and TE-14.
howToFind: Seated, with the upper limb relaxed, first locate Nao Hui (TE-13) at the intersection between the humerus and the posteroinferior border of the deltoid muscle. Locate TE-12 at the midpoint of the line connecting Qing Leng Yuan (TE-11) and Nao Hui (TE-13).
TE-12.anatomy: Triceps brachii muscle (lateral head). Innervated by the posterior brachial cutaneous nerve and the radial nerve.
actions: Activates the channel and relieves pain
TE-12.etymology: Xiao (消), receding water; Luo (濼), shallow lake, marsh. This point is a small depression and has the function of regulating the passage of waters.
TE-12.clinicalNotes: This point is used mainly to treat pain. The indications follow the principle of the meridian pathway.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-13.category: Meeting Point of the Sanjiao and Yang Linking (Yang Wei) Vessel
TE-13.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the arm, 3 cun distal to the lateral end of the acromion (TE-14), on the line connecting TE-14 and the olecranon, at the junction of this line with the margin of the deltoid muscle.
howToFind: With the elbow relaxed, locate the point 3 cun below Jian Liao (TE-14), which lies on the posterior aspect of the shoulder, on the same line as Tian Jing (TE-10).
TE-13.anatomy: Posterior border of the deltoid, lateral head of the triceps. Innervated by the posterior brachial cutaneous nerve and the radial nerve.
TE-13.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion of 1 to 2 cun.
actions: activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: pain in the shoulder and arm
Stiffness and pain of the nape and back with inability to turn the head
pain in the shoulder and arm
westernIndications: myofascial trigger points in the deltoid
TE-13.etymology: Nao (臑), arm; Hui (会), meeting point. The point lies on the muscular prominence of the arm. Meeting point of the Hand Shao Yang Meridian with the Yang Wei Mai, hence called the meeting of the arm.
TE-13.clinicalNotes: This is one of the points commonly used to treat pain in the arm and scapula. Its needling promotes drainage and activation of the meridian, regulating the flow of Qi to promote analgesia. See Wai Guan (TE-5) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-14.locationClassical: On the posterior aspect of the shoulder, in the depression posterior and inferior to the acromion. With the arm abducted at 90 degrees, it is in the posterior depression (LI-15 lies in the anterior depression).
howToFind: With the arm abducted, locate the point in the posterior depression of the shoulder joint.
With the shoulder relaxed, locate the point 2 cun immediately below the posterior border of the acromioclavicular joint, between the acromion and the greater tubercle of the humerus.
TE-14.anatomy: Motor point of the posterior deltoid. Muscular branch of the axillary nerve. Muscular branch of the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
TE-14.needling: With the affected arm abducted, insert the needle perpendicularly between the acromion and the greater tubercle of the humerus, pointing toward Jiquan (HT-1), for 1 to 1.5 cun.
tcmIndications: Pain and motor impairment of the shoulder and arm
Capsulitis of the shoulder, frozen shoulder.
TE-14.etymology: Jian (肩), shoulder; Liao (髎), cleft, foramen. The point is a foramen in the shoulder.
TE-14.clinicalNotes: Point used to treat pain and difficulty moving the shoulder. Used in combination with Jian Yu (LI-15) to promote the circulation of Qi and Xue around the shoulder. An additional needle between Jian Liao (TE-14) and Jian Yu (LI-15) is frequently used, providing better effects. The three points together are called "Jian San Zhen."

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-15.locationClassical: In the supraspinous region, in the depression midway between GB-21 and SI-13, over the superior angle of the scapula.
howToFind: With the shoulder relaxed, locate the point at the superomedial angle of the scapula.
TE-15.anatomy: Trapezius and levator scapulae muscles. Innervated by the accessory nerve and the dorsal scapular nerve.
TE-15.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion directed inferiorly, 0.5–1.0 cun.
TE-15.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Deep perpendicular or anterior insertion is contraindicated.
actions: activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: Pain in the shoulder and neck
Pain in the shoulder and arm
stiffness and pain in the neck
pain in the supraclavicular fossa. Agitation and oppression in the chest
heat and fullness in the chest
oppression of the Heart with absence of sweating
heat in the body with absence of sweating
chills and fever and febrile diseases.
westernIndications: trigger points in the upper trapezius
TE-15.etymology: Tian (天), heaven, upper part; Liao (髎), cleft, foramen. The point lies in a foramen above the scapula.
TE-15.clinicalNotes: The point corresponds to the projection of the apex of the lung on the chest, located near the shoulder and neck. The indications follow the principle of the local point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-16.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the neck, directly below the posterior border of the mastoid process, at the level of the angle of the mandible and on the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle.
howToFind: Seated, with the head erect, locate the point at the level of the angle of the mandible, on the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
TE-16.anatomy: Posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM), splenius capitis. Innervated by the lesser occipital nerve and the great auricular nerve.
TE-16.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the great cervical vessels.
actions: Benefits the head and the sense organs, regulates and descends Qi.
TE-16.etymology: Tian (天), heaven, upper part; You (牖), window. Treats diseases in the cephalic segment.
TE-16.clinicalNotes: Crossing point of the Hand and Foot Shao Yang Meridians with the Yang Wei Mai. The San Jiao Meridian passes along the posterior border of the ear. A branch penetrates the ear and emerges at the lateral commissure of the eyelid. This tendinomuscular meridian runs along the root of the tongue. It can be used to treat sore throat and disorders of the sense organs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-17.category: Meeting Point of the Sanjiao and Gall Bladder Channels
TE-17.locationClassical: Posterior to the earlobe, in the depression between the mastoid process and the angle of the mandible.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, with the earlobe folded slightly inward, the point is located anterior to the mastoid process.
TE-17.anatomy: The external jugular vein, the great auricular nerve, the trunk of the facial nerve (located more deeply at its emergence from the stylomastoid foramen), and the posterior auricular artery.
TE-17.needling: Insert the needle 0.5 to 1 cun toward the contralateral eyeball (to treat facial paralysis).
TE-17.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may cause an electric-shock sensation owing to the facial nerve.
actions: Benefits the ears (principal local point for all ear disorders)
tcmIndications: otalgia and purulent discharge of the ear.
westernIndications: Facial nerve paralysis and temporomandibular arthritis.
TE-17.etymology: Yi (翳), verb meaning to shelter, hide, protect; Feng (風), pathogenic wind. The point lies behind the earlobe in a location sheltered from pathogenic wind.
TE-17.clinicalNotes:
1. An important point for treating diseases of the head, face, and sense organs. It has the function of eliminating wind and heat and draining the meridians and collaterals. It can be needled in different directions to treat different diseases.

2. Needling toward Xia Guan (ST-7), the Qi sensation may radiate to the ear region and to the anterior part of the tongue. Used to treat diseases of the ear, tongue, and jaw.

3. Needling toward Da Ying (ST-5), the Qi sensation may reach the lower dental arch. Used to treat diseases of this region.

4. Needling toward the tip of the nose, the Qi sensation may reach the throat, treating cough resulting from local itching. It can be employed to treat diseases of the throat and cheek region.

5. Due to stagnation of perverse heat, a small local bleeding upon withdrawal of the needle may produce a better effect in the treatment of hearing deficit, tinnitus, and mumps.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-18.locationClassical: Posterior to the ear, at the center of the mastoid process, in the lower third of the curve connecting TE-17 and TE-20.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point at the intersection of the retroauricular hairline and the line of the opening of the external auditory canal.
TE-18.anatomy: Posterior auricular muscle. Innervated by the great auricular nerve. Posterior auricular artery.
TE-18.etymology: Chi (瘈), convulsion; Mai (脉), blood vessel. The point lies behind the ear, where the collaterals are distributed. It is used for the treatment of convulsions.
TE-18.clinicalNotes: Used principally to treat hearing disorders. For infantile convulsion, vomiting, diarrhea, and dysentery, bleeding methods can be employed by needling the point or the smaller collaterals around the point with three-edged needles. It can also be used in the treatment of emergencies.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-19.locationClassical: Posterior to the ear, in the upper third of the curve connecting TE-17 and TE-20, posterior to the root of the auricle.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point on the posterior auricular hairline, at the midpoint of the line connecting Chi Mai (TE-18) and Jiao Sun (TE-20) along the helix.
TE-19.anatomy: Posterior auricular muscle. Innervated by the lesser occipital nerve. Posterior auricular artery.
TE-19.etymology: Lu (顱), fontanelle; Xi (息), sign. Note: there is a translation error here in Chinese. The point lies on the skull and is used to treat infantile convulsion.
TE-19.clinicalNotes: See Chi Mai (TE-18) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-20.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, directly at the level of the apex of the ear when it is folded forward.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, folding the ear forward, locate the point on the hairline, immediately above the ear. This area is felt when opening or closing the mouth.
TE-20.anatomy: The branches of the auriculotemporal nerve containing fibers from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve innervate the skin.
TE-20.needling: Transverse insertion 0.5–1.5 cun; inserted in the subcutaneous layers near the bone of the skull, directed toward the disorder. Or horizontal insertion of 0.3 to 0.5 cun.
actions: Benefits the ears and eyes and clears Heat, especially of the mouth.
tcmIndications: redness and pain of the eyes
purulent discharge of the ear and redness and swelling at the back of the ear.
westernIndications: tension headache in the temporal muscle
TE-20.etymology: Jiao (角), angle; Sun (孫), small vessel (at the apex of the ear). The point lies in the temporal region, corresponding to the apex of the ear, where the network of meridians is distributed.
TE-20.clinicalNotes: This point removes heat and eliminates wind. The combination of bleeding and moxibustion with the method of sedation by filiform needles is effective and frequently used.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-21.locationClassical: In the middle of the depression anterior to the supratragic notch and slightly superior to the condyloid process of the mandible. Located with the mouth open.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, with the mouth slightly open, locate the point in the depression anterior to the notch above the tragus,
5 cun cranial to the line of Lu Xi (TE-19).
TE-21.anatomy: Temporomandibular joint capsule. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve. The superficial temporal artery and vein are directly adjacent/anterior.
TE-21.needling: Insert the needle perpendicularly and slightly downward toward Tinggong (SI-19) and Tinghui (GB-2), 1.5 to 2.5 cun. Or 0.5 cun perpendicularly or subcutaneously in a caudal direction. Needled with the mouth open.
TE-21.safetyWarning: Take care with the superficial temporal artery and vein. Ensure that the patient does not abruptly close the jaw during needling.
tcmIndications: pain from dental caries and temporomandibular arthritis.
TE-21.etymology: Er (耳), ear; Men (門), gate. The point lies in front of the ear and functions as a gate to it.
TE-21.clinicalNotes: Point used for the treatment of ear disorders, according to the theory of the local point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-22.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, at the level of the root of the auricle, posterior to the superficial temporal artery.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point anterosuperior to Er Men (TE-21), at the same level as the root of the ear, at the location where the pulsation of the artery can be felt, on the posterior border of the hairline, at the temple.
TE-22.anatomy: Temporalis muscle. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve and the temporal branches of the facial nerve.
TE-22.safetyWarning: Avoid the superficial temporal artery, which is palpable at this location.
westernIndications: myofascial pain in the temporalis muscle
TE-22.etymology: Er (耳), ear; He (和), harmony; Liao (髎), foramen. The point lies in the depression in front of the tragus, used to improve hearing.
TE-22.clinicalNotes: Point indicated for excess syndrome by eliminating heat and expelling wind.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

TE-23.locationClassical: On the face, in the depression at the lateral end of the eyebrow.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point at the lateral border of the zygomatic process on the frontal bone, in the depression at the end of the eyebrow.
TE-23.anatomy: Orbicularis oculi muscle. Innervated by the zygomaticotemporal nerve and the facial nerve.
TE-23.needling: Transverse (subcutaneous) insertion directed posteriorly or medially, 0.3–0.5 cun.
TE-23.safetyWarning: Vascular area; prone to bruising. According to several classical texts, this point is contraindicated to moxibustion.
tcmIndications: redness and pain of the eyes
TE-23.etymology: Sizhu (絲竹), thin bamboo (indicates eyebrow); Kong (空), cleft. The point lies at the lateral end of the eyebrow, in a depression.
TE-23.clinicalNotes: The point is located in the eye region. Used principally to treat diseases of the head and eyes. Si Zhu Kong (TE-23) is needled directed toward Shuai Gu (GB-8) to treat migraines, and from Si Zhu Kong (TE-23) toward Zan Zhu (BL-2) to treat pain in the forehead.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-1.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-1.locationClassical: On the face, in the depression on the lateral aspect of the orbit, approximately 0.5 cun lateral to the outer canthus of the eye.
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest and the eyes closed, locate the point
5 cun lateral to the lateral margin of the orbit, in the depression beside the lateral commissure of the eyelid.
GB-1.anatomy: Orbicularis oculi muscle. Innervated by the zygomaticofacial nerve (trigeminal) and the facial nerve.
GB-1.needling: Transverse (subcutaneous) insertion directed posteriorly or toward neighboring points (e.g., Taiyang), 0.3–0.5 cun.
GB-1.safetyWarning: Highly vascular area; prone to bruising.
tcmIndications: Redness and pain in the eyes
deviation of the mouth and eye
GB-1.etymology: Tong Zi (瞳子), pupil; Liao (髎), foramen. The point is located in the depression beside the lateral commissure of the eyelid, at the level of the pupil.
GB-1.clinicalNotes:
This point is located around the eyes and has the function of eliminating wind and heat, improving vision, and relieving ocular pain. It is generally used in the treatment of eye diseases.

Chronic headache can be treated by the bleeding method, which has the function of activating the flow of Qi in the meridians and collaterals.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-2.locationClassical: On the face, anterior to the intertragic notch, on the posterior border of the condyloid process of the mandible. Locate with the mouth open.
howToFind: Seated with the head at rest or in lateral decubitus. With the mouth open, locate the point in the depression posterior to the condyloid process of the mandible.
GB-2.anatomy: Parotid gland, temporomandibular joint capsule. Innervated by the great auricular nerve and the facial nerve. The superficial temporal artery and vein lie adjacent.
GB-2.needling: With the patient’s mouth open, perpendicular insertion 0.5–1.0 cun.
GB-2.safetyWarning: Take care with the superficial temporal vessels. Instruct the patient not to forcefully close the jaw while the needle is inserted.
tcmIndications: motor impairment of the temporomandibular joint
GB-2.etymology: Ting (听), hearing; Hui (会), convergence/capacity. The point is located anterior to the ear. Its function is to treat hearing impairment.
GB-2.clinicalNotes: It has the function of arousing and calming the mind and improving hearing.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-3.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-3.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, anterior to the ear, in the depression directly above ST-7, on the upper border of the zygomatic arch.
howToFind: Seated with the head at rest or in lateral decubitus. With the mouth open, locate the point in the preauricular region, in the upper sulcus of the zygomatic arch, immediately above Xia Guan (ST-7).
GB-3.anatomy: Temporalis muscle and fascia. Innervated by the zygomaticotemporal nerve and the facial nerve.
GB-3.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may cause significant discomfort.
tcmIndications: deviation of the mouth and eye
GB-3.etymology: Shang (上), upper; Guan (关), boundary or gate. Guan refers to the zygomatic arch. The point is located on the upper margin of the zygomatic arch.
GB-3.clinicalNotes: Promotes the circulation of Qi flow in the meridians and clears the mind.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-4.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-4.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, within the hairline, at the junction of the upper one-quarter and lower three-quarters of the curved line connecting ST-8 and GB-7.
howToFind: Seated with the head at rest or in lateral decubitus. Locate the point 1 cun inferior and posterior to Tou Wei (ST-8). At this site, a slight movement is perceived during chewing.
GB-4.anatomy: Temporalis muscle. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve. Branches of the superficial temporal artery.
tcmIndications: pain at the outer canthus of the eye
westernIndications: myofascial pain in the temporalis muscle
GB-4.etymology: Han (颔), to sway; Yan (厌), to inhibit. The point treats tremors of the head caused by Liver fire.
GB-4.clinicalNotes: Han Yan (GB-4) is located near the eyes. Its meridian enters the ear, passes through Jia Che (ST-6), and crosses with the Stomach Meridian, Foot Yang Ming, which penetrates the teeth. This point is used to eliminate wind and heat and to relieve pain. The Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, and its collaterals are distributed over the face and eyes, so the point may be indicated to treat disorders of the head, face, and sense organs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-5.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-5.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, within the hairline, midway along the curved line connecting ST-8 and GB-7.
howToFind: On the head, above the temple, locate the point at the midpoint of the distance between Tou Wei (ST-8) and Qu Bin (GB-7).
GB-5.anatomy: Temporalis muscle. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve.
tcmIndications: redness and swelling of the eyes
westernIndications: myofascial pain in the temporalis muscle
GB-5.etymology: Xuan (悬), to suspend; Lu (颅), skull. The point is located on the temple. It is as if the skull were suspended by the points, one on each side of the temples.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-6.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-6.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, within the hairline, at the junction of the lower one-quarter and upper three-quarters of the curved line connecting ST-8 and GB-7.
howToFind: Seated with the head at rest or in lateral decubitus. Locate the point at the junction of the upper three-quarters and the lower one-quarter of the curved line that connects Tou Wei (ST-8) and Qu Bin (GB-7), or at the midpoint of the distance between Xuan Lu (GB-5) and Qu Bin (GB-7).
GB-6.anatomy: Temporalis muscle. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve.
tcmIndications: pain at the outer canthus of the eye
GB-6.etymology: Xuan (悬), to suspend; Li (厘), to arrange, to correct. The point is located on the temple and has the function of relieving headache and improving dizziness.
GB-6.clinicalNotes:
It is a Crossing point with the Stomach Meridian, Foot Yang Ming, which has the function of regulating the Wei (Stomach) and the Pi (Spleen). According to the principle that a point treats disorders of the interconnected meridians, this point may be indicated for treating fever and disorders of the digestive system.

The point has the function of eliminating pathogenic wind and heat and activating the flow of Qi in the collaterals to relieve pain; therefore, it may be used in the treatment of disorders of the head, face, sense organs, and convulsions.

See Han Yan (GB-4) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-7.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels
GB-7.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, within the hairline, at the intersection of a vertical line posterior to the temple and a horizontal line through the apex of the ear.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 1 cun superior and anterior to the ear, at the hairline, approximately 1 cun anterior to Jiao Sun (TE-20).
GB-7.anatomy: Anterior auricular and temporalis muscles. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve.
westernIndications: spasm of the masseter and spasm of the temporalis muscle
GB-7.etymology: Qu (曲), curve; Bin (鬢), hair on the temple. The point is located at the hairline, on the temple, above the ear.
GB-7.clinicalNotes: Crossing point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, and the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, which are distributed over the head, neck, and eyes. This point has the function of eliminating wind and heat and activating the flow of Qi in the collaterals to relieve pain. It is generally indicated in the treatment of disorders of the head, face, and sense organs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-8.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels
GB-8.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, directly superior to the apex of the ear, 1.5 cun within the hairline.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point
5 cun directly above the apex of the ear.
GB-8.anatomy: Temporalis muscle and epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve.
westernIndications: Extremely important local point for migraines
Strong correlation with trigger points in the temporalis muscle.
GB-8.etymology: Shuai (率), along; Gu (谷), valley. The point is located in a depression above the ear.
GB-8.clinicalNotes:
This point belongs to the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang. The sensation of fullness in the chest and the vomiting accompanied by anorexia are due to fire in the Wei (Stomach) caused by the stagnation of fire in the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang.

Cough and expectoration are caused by deficiency of the Pi (Spleen). The point has the function of eliminating heat, removing stagnation and phlegm, and regulating the Wei (Stomach). Thus, it may be indicated in the treatment of disorders of the digestive and respiratory systems and of acute or recurrent infantile convulsions caused by phlegm-heat.

The Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, originates beside the eye and enters the ear. Therefore, it may be used to treat disorders of the head, face, and sense organs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-9.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels
GB-9.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, 0.5 cun posterior to GB-8, 2 cun directly above the posterior border of the root of the auricle.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 2 cun directly above the posterior margin of the root of the ear, approximately
5 cun obliquely and posteriorly to Shuai Gu (GB-8).
GB-9.anatomy: Posterior auricular muscle. Innervated by the lesser occipital nerve.
tcmIndications: swelling and pain of the gums
GB-9.etymology: Tian (天), heaven; Chong (沖), in contact. Tian refers to the head. The name of the point relates to intense headache.
GB-9.clinicalNotes: See Shuai Gu (GB-8) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-10.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels
GB-10.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, posterior to the ear, along the curve joining GB-9 and GB-12, approximately 1 cun inferior to GB-9.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 1 cun obliquely-posteriorly to the Shuai Gu point (GB-8).
GB-10.anatomy: Posterior auricular muscle. Innervated by the lesser occipital nerve.
GB-10.etymology: Fu (浮), superior; Bai (白), brightness. The point is located on the upper part of the head, easily visualized.
GB-10.clinicalNotes: Fu Bai (GB-10) is the Crossing point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, and the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, which are distributed across the neck, shoulders, and legs. For this reason, this point can treat disorders of the shoulders, arms, and lower limbs. See Shuai Gu (GB-8) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-11.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-11.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the head, posterior to the ear, along the curve joining GB-9 and GB-12, approximately 1 cun superior to GB-12.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point in the posterosuperior region of the mastoid bone, at the midpoint of the distance between Fu Bai (GB-10) and Wan Gu (GB-12).
GB-11.anatomy: Splenius capitis, upper border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM). Innervated by the lesser occipital and great auricular nerves.
westernIndications: myofascial pain in the SCM and splenius capitis
GB-11.etymology: Tou (头), head; Qiao (窍), orifice; Yin (阴), Yin of Yin-Yang. The point is indicated in the treatment of disorders of the ear, eye, head, and throat.
GB-11.clinicalNotes: See Fu Bai (GB-10) and Wan Gu (GB-12) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-12.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels
GB-12.locationClassical: In the depression posterior and inferior to the mastoid process.
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point in the posteroinferior depression of the mastoid process of the temporal bone.
GB-12.anatomy: Insertion of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and splenius capitis muscles. Innervated by the lesser occipital nerve. Posterior auricular artery.
tcmIndications: deviation of the mouth and eye
westernIndications: Direct access to the insertion of the SCM.
GB-12.etymology: Wan Gu (完骨), mastoid process. The point is located on the inferior margin of the mastoid process of the temporal bone.
GB-12.clinicalNotes:
1. The Divergent Meridian of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, ascends to the nasopharynx, emerges in the lower region of the cheek, and spreads over the face. The points of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, are generally used to treat throat inflammation, edema, and pain in the head and face.

2. Insomnia is often caused by disturbance of mental activities resulting from heat stagnated in the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang. This point eliminates heat and calms the mind.

3. Malaria is caused mainly by a pathogenic factor alternating between the superficial and deep layers of the body, disharmony between Ying and Wei, and conflict between the pathogenic factor and the vital Qi. This disease is in the Shao Yang Meridian. Thus, the point treats the symptoms of malaria and Shao Yang–mediated disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-13.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
GB-13.locationClassical: On the forehead, 0.5 cun within the anterior hairline, 3 cun lateral to the anterior midline (or two-thirds of the distance between the midline and ST-8).
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest, locate the point 3 cun lateral to the midline,
5 cun posterior to the anterior hairline.
GB-13.anatomy: Frontalis muscle. Innervated by the frontal nerve (trigeminal).
actions: concentrates the essence in the head
GB-13.etymology: Ben (本), talent, capacity; Shen (神), mind. The point is located lateral to Shen Ting (GV-24), in the cephalic region, considered the residence and governor of the mind. Indicated in the treatment of psychic disorders.
GB-13.clinicalNotes: See Fu Bai (GB-10) and Wan Gu (GB-12) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-14.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-14.locationClassical: On the forehead, 1 cun superior to the middle of the eyebrow, directly above the pupil when the eyes are looking straight ahead.
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest, locate the point 1 cun above the midpoint of the eyebrow.
GB-14.anatomy: Frontalis muscle. Innervated by the supraorbital nerve (branch of the trigeminal).
GB-14.needling: Transverse (subcutaneous) insertion directed inferiorly or toward neighboring points, 0.3–0.5 cun.
GB-14.etymology: Yang (阳), Yang of Yin-Yang; Bai (白), white, brightness. Yang brightness in the frontal region of the head.
GB-14.clinicalNotes: Yang Bai (GB-14) is located in the frontal region and is generally used to treat disorders of the eyelid. This point can treat blepharoptosis and palpebral tremor when needled subcutaneously in a caudal direction, approximately 0.8 to 1 cun. It also treats headache, migraine, and trigeminal neuralgia. Note: Diagnostic investigation is necessary to clarify the cause of blepharoptosis. (Translator’s note.)

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-15.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
GB-15.locationClassical: On the head, directly above the pupil, 0.5 cun within the anterior hairline, midway between GV-24 and ST-8.
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest, locate the point
5 cun posterior to the anterior hairline, on the vertical line that passes through the pupil, or locate the point at the midpoint of the line connecting Shen Ting (GV-24) and Tou Wei (ST-8).
GB-15.anatomy: Frontalis muscle and epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the supraorbital nerve.
tcmIndications: pain at the outer canthus of the eye
GB-15.etymology: Tou (头), head; Lin (临), from above to below; Qi (泣), tears. The point is located on the head and is indicated in the treatment of eye disorders.
GB-15.clinicalNotes: The Divergent Meridian of the Gallbladder, Foot Shao Yang, passes through the Xin (Heart). The Xin (Heart) controls mental activities and the circulation of Xue (Blood). Thus, this point may be indicated in the treatment of disorders of the circulatory system and neuropsychiatric disturbances.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-16.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
GB-16.locationClassical: On the head, 1.5 cun posterior to GB-15, along the line that extends directly posterior to the pupil.
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest, locate the point
5 cun directly above the anterior hairline, 1 cun posterior to Tou Lin Qi (GB-15).
GB-16.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the supraorbital nerve.
tcmIndications: redness and swelling of the eyes
GB-16.etymology: Mu (目), eye; Chuang (窗), window. The point is located above the eye, like a window for the eyes, indicated for ocular disorders.
GB-16.clinicalNotes: Mu Chuang (GB-16) is the Crossing point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, with the Yang Wei Mai. It can be used to treat aversion to cold, fever, and nasal obstruction.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-17.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
GB-17.locationClassical: On the head, 1.5 cun posterior to GB-16, along the line that extends directly posterior to the pupil.
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest, locate the point 2 cun directly superior to Tou Lin Qi (GB-15).
GB-17.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the supraorbital and greater occipital nerves.
GB-17.etymology: Zheng (正), convergence; Ying (营), union. This point is the meeting place of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, with the Yang Wei Mai.
GB-17.clinicalNotes: See Mu Chuang (GB-16) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-18.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
GB-18.locationClassical: On the head, 1.5 cun posterior to GB-17, along the line that extends directly posterior to the pupil.
howToFind: Seated, with the head at rest, locate the point
5 cun directly superior to Tou Lin Qi (GB-15), at the level of Tong Tian (BL-7).
GB-18.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve.
GB-18.etymology: Cheng (承), to receive; Ling (灵), spirit. The brain dominates the mind; thus, this point treats neuropsychiatric disorders, calming the head and the mind.
GB-18.clinicalNotes: See Mu Chuang (GB-16) and Shuai Gu (GB-8) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-19.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
GB-19.locationClassical: In the occipital region, directly superior to GB-20, at the level of GV-17 (upper border of the external occipital protuberance).
howToFind: Seated or in ventral decubitus, locate the point
25 cun lateral to Nao Hu (GV-17) or
5 cun above the Feng Chi point (GB-20).
GB-19.anatomy: Occipitalis muscle. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve. Occipital artery.
GB-19.etymology: Nao (脑), brain; Kong (空), cavity, depression. The point is located in the depression lateral to the occipital bone.
GB-19.clinicalNotes: See Mu Chuang (GB-16) and Shuai Gu (GB-8) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-20.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Triple Burner channels with the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) and Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessels
GB-20.locationClassical: Suboccipital region, in the depression between the superior attachments of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and trapezius muscles, at the level of GV-16.
howToFind: With the patient seated or prone, locate the point in the inferior depression of the occipital bone, between the superior attachments of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
GB-20.anatomy: Splenius capitis, rectus capitis posterior major and minor. Nerve supply: lesser occipital nerve and greater occipital nerve. The occipital artery and vertebral artery lie deep to this point.
GB-20.needling: Oblique insertion directed toward the tip of the nose or the contralateral orbit, 0.8–1.2 cun.
GB-20.safetyWarning: HIGH RISK. Deep needling directed medially and superiorly can enter the foramen magnum and penetrate the spinal cord or medulla oblongata.
actions: descends Yang. (Principal point for all Wind disorders)
GB-20.etymology: Feng (风): pathogenic wind; Chi (池): pool or depression. This is a key point for eliminating pathogenic wind.
GB-20.clinicalNotes:
1. Feng Chi (GB-20) is used for both exogenous and endogenous wind. Wind, the principal pathogenic factor in TCM, frequently combines with cold, heat, dampness, and phlegm to produce a wide range of disorders. Symptoms of exogenous wind invasion include fever with chills, cervical stiffness with headache, peripheral facial paralysis, throat pain and swelling, and skin conditions. This point is also indicated for headache, vertigo, and post-stroke sequelae caused by endogenous wind.

2. This point is frequently indicated for eye disorders such as blepharoptosis, and may be used alone or combined with Yang Bai (GB-14) and Xian Gu (ST-43). Note: A diagnostic workup is required to identify the underlying cause of blepharoptosis. (Translator's note.)

3. It may be effective for throat inflammation and dysphagia. In these cases, the needle tip should be directed toward the cricoid cartilage.

combinations.indication: Headache, neck stiffness, wind disorders, occipital pain

GB-21.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-21.locationClassical: On the shoulder, directly above the nipple, at the midpoint of the line connecting the spinous process of C7 (GV-14) and the lateral end of the acromion.
howToFind: Seated, locate the point at the midpoint of the line connecting the highest part of the spinous process of the seventh cervical vertebra and the acromial extremity of the clavicle.
GB-21.anatomy: Upper trapezius, levator scapulae, supraspinatus. Innervated by the accessory nerve and the supraclavicular nerve. Transverse cervical artery.
GB-21.safetyWarning: HIGH RISK OF PNEUMOTHORAX. Do not needle deeply, especially in thin patients. The apex of the lung lies directly beneath this region. CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY (strongly promotes labor/downward movement).
tcmIndications: Pain and stiffness in the neck and shoulder
GB-21.etymology: Jian (肩), shoulder; Jing (井), well. The point is located on the shoulder, in the depression of the trapezius muscle.
GB-21.clinicalNotes:
1. Crossing point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, with the Yang Wei Mai and with the San Jiao Meridian, Hand Shao Yang. It is generally used to treat shoulder pain, dorsalgia, torticollis, and flaccidity of the lower limbs. The Ba Zong Xue Ge says: "Jiang Jing is principally used to treat disorders of the feet." It is recommended in the treatment of flaccidity of the lower limbs caused by psychic disorders. The tip of the needle should be directed posteriorly.

2. This point has the function of regulating the flow of Qi and promoting blood circulation, removing the stasis of Xue (Blood). The Tendinous Meridian of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, connects with the pectoral muscle. Thus, it is indicated to treat acute mastitis and postoperative symptoms. Directing the tip of the needle anteriorly increases the therapeutic effect.

3. Epigastralgia can be relieved rapidly by massaging Jian Jing (GB-21) on the left side with the right thumb and the abdomen with the palm of the left hand.

4. It is widely used to treat torticollis and shoulder pain. The best method is to needle obliquely, directing the tip of the needle toward the affected region.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-22.locationClassical: On the midaxillary line, in the fourth intercostal space, approximately 3 cun inferior to the apex of the axilla (with the arm raised).
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, locate the point on the midaxillary line, in the fourth intercostal space, 3 cun below the axilla.
GB-22.anatomy: Serratus anterior muscle, intercostal muscles. Innervated by the long thoracic nerve and the 4th intercostal nerve.
GB-22.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space, 0.5–0.8 cun.
GB-22.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Deep perpendicular insertion is strictly contraindicated.
tcmIndications: Fullness and pain in the chest and hypochondrium
westernIndications: myofascial pain in the serratus anterior
GB-22.etymology: Yuan (渊), deep; Ye (腋), axilla. The point is located in the lower part of the axilla.
GB-22.clinicalNotes: This point is used to eliminate heat, promote the dispersing function of the Fei (Lung), regulate menstruation, and relieve dysmenorrhea.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-23.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels
GB-23.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the chest, in the fourth intercostal space, 1 cun anterior to GB-22 (at the level of the nipple).
howToFind: Seated or in lateral decubitus, with the upper limb abducted, locate the point 1 cun anterior to Yuan Ye (GB-22), in the depression between Yuan Ye (GB-22) and Tian Xi (SP-18). In men, the point is located at the level of the nipple.
GB-23.anatomy: Serratus anterior muscle, intercostal muscles. Innervated by the 4th intercostal nerve and the long thoracic nerve.
GB-23.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space, 0.5–0.8 cun.
GB-23.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Deep perpendicular insertion is strictly contraindicated.
westernIndications: myofascial pain in the serratus anterior
GB-23.etymology: Zhe (辄), an ancient curved cart-piece resembling a rib; Jin (筋), tendon. The point is located in the intercostal space.
GB-23.clinicalNotes:
1. Stagnation of the Qi of the Gan (Liver) and the Qi of the Dan (Gallbladder) can cause dysfunction of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach). This point has the function of regulating the flow of Qi and calming the Gan (Liver); therefore, it is indicated in the treatment of disorders of the digestive system.

2. This point is located in the lung region, so it can treat pulmonary disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-24.category: Front-Mu Point of the Gall Bladder
GB-24.locationClassical: On the anterior wall of the chest, in the seventh intercostal space, directly below the nipple (4 cun lateral to the anterior midline).
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the seventh intercostal space, on the midclavicular line, 4 cun lateral to the anterior midline.
GB-24.anatomy: External oblique and internal intercostal muscles. Innervated by the 7th intercostal nerve.
GB-24.needling: Transverse-oblique insertion along the intercostal space, 0.5–0.8 cun.
GB-24.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Deep insertion may also puncture the liver on the right side. Hazardous point (risk of pneumothorax).
actions: promotes the flow of Gallbladder Qi
GB-24.etymology: Ri (日), sun; Yue (月), moon. Ri is Yang, and one of the functions of the Dan (Gallbladder) is the clarity to make decisions. The Chinese ideogram corresponding to clarity is composed of two ideograms — the Sun and the Moon.
GB-24.clinicalNotes:
1. It is the Front-Mu point of the Dan (Gallbladder), the place where the Jing (essence) and the Qi of the Dan (Gallbladder) accumulate. The Gan (Liver) and the Dan (Gallbladder) are paired meridians. Dysfunction of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach) is consequent to stagnation of the Qi of the Gan (Liver) and the Dan (Gallbladder). This point has the function of calming the Gan (Liver), normalizing the secretion of the Dan (Gallbladder), promoting the circulation of Qi, and relieving stagnation. It is indicated in the treatment of disorders of the Pi (Spleen) and the Wei (Stomach) resulting from stagnation of Dan (Gallbladder) Qi. Currently, Ri Yue (GB-24) is needled on the right side to treat gallbladder disorders such as cholecystitis, gallbladder colic, and symptoms of acute and chronic hepatitis.

2. This point calms the Gan (Liver) and regulates the circulation of Qi. It is one of the points used to treat pain and distension in the hypochondriac region, sighing, and susceptibility to melancholy resulting from stagnation of Liver Qi.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-25.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the abdomen, on the lower border of the free end of the twelfth rib.
howToFind: In lateral or ventral decubitus, locate the point at the free end of the twelfth (floating) rib on the lateral aspect of the waist,
8 cun posterior to Zhang Men (LR-13).
GB-25.anatomy: External and internal oblique muscles, latissimus dorsi, quadratus lumborum. Innervated by the 11th intercostal and subcostal nerves.
GB-25.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a substantial risk of puncturing an enlarged kidney or the spleen (on the left).
tcmIndications: and Kidney deficiency conditions (when used with BL-23 Shenshu and moxibustion).
westernIndications: trigger points in the quadratus lumborum
GB-25.etymology: Jing (京门), capital, important; Men (门), gate. As the Front-Mu point of the Shen (Kidney), it has an important role in the treatment of dysfunction of the Water pathway.
GB-25.clinicalNotes:
Jing Men (GB-25) is the Front-Mu point of the Shen (Kidney), where the Jing (essence) and Qi of the Shen (Kidney) gather. It is used to treat urinary disorders such as difficulty in micturition and "dark urine with edema of the face."

Pain in the hypochondriac region can be treated by tonifying the Shen (Kidney) to promote the circulation of local Qi.

See Ri Yue (GB-24) and Zhe Jin (GB-23) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-26.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Girdling (Dai) vessel
GB-26.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the abdomen, directly below the free end of the eleventh rib, at the level of the umbilicus.
howToFind: In lateral decubitus, locate the point at the intersection of the midaxillary line with the horizontal line passing through the umbilical scar,
8 cun below Zhang Men (LR-13).
GB-26.anatomy: External and internal oblique muscles, transverse abdominis. Innervated by the subcostal nerve.
GB-26.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may perforate the peritoneal cavity.
tcmIndications: pain in the lumbar and hypochondriac regions
intestinal disease and sensation of distension in the abdomen.
GB-26.etymology: Dai (带), belt; Mai (脉), vessels. This point is located at the waist, the place through which the Qi of the Dai Mai passes.
GB-26.clinicalNotes:
1. The Dai Mai emerges from the second lumbar vertebra, where Ming Men (GV-4) is located, passing through the lumbar and abdominal region. Chong Mai, Ren Mai, and Du Mai originate in the uterus, and the Qi of these meridians emerges in the abdomen and lumbar region. Thus, the Dai Mai is directly related to them. For this reason, the point is indicated to treat gynecological disorders.

2. The Dai Mai passes around the waist like a belt and has the function of controlling several meridians. The Nei Jing says: "Flaccidity of the foot is caused by dysfunction of the Dai Mai, secondary to deficiency of the Yang Ming Meridian." Disorders of the Dai Mai cause fullness in the abdomen and lumbar laxity. The point can be used to treat muscular weakness in the lumbar region, abdomen, and lower limbs.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-27.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Girdling (Dai) vessel
GB-27.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the abdomen, anterior to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), 3 cun below the level of the umbilicus.
howToFind: In lateral decubitus, locate the point
5 cun anterior to the anterior superior iliac spine, 3 cun below the umbilical scar and 3 cun anteroinferior to the Dai Mai point (GB-26).
GB-27.anatomy: External and internal oblique muscles. Innervated by the iliohypogastric nerve.
GB-27.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may perforate the peritoneal cavity.
westernIndications: lower crossed syndrome (tension in the iliopsoas and obliques)
GB-27.etymology: Wu (五), five; Shu (枢), pivot. Wu also means the place of intersection of several lines. The point is located where several meridians pass.
GB-27.clinicalNotes: Wu Shu (GB-27) on the left side is located in the area of the descending colon, so it is generally used to treat constipation and dysentery.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-28.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Girdling (Dai) vessel
GB-28.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the abdomen, anterior and inferior to the ASIS, 0.5 cun anterior and inferior to GB-27.
howToFind: In lateral decubitus, locate the point
5 cun anteroinferior to Wu Shu (GB-27), close to the inguinal region.
GB-28.anatomy: External and internal oblique muscles. Innervated by the ilioinguinal nerve.
GB-28.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may perforate the peritoneal cavity.
GB-28.clinicalNotes: See Wu Shu (GB-27) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-29.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder channel with the Yang Motility (Yang Qiao) vessel
GB-29.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the hip, in the depression at the midpoint of a line drawn between the ASIS and the most prominent point of the greater trochanter.
howToFind: In lateral decubitus, locate the point 3 cun posteroinferior to Wei Dao (GB-28) or in the depression at the midpoint of the line connecting the anterior superior iliac spine and the highest point of the greater trochanter.
GB-29.anatomy: Tensor fasciae latae, gluteus medius and minimus muscles. Innervated by the superior gluteal nerve.
tcmIndications: Pain and motor impairment of the hip and lower limbs
westernIndications: Myofascial pain syndrome of the gluteus medius and minimus
tension in the tensor fasciae latae
GB-29.etymology: Ju (居), to reside; Liao (髎), fossa. The point is located in the depression of the hip bone.
GB-29.clinicalNotes:
1. Ju Liao (GB-29) is the Crossing point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, with the Yang Qiao Mai. According to the principle that a point can treat disorders manifested along its own meridian, this point can be used to treat disorders of the lower limbs. According to the principle of correspondence, Ju Liao (GB-29) is indicated to treat shoulder pain.

2. The Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, crosses with the Dai Mai. Thus, this point can be used in the treatment of disorders of the genitourinary system.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-30.category: Meeting Point of the Gall Bladder and Bladder channels
GB-30.locationClassical: On the posterolateral aspect of the hip, at the junction of the lateral one-third and the medial two-thirds of the line connecting the most prominent point of the greater trochanter and the sacral hiatus.
howToFind: In lateral decubitus, locate the point in the posterior depression of the greater
trochanter, at the junction of the lateral one-third with the middle one-third of the distance between the greater
trochanter of the femur and the intergluteal cleft. (Fig.
GB-30.anatomy: Gluteus maximus and piriformis muscles. The thickest part of the sciatic nerve passes directly deep to this point. Innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.
GB-30.needling: Perpendicular insertion directed slightly inferiorly, 1.5–3.0 cun.
GB-30.safetyWarning: Deep needling will directly contact the sciatic nerve (causing a strong electrical sensation in the leg). Ensure the sensation is not excessively painful.
actions: benefits the hip joint and the leg
tcmIndications: pain in the lumbar region and the thigh
westernIndications: Principal target in piriformis syndrome. Deep gluteal syndrome
GB-30.etymology: Huan (环), a ring; Tiao (跳), to jump. The point is located at the hip joint, which is responsible for the act of jumping.
GB-30.clinicalNotes:
1. In addition to the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, crossing with the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang, it also crosses with the Yang Wei Mai and the Yang Qiao Mai. The point can treat disorders manifested along the trajectory of its own meridian; thus, this point is generally used to treat disorders of the lower limbs, lumbar pain, lumbosciatica, Bi syndrome (arthralgia), and Wei syndrome (flaccidity).

2. In clinical practice, when the tip of the needle is directed slightly behind the classical point, the needling response or De Qi sensation descends along the posterior aspect of the lower limb, and when directed slightly forward, the needling response descends along the lateral aspect of the lower limb. According to the location of the pain, this point can be needled with different manipulations, making the De Qi sensation reach the site of pain.

3. This point is one of the points of the Four-Yang and Nine-Needles method and is indicated to treat collapse of Yang. Note: Four-Yang and Nine-Needles are likely therapeutic methods, where Four-Yang means Zu San Li (ST-36), Wei Zhong (BL-40), Lie Que (LU-7), and He Gu (LI-4), and Nine-Needles means Ya Men (GV-15), Lao Gong (PC-8), San Yin Jiao (SP-6), Hui Yin (CV-1), Tai Xi (KI-3), Zhong Wan (CV-12), Huan Tiao (GB-30), Zu San Li (ST-36), and He Gu (LI-4).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-31.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the thigh, 7 cun superior to the transverse popliteal crease. With the patient standing and the hands relaxed at the sides of the body, the point lies where the tip of the middle finger touches.
howToFind: With the patient standing and both arms relaxed at the sides of the body, locate the point where the tip of the patient’s middle finger touches the leg.
In lateral decubitus, locate the point 7 cun above the popliteal fossa, on the lateral midline of the femur.
GB-31.anatomy: Iliotibial tract (ITT), vastus lateralis muscle. Innervated by the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and branches of the femoral nerve.
tcmIndications: Pain and soreness in the thigh and knee
westernIndications: trigger points in the vastus lateralis
GB-31.etymology: Feng (风), pathogenic wind; Shi (市), market. An important point for removing pathogenic wind.
GB-31.clinicalNotes:
Feng Shi (GB-31) in Chinese means "wind market." The function of this point is to eliminate wind. Generalized itching, flaccidity, pain, and numbness in the lower limbs are related to pathogenic wind. Therefore, this point may be used to treat disorders of the lower limbs.

It eliminates wind-dampness, regulates Qi and Xue (blood), and activates the flow of Qi in the meridians and collaterals. The Tendinous Meridian of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, passes through the buttock, so Feng Shi (GB-31) may be used in the treatment of acute low back pain.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-32.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the thigh, 2 cun inferior to GB-31 (5 cun superior to the popliteal crease).
howToFind: In lateral decubitus, locate the point 5 cun above the popliteal fossa, on the midline of the lateral aspect of the femur.
GB-32.anatomy: Iliotibial tract, vastus lateralis. Innervated by the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
tcmIndications: Pain and soreness in the thigh and knee
westernIndications: Myofascial pain in the vastus lateralis
GB-32.etymology: Zhong (中), middle; Du (渎), small water channel. The point lies between the tendons on the lateral aspect of the thigh, like a small stream.
GB-32.clinicalNotes:
1. This point may be used to eliminate wind, remove dampness, and activate the flow of Qi in the meridians and their collaterals.

2. In biliary colic, a good analgesic effect can be achieved by needling the most painful point on digital pressure between Zhong Du (GB-32) and Liang Qiu (ST-34).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-33.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the knee, in the depression 3 cun superior to GB-34, directly above the lateral epicondyle of the femur.
howToFind: With the knee flexed, locate the point at the midpoint between the depression on the anterior aspect of the lateral epicondyle of the femur and the biceps femoris tendon, 3 cun above Yang Ling Quan (GB-34).
GB-33.anatomy: Posterior border of the iliotibial tract, anterior to the biceps femoris tendon. Innervated by the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
tcmIndications: Swelling and pain of the knee
contracture of the tendons in the popliteal fossa
GB-33.etymology: Xi (膝), knee; Yang (阳), Yang of Yin-Yang; Guan (关), joint. The point is located on the lateral aspect of the knee joint.
GB-33.clinicalNotes: Dysfunctions of the Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach) are caused by stagnation of Qi in the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang. The function of the point is to calm the Gan (Liver), regulate the Dan (Gallbladder), tonify the Pi (Spleen), and remove dampness. For this reason, it may be used in the treatment of vomiting and excessive salivation.
