combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-34.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the leg, in the depression anterior and inferior to the head of the fibula.
howToFind: Seated, with the knees flexed and the feet relaxed, locate the point in the depression anterior and inferior to the head of the fibula.
GB-34.anatomy: Fibularis longus and extensor digitorum longus muscles. The common fibular nerve bifurcates into the deep and superficial fibular nerves near this point.
GB-34.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion directed posteriorly, 1.0–1.5 cun.
GB-34.safetyWarning: Avoid direct trauma to the common fibular nerve.
actions: promotes the smooth flow of Liver Qi
clears Damp-Heat from the Liver and Gallbladder
tcmIndications: numbness and pain in the lower limbs
swelling and pain of the knee
A very important point for muscles and tendons.
westernIndications: Master point for all tendon and ligament disorders. Knee osteoarthritis
GB-34.etymology: Yang (阳), Yang of Yin-Yang; Ling (陵), mound; Quan (泉), spring. The head of the fibula, located on the lateral aspect of the knee, is prominent like a mound. Below it lies a depression, like a spring, where the point is located.
GB-34.clinicalNotes:
1. As the Lower He-Sea Point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, it may be used to treat cholecystitis and other digestive disorders caused by gallbladder pathology, such as abdominal distension, borborygmus, and jaundice. The point has the function of calming the Gan (Liver), normalizing the secretion of the Dan (Gallbladder), promoting the flow of Qi, and eliminating stagnation.

2. As the Influential Point of the Tendons, it is indicated for the treatment of weakness, Bi syndrome (arthralgia), Wei syndrome (flaccidity), pain and numbness in the lower limbs, and hemiplegia.

3. The Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, connects with the San Jiao Meridian, Hand Shao Yang, which is distributed over the shoulder. It may therefore be indicated to treat shoulder pain.

4. The Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, runs along the lateral aspect of the head, thorax, and hypochondrium. The point may be used in the treatment of disorders of the head, face, and sense organs, and of pain in the thorax and hypochondrium. Needling Yang Ling Quan (GB-34) toward Zu San Li (ST-36) can treat all types of hypochondriac pain, as well as hypochondriac pain aggravated by coughing.

combinations.indication: Musculoskeletal pain, tendon and sinew disorders, hypochondriac pain

GB-35.category: Xi-Cleft Point of the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel
GB-35.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the leg, 7 cun superior to the prominence of the lateral malleolus, on the posterior border of the fibula.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 7 cun above the lateral malleolus, on the posterior border of the fibula.
GB-35.anatomy: Fibularis brevis and soleus muscles. Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: Fullness of the chest and hypochondrium
pain on the lateral aspect of the leg
GB-35.etymology: Yang (阳), Yang of Yin-Yang; Jiao (交), crossing. The point is located on the lateral aspect of the leg, where the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, crosses with the Yang Wei Mai.
GB-35.clinicalNotes:
1. This point may be used to treat flaccidity of the lower limbs and hemiplegia by activating the circulation of Qi in the meridian and its collaterals.

2. The Divergent Meridian of the Gallbladder, Foot Shao Yang, ascends to the throat, so it may be indicated to treat inflammation of the throat and dysphonia.

3. The point has the function of calming the Gan (Liver), normalizing the function of the Dan (Gallbladder), calming phobia, and eliminating wind.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-36.category: Xi-Cleft Point of the Gall Bladder channel
GB-36.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the leg, 7 cun superior to the prominence of the lateral malleolus, at the level of GB-35, but on the anterior border of the fibula.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 7 cun above the apex of the lateral malleolus, on the anterior border of the fibula, at the level of Yang Jiao (GB-35).
GB-36.anatomy: Fibularis longus and extensor digitorum longus muscles. Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: pain on the lateral aspect of the leg
GB-36.etymology: Wai (外), lateral; Qiu (丘), mound. The point lies above the lateral malleolus, where the local muscle is prominent like a mound.
GB-36.clinicalNotes: See Yang Jiao (GB-35) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-37.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the leg, 5 cun superior to the prominence of the lateral malleolus, on the anterior border of the fibula.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 5 cun above the apex of the lateral malleolus, on the anterior border of the fibula.
GB-37.anatomy: Fibularis brevis and extensor digitorum longus muscles. Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve.
GB-37.etymology: Guang (光), light; Ming (明), bright. Indicated in eye disorders, as it is the Luo (Connecting) point of the Gallbladder Meridian.
GB-37.clinicalNotes:
1. The point Guang Ming (GB-37) is the Luo (Connecting) point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, with the Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin. The Gallbladder Meridian begins at the lateral commissure of the eyelid and connects with the Liver Meridian, which passes through the ocular system and opens into the eyes. Therefore, this point treats ophthalmic disorders.

2. The Tendinous Meridian of the Gallbladder Meridian spreads over the chest and hypochondrium. The function of this point is to calm the Gan (Liver) and regulate Qi circulation. In general, it is used to treat painful distension of the breasts and a sensation of fullness in the chest and hypochondrium.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-38.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the leg, 4 cun superior to the prominence of the lateral malleolus, slightly anterior to the anterior border of the fibula.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 4 cun above the apex of the lateral malleolus, on the anterior border of the fibula.
GB-38.anatomy: Fibularis brevis and extensor digitorum longus muscles. Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve.
tcmIndications: pain at the outer canthus of the eye
pain on the lateral aspect of the lower limb
GB-38.etymology: Yang (阳), Yang of Yin-Yang; Fu (辅), fibula. The point is located anterior to the fibula, on the lateral aspect of the leg.
GB-38.clinicalNotes: See Xuan Zhong (GB-39) and Tou Lin Qi (GB-15) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-39.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the leg, 3 cun superior to the prominence of the lateral malleolus, between the posterior border of the fibula and the tendons of the fibularis longus and brevis muscles.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or in lateral decubitus, locate the point 3 cun above the lateral malleolus, on the anterior border of the fibula.
GB-39.anatomy: Fibularis brevis muscle. Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve and the sural nerve.
tcmIndications: Stiffness of the neck (principal distal point)
pain in the neck and back
westernIndications: Cervical spondylosis (highly effective distal point for cervical stiffness)
GB-39.etymology: Xuan (悬), suspended; Zhong (钟), bell. The point lies above the lateral malleolus, where children long ago used to hang a bell. This point is also called Jue Gu, which means "severed bone."
GB-39.clinicalNotes:
1. The Divergent Meridian of the Gallbladder, Foot Shao Yang, runs along the throat. Heat from the Dan (Gallbladder) attacking the head results in increased nasal discharge. Needling Xuan Zhong (GB-39) eliminates heat and wind, and can therefore reduce fever. It is also the Influential Point of the Marrow, so it may be selected to treat sinusitis, epistaxis, painful inflammation of the throat, and fever caused by exogenous wind.

2. The Tendinous Meridian of the Gallbladder Meridian runs posteriorly and reaches the sacrum. The straight branch ascends through the ribs, distributes around and anterior to the axilla, connecting first with the breast region, chest, and supraclavicular region, and then joins Que Pen (ST-12). According to the principle that a point can treat disorders manifesting along the course of its own meridian, Xuan Zhong (GB-39) may be used to treat pain in the chest, hypochondrium, supraclavicular fossa, and lumbosacral pain, in accordance with its location.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-40.locationClassical: Anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus; at the intersection of the line drawn along the anterior and inferior borders of the lateral malleolus.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported or in lateral decubitus, locate the point in the anterior and inferior region to the lateral malleolus, on the lateral aspect of the tendon of the extensor digitorum longus muscle, in the depression of the talocalcaneal joint.
Locate the point at the intersection of the lines passing along the anterior border and inferior border of the lateral malleolus.
GB-40.anatomy: Extensor digitorum brevis muscle. Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve.
GB-40.needling: Perpendicular insertion directed toward the medial malleolus, 0.5–1.5 cun.
GB-40.safetyWarning: Avoid the dorsalis pedis artery during deep insertion.
actions: Promotes the smooth flow of Liver Qi
tcmIndications: Pain and swelling of the lateral ankle
sprain of the ankle joint and leg ulcers
important distal point for chest pain and mastitis.
westernIndications: Principal point for lateral ankle sprains (ATFL injuries). Ankle osteoarthritis
GB-40.etymology: Qiu (丘), mound; Xu (丘墟), great mound. Here it refers to the malleolus.
GB-40.clinicalNotes:
1. Qiu Xu (GB-40) is the Yuan (Source) point of the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang. According to the principle that a point can treat diseases manifesting in its own meridian and that points in the lower portion can be selected to treat upper disorders, Qiu Xu (GB-40) is frequently used to treat hemicranial migraine and pain and fullness in the chest and hypochondrium.

2. The Su Wen states "Disorders of any of the five Zang and six Fu may result in cough." The Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, passes through the hypochondrium and connects with the Fei (Lung). Qiu Xu (GB-40) has the function of eliminating heat from the Dan (Gallbladder) and eliminating Qi stagnation of the Gan (Liver). Therefore, this point may be indicated to treat cough and other respiratory disorders resulting from Gan (Liver) fire attacking the Fei (Lung) and retention of heat in the Gan (Liver) and Dan (Gallbladder).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-41.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, in the depression distal to the junction of the 4th and 5th metatarsal bones, on the lateral side of the tendon of the extensor digitorum longus (the branch to the little toe).
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported, locate the point on the lateral border of the dorsum of the foot, between the fourth and fifth metatarsals, proximal to the metatarsophalangeal joint of the fourth and fifth toes, on the lateral aspect of the tendon of the extensor digitorum longus muscle.
GB-41.anatomy: Fourth dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve (a branch of the superficial fibular nerve).
GB-41.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion, 0.5–0.8 cun.
tcmIndications: pain at the outer canthus of the eye
pain on the dorsum of the foot
westernIndications: pain on the dorsum of the foot
GB-41.etymology: Zu (足), foot; Lin (临), treatment; Qi (泣), to weep. Although the point lies on the foot, it is indicated in the treatment of lacrimation and other eye disorders.
GB-41.clinicalNotes: See Qiu Xu (GB-40) and Xuan Zhong (GB-39) for further details.

combinations.indication: Temporal headache, ear disorders, hypochondriac pain

GB-42.english: Five Meeting Places on the Ground
GB-42.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, between the 4th and 5th metatarsal bones, in the depression proximal to the metatarsophalangeal joints.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported, locate the point between the fourth and fifth metatarsal bones, medial to the tendon of the extensor digitorum longus,
5 cun proximal to the interdigital fold.
GB-42.anatomy: Fourth dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve.
tcmIndications: Pain at the outer canthus of the eye
swelling and pain on the dorsum of the foot
GB-42.etymology: Di (地), ground; Wu (五), five; Hui (会), confluence. Di Wu Hui (GB-42) is the point that treats arthralgia of the five toes.
GB-42.clinicalNotes: See Qiu Xu (GB-40) and Xuan Zhong (GB-39) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-43.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, between the 4th and 5th toes, 0.5 cun proximal to the margin of the interdigital fold.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported, locate the point between the fourth and fifth toes, at the transition between the lighter and darker skin.
GB-43.anatomy: Dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the dorsal digital nerve from the superficial fibular nerve.
GB-43.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion directed proximally, 0.3–0.5 cun.
actions: indicated for Liver and Gallbladder Heat ascending along the channel to the head.
tcmIndications: pain at the outer canthus of the eye
redness and pain at the outer canthus of the eye and itching of the eye.
GB-43.etymology: Xia (侠), to squeeze on both sides; Xi (溪), stream, depression. The point lies in the space between the fourth and fifth toes.
GB-43.clinicalNotes:
1. Xia Xi (GB-43) belongs to the Gallbladder Meridian, Foot Shao Yang, and has the function of eliminating pathogenic heat from the Shao Yang. It is therefore indicated to treat Shao Yang disorders such as: malaria-like symptoms and fever from exogenous cold.

2. The Gan (Liver) has the function of calming and regulating the flow of Qi and Xue (blood) and is the coupled organ of the Dan (Gallbladder). Therefore, the points of the Gallbladder Meridian also have the function of removing Qi stagnation of the Gan (Liver). Thus, Xia Xi (GB-43) may be used to treat amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, and other gynecological disorders caused by Qi stagnation of the Gan (Liver).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GB-44.locationClassical: On the dorsal aspect of the 4th toe, 0.1 cun from the lateral (fibular) corner of the nail.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported, locate the point at the intersection of the lines passing along the lateral border and the base of the nail of the fourth toe.
GB-44.anatomy: Nail bed. Innervated by the dorsal digital nerve.
GB-44.needling: Perpendicular or oblique insertion directed proximally, 0.1–0.2 cun, or prick to bleed.
actions: clears the head and benefits the sensory orifices
GB-44.etymology: Zu (足), foot; Qiao (窍), opening; Yin (阴), Yin of Yin-Yang. The Shen (Kidney) and Gan (Liver) belong to Yin and open into the ears and eyes, respectively. The point is indicated to treat disorders of the ears and eyes.
GB-44.clinicalNotes: Zu Qiao Yin (GB-44) is the Jing-Well (terminal) point of the Gallbladder Meridian, classified in Ling Shu chapter 1. By Five-Shu theory its action is to restore consciousness, clear Heat from the head and eyes, and treat "fullness below the Heart" — hence its central role in acute temporal migraine, retro-orbital headache, acute conjunctivitis, sudden deafness, and recent-onset tinnitus (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 487–488). The Jia Yi Jing adds high fever with restlessness, disturbing dreams, and nightmares from upward-rising Heat. Common combinations: Zu Qiao Yin (GB-44) + Tai Yang (Extra) + Shuai Gu (GB-8) for acute temporal migraine; with Tai Chong (LR-3) and He Gu (LI-4) in the "Four Gates" combination for crises with an irritability-tension component; and as a distal bleeding point for acute conjunctivitis and stubborn headache (Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, Foreign Languages Press, Beijing). It is preferred for acute, not chronic, presentations. Critical safety note: as a Jing-Well, insertion is superficial, perpendicular or slightly oblique, limited to 0.1 cun (1–2 mm). Its most relevant modern role is bleeding-letting: a three-edged needle (san leng zhen) or disposable lancet, expressing 1 to 2 drops of blood, classically indicated for hypertensive crisis, refractory migraine, and high fever. The area is highly sensitive — inform the patient beforehand (Deadman, op. cit.; Cheng Xinnong, op. cit.). Frequently paired with Xuan Zhong (GB-39), Qiu Xu (GB-40), and Xia Xi (GB-43); see technical details under those points.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-1.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect/tip of the great toe, approximately 0.1 cun proximal and lateral to the corner of the nail, or among the hairs.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported, locate the point on the great toe, at the intersection of the lines passing through the lateral margin and the base of the nail.
LR-1.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, branches of the dorsal digital nerves and veins of the great toe, dorsal digital branches of the superficial fibular nerve, dorsal digital artery, and distal phalanx of the great toe.
LR-1.needling: Perpendicular insertion or oblique insertion in a proximal direction, 0.1–0.2 cun, or pricking to bleed.
LR-1.safetyWarning: Very painful point. Avoid needling the perionychium.
tcmIndications: swelling and pain of the genitals
pain in the lateral costal region
heat in the hands and feet
LR-1.etymology: Da (大), great; Dun (敦), thickness. Da Dun refers to the great toe. The point is located on the medial aspect of the great toe, where the region is thick.
LR-1.clinicalNotes:
1. The Da Dun point (LR-1) is the Jing (Well) point of the Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, and is therefore indicated to restore consciousness.

2. Hyperactivity of Gan (Liver) Qi and the inability of the Gan (Liver) to regulate the flow of Xue (Blood) can cause various types of hemorrhage. Thus, in clinical practice, this point can be used in the treatment of metrorrhagia, metrostaxis, hematochezia, and hematuria.

3. The Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, circulates around the external genitalia and is the only meridian directly connected to the vulva. For this reason, Da Dun (LR-1) can be used in the treatment of diseases of the genitourinary system, such as vulvar pruritus, "uterine prolapse," and in the symptoms of inguinal hernia.

4. Dysfunction of the Gan (Liver) can cause the formation of Wind, so the point can be indicated in the treatment of bipolar disorder, epilepsy, sequelae of stroke, among others.

5. The Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, circulates around the stomach and has the function of softening and regulating the circulation of Qi and Xue (Blood) and of favoring digestion and absorption, relating directly to the functions of Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach). Therefore, Da Dun (LR-1) can be indicated in the treatment of diseases of the digestive system.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-2.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, between the 1st and 2nd toes, 0.5 cun proximal to the margin of the interdigital web.
howToFind: Seated with the feet supported, locate the point on the dorsum of the foot, in the depression between the great toe and the second toe, proximal to the margin of the interosseous web.
LR-2.anatomy: Dorsal interosseous muscle. Innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
LR-2.needling: 0.3–0.5 cun obliquely toward the heel or vertically, or 0.5–1.0 cun perpendicularly.
actions: clears Heat from the Lower Jiao (principal point for clearing excess Liver Heat)
cools Heat and Heat in the Blood
tcmIndications: redness and swelling of the eyes
lumbar pain due to contracture of the tendons
LR-2.etymology: Xing (行), walking; Jian (间), between. This point is located between the great toe and the second toe, in the depression anterior to the first and second metatarsophalangeal joints.
LR-2.clinicalNotes: Xing Jian (LR-2) is the Ying-Spring and Fire point of the Liver Meridian, classified in Ling Shu chapter 1. As Fire on a Wood meridian it is the classical sedation (child) point of the Liver: its central action is to sedate Liver Fire — the primary indication for Liver Fire / Liver Yang-rising patterns (red eyes, vertex headache from rising Yang, hypertensive crisis with hot facies, explosive irritability, and rage attacks) and for Lower-Jiao Heat patterns (urethritis with dysuria, right hypochondrial pain, genital pruritus) (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 469–470). Common combinations: Xing Jian (LR-2) + Tai Chong (LR-3) + Bai Hui (GV-20) for vertex headache from rising Yang; Xing Jian (LR-2) + Tai Xi (KI-3) for rising Yang on a Kidney-Yin-deficient base (the classical Yin-root/Yang-canopy combination); Xing Jian (LR-2) + Zu Qiao Yin (GB-44) bled, or bilateral Xing Jian, for acute red eye from Liver Heat. It is eclipsed by Tai Chong (LR-3), the Yuan-Source and Shu-Stream point and the most-used point of the meridian, which concentrates general Liver-Qi regulation in modern practice — hence Xing Jian is reserved for acute Heat/Fire presentations rather than baseline tonic regulation. Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion of 0.3–0.5 cun.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-3.locationClassical: On the dorsum of the foot, 1.5 to 2 cun above the interdigital web, in the pronounced groove distal to the junction of the bases of the first and second metatarsal bones.
howToFind: Seated with the foot supported and in slight dorsiflexion, locate the point on the dorsum of the foot, in the groove proximal to the junction of the bases of the first and second metatarsal bones, approximately
5 to 2 cun proximal to the interdigital fold, palpating the depression between the two metatarsals (WHO 2008, §LR-3).
LR-3.anatomy: Motor point of the first dorsal interosseous muscle, located between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals and the lateral border of the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. Dorsal metatarsal nerve from the deep fibular nerve, dorsal venous plexus of the foot, and first dorsal metatarsal artery.
LR-3.needling: Vertically or slightly oblique 0.5–1.0 cun, or toward Yongquan KI-1 by 0.5–1.5 cun.
LR-3.safetyWarning: Avoid puncturing the dorsal artery of the foot. Caution in pregnancy.
actions: relieves pain (the most important point for all Liver patterns)
tcmIndications: distension and pain in the head, throat, chest, breasts, epigastrium, abdomen, uterus, or genitals
swelling and pain on the dorsum of the foot
LR-3.etymology: Tai (太), great, supreme; Chong (衝), surge, thoroughfare, rushing. The Qi of the Liver channel surges forth strongly at this point — the name records the image of a current that breaks out vigorously. Tai Chong is also one of the classical names of the Chong Mai (Penetrating Vessel), with which the point shares a functional relationship through its action of regulating the Blood (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 470; Ling Shu, chapter 1).
LR-3.clinicalNotes: Tai Chong (LR-3) is at once the Yuan-Source point and the Shu-Stream (Earth) point of the Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, and one of Ma Dan Yang's Heavenly Star points (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 470–473). It is the principal distal point for vigorously regulating Liver Qi, subduing ascending Liver Yang, pacifying internal Wind, and nourishing Liver Blood and Yin — covering the classical triad of channel actions: regulating the free flow of Qi, storing the Blood, and governing the sinews (Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015). Core indications include vertex headache, migraine, dizziness, irritability, depression, and essential hypertension from ascending Liver Yang; menstrual irregularity, dysmenorrhea, and premenstrual syndrome from Liver-Qi Stagnation; and convulsions from internal Wind. Combined bilaterally with He Gu (LI-4) it forms the "Four Gates" (Si Guan), a powerful combination for regulating Qi and Blood throughout the body, classically indicated for refractory pain, emotional disorders, and patterns of diffuse Stagnation. Other common combinations: Tai Chong (LR-3) + Tai Xi (KI-3) for subduing Yang with Yin Deficiency; with Yang Ling Quan (GB-34) for radiating pain from Shao Yang sinew contracture; with San Yin Jiao (SP-6) for dysmenorrhea. Caution: avoid puncturing the dorsalis pedis artery and use with care in pregnancy (WHO 2008, §LR-3).

combinations.indication: Pain, stress, emotional regulation, headache
Musculoskeletal pain, tendon and sinew disorders, hypochondriac pain
Gynecological disorders, menstrual irregularities, Liver Qi stagnation

LR-4.locationClassical: At the ankle, 1 cun anterior to the prominence of the medial malleolus, in the significant depression just medial to the tendon of the tibialis anterior when the ankle is in extension/dorsiflexion.
howToFind: With the foot in dorsiflexion (pulling the toes toward the tibia to bring out the tibialis anterior tendon), locate the point anterior and inferior to the medial malleolus, in the significant depression medial to the tibialis anterior tendon, approximately 1 cun anterior to the malleolar prominence (WHO 2008, §LR-4).
LR-4.anatomy: Medial to the tendon of the tibialis anterior. Innervated by the saphenous nerve and the deep fibular nerve.
LR-4.needling: Perpendicular insertion 0.3–0.5 cun, or oblique insertion medially or laterally.
LR-4.safetyWarning: No special precautions. It is important to extend (dorsiflex) the ankle by pulling the toes toward the tibia before locating this point.
actions: clears Heat from the Liver channel
tcmIndications: pain and retraction of the genitals
LR-4.etymology: Zhong (中), middle; Feng (封), mound, seal. The point lies at the ankle, between the tendons of the tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus, as in a depression between two mounds — hence the name "middle seal" (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 473).
LR-4.clinicalNotes: Zhong Feng (LR-4) is the Jing-River (Metal) point of the Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin. By Five-Shu theory, Jing-River points are classical for disorders of the sinews and voice, and — through the Metal–Lung correspondence — for draining Damp-Heat from the paired channel via the generating and controlling cycles (Deadman, A Manual of Acupuncture, 2007, p. 473–475). In contemporary practice its main indications are disorders along the Liver-channel trajectory across the genitals and lower abdomen — inguinal hernia, genital pain, urinary retention, seminal emission — and jaundice from Damp-Heat in the Liver and Gallbladder. As a local ankle point it is also an option for anterior ankle impingement and medial joint-line pain. Common combinations: Zhong Feng (LR-4) + Tai Chong (LR-3) for hernia and genital pain from Liver-Qi Stagnation in the Lower Jiao; with Zhi Yin (BL-67) and San Yin Jiao (SP-6) for urinary retention; with Dan Shu (BL-19) and Yang Ling Quan (GB-34) for Damp-Heat jaundice (Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed., 2015).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-5.locationClassical: 5 cun above the prominence of the medial malleolus, immediately posterior to the medial crest of the tibia, in the depression between the medial crest of the tibia and the gastrocnemius muscle.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point alongside the medial margin of the tibia, 5 cun above the apex of the medial malleolus.
LR-5.anatomy: Directly over the medial surface of the tibia. Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
LR-5.needling: 0.5–1.0 cun vertically or obliquely in a posterior direction toward the fibula, or transversely (subcutaneously) along the tibia. Alternatively, perpendicular insertion 0.5–1.0 cun, or oblique insertion in a proximal direction 1–2 cun.
LR-5.safetyWarning: The bone lies directly beneath; do not needle perpendicularly.
actions: clears Damp-Heat from the Lower Jiao (principal point for genital/urogenital pruritus and discharge)
tcmIndications: pruritus, swelling, and pain of the genitals
sudden pain and swelling of the testicles
LR-5.etymology: Li (蠡), orifice; Gou (沟), depression. The point is located in a depression on the medial margin of the tibia, resembling an orifice.
LR-5.clinicalNotes: The Gan (Liver) controls the drainage and storage of Xue (Blood). Its meridian passes around the external genitalia. Stagnation of Gan (Liver) Qi can cause accumulation of damp-heat in the Lower Jiao, resulting in diseases of the genitourinary system. Li Gou (LR-5) removes stagnation of Gan (Liver) Qi, eliminates heat, and removes pathogenic dampness, and is therefore indicated in the treatment of various diseases of the genitourinary system. In clinical practice, Li Gou (LR-5) is commonly used to treat strangury and serosanguineous leukorrhea.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-6.locationClassical: 7 cun above the prominence of the medial malleolus, immediately posterior to the medial border of the tibia, in the depression between the medial border of the tibia and the gastrocnemius muscle.
howToFind: Seated or in dorsal decubitus, locate the point 7 cun above the apex of the medial malleolus, alongside the medial margin of the tibia.
LR-6.anatomy: Directly over the medial surface of the tibia. Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
LR-6.needling: 0.5–1.0 cun vertically or obliquely in a posterior direction toward the fibula, or transversely (subcutaneously) in a proximal direction.
actions: treats acute conditions, pain, and Blood disorders
LR-6.etymology: Zhong (中), middle; Du (都), confluence. The point is located halfway along the anteromedial surface of the leg.
LR-6.clinicalNotes: See Li Gou (LR-5) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-7.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the leg, posterior and inferior to the medial condyle of the tibia, 1 cun posterior to SP-9.
howToFind: With the knee flexed, first locate Yin Ling Quan (SP-9) at the inferior border of the medial condyle of the tibia. Locate the Xi Guan point (LR-7) 1 cun posterior to Yin Ling Quan (SP-9).
LR-7.anatomy: Medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle. Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
actions: benefits the knee and relaxes the tendons
tcmIndications: Swelling and pain of the knee
pain on the medial aspect of the leg
westernIndications: Sprain of the medial collateral ligament (MCL)
LR-7.etymology: Xi (膝), knee; Guan (关), joint. The point is located near the joint and treats diseases of the knee.
LR-7.clinicalNotes: This point can be used to treat local diseases, according to the principle of treating the local point.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-8.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the knee, in the depression superior to the medial end of the transverse popliteal crease, posterior to the medial epicondyle of the tibia. Locate with the knee flexed.
howToFind: With the knee flexed, locate the point at the medial end of the popliteal fossa, in the depression between the medial condyle of the femur and the tendon of the semimembranosus muscle.
LR-8.anatomy: Anterior to the tendons of the semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Innervated by the saphenous nerve.
actions: Clears Damp-Heat from the Lower Jiao
benefits the Bladder and the genitals
eliminates Dampness and Damp-Heat from the Lower Jiao (principal action)
benefits the genitals and the uterus
tcmIndications: Dampness disorders of the Lower Jiao
Liver Damp-Heat descending to the genitals
LR-8.etymology: Qu (曲), curved; Quan (泉), source, spring. The point is located at the medial end of the popliteal fossa, in a depression that appears when the knee is flexed, resembling a spring.
LR-8.clinicalNotes: Qu Quan (LR-8) has the function of eliminating damp-heat and regulating the Lower Jiao. Thus, it can be indicated in the treatment of diseases of the genitourinary system caused by accumulation of damp-heat in the Lower Jiao.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-9.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the femur, 4 cun proximal to the medial condyle of the femur (or 4 cun above LR-8), between the sartorius and vastus medialis muscles.
howToFind: With the knee flexed, locate the point 4 cun immediately above Qu Quan (LR-8), or 5 cun above the popliteal fossa, between the vastus medialis and sartorius muscles.
LR-9.anatomy: Sartorius, vastus medialis, and adductor longus muscles. Innervated by the anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve and by the obturator nerve.
tcmIndications: pain in the lumbosacral region radiating to the lower abdomen
westernIndications: trigger points in the vastus medialis
LR-9.etymology: Yin (阴), medial aspect; Bao (包), interior, wrapping. The point is located on the medial aspect of the thigh, between the Spleen Meridian (Foot Tai Yin) and the Kidney Meridian (Foot Shao Yin).
LR-9.clinicalNotes: See Qu Quan (LR-8) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-10.locationClassical: On the medial aspect of the thigh, 3 cun inferior to ST-30, on the lateral border of the adductor longus muscle.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, first locate Qi Chong (ST-30). Locate the point 3 cun immediately below Qi Chong (ST-30).
LR-10.anatomy: Adductor longus and adductor brevis muscles. Innervated by the obturator nerve and by the genitofemoral nerve.
LR-10.safetyWarning: Avoid the femoral artery, which lies lateral to this point.
actions: Clears Damp-Heat from the Lower Jiao
tcmIndications: Fullness and pain in the lower abdomen
LR-10.etymology: Zu (足), foot; Wu (五), five; Li (里), measure of length.
LR-10.clinicalNotes: Zu Wu Li (LR-10) has the function of removing damp-heat and may be effective in treating leukorrhea, eczema, and scrotal pruritus.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-11.locationClassical: In the middle of the inguinal crease, 2 cun inferior to ST-30 (which lies at the level of the upper border of the pubic symphysis), on the lateral border of the adductor longus muscle, where the femoral artery can be palpated.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, first locate Qi Chong (ST-30). Locate the Yin Lian point (LR-11) 2 cun immediately below Qi Chong (ST-30).
LR-11.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, branch of the obturator nerve, branch of the femoral nerve, femoral artery and vein, ilioinguinal nerve, branch of the genitofemoral nerve, adductor longus and pectineus muscles.
actions: Regulates the Conception and Penetrating vessels
benefits the uterus and the ligaments
tcmIndications: pain in the thigh and knee
pain on the inner aspect of the thigh and knee
LR-11.etymology: Yin (阴), medial aspect; Lian (廉), corner. The point is located on the medial aspect of the thigh, near the genitalia.
LR-11.clinicalNotes: See Zu Wu Li (LR-10) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-12.locationClassical: In the inguinal crease, 2.5 cun lateral to the midline and 1 cun inferior to the upper border of the symphysis (Qugu CV-2), medial to the femoral vein/artery.
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the inguinal groove,
5 cun lateral to the anterior midline, at the level of the inferior margin of the pubic symphysis, lateral and inferior to Qi Chong (ST-30).
LR-12.anatomy: Pectineus muscle, obturator externus muscle. The femoral vein and artery lie laterally. Innervated by the ilioinguinal nerve.
LR-12.safetyWarning: HIGH RISK. Avoid the femoral artery and vein. Avoid the spermatic cord. The femoral vein lies medial to the artery. To avoid injury, do not needle medial to the artery.
actions: Eliminates Cold from the Liver channel
tcmIndications: pain on the inner aspect of the thigh
LR-12.etymology: Ji (急), urgent, movement; Mai (脉), artery. This point is located on the medial aspect of the thigh, alongside the femoral artery.
LR-12.clinicalNotes: See Zu Wu Li (LR-10) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-13.locationClassical: On the lateral aspect of the abdomen, directly anterior and inferior to the free end of the 11th rib (approximately 2 cun above the umbilicus and 6 cun lateral to the midline).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point on the midaxillary line, below the tip of the eleventh rib, or at the level of the olecranon when the elbow is flexed.
LR-13.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, thoracoepigastric vein, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, subcostal and lower intercostal arteries, lateral thoracic artery, and lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves.
LR-13.needling: 0.5–1.0 cun vertically or obliquely in a lateral direction, or 0.5 cun obliquely.
LR-13.safetyWarning: Deep perpendicular insertion carries a high risk of puncturing an enlarged liver (on the right) or an enlarged spleen (on the left).
actions: regulates the Middle and Lower Jiao
LR-13.etymology: Zhang (章), clarity; Men (门), gate. The point belongs to the Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, responsible for growth and clarity.
LR-13.clinicalNotes:
1. Zhang Men (LR-13) is the Front-Mu point of the Pi (Spleen). The Pi (Spleen) is responsible for the transport and transformation of water and food, being the principal source of acquired nutrients. For this reason, this point can be indicated in the treatment of diseases of the digestive system, consumptive diseases, lassitude, and weight loss resulting from a lack of acquired Jing (essence).

2. Earth generates Metal. Thus, this point can be indicated in the treatment of diseases of the respiratory system.

3. The Pi (Spleen) controls the circulation of Xue (Blood). Symptoms of abdominal masses and hepatosplenomegaly caused by stagnation of Qi and Xue (Blood) can be treated with direct moxibustion at Zhang Men (LR-13) and Pi Gen (EX-DL 4).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

LR-14.locationClassical: On the anterior wall of the chest/mammillary line, in the 6th intercostal space, 4 cun lateral to the midline (directly below the nipple).
howToFind: In dorsal decubitus, locate the point in the sixth intercostal space, immediately below the nipple. In women, the point is located in the sixth intercostal space, on the midclavicular line.
LR-14.anatomy: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, thoracoepigastric vein, lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves, intercostal nerves, arteries and veins, and intercostal muscle.
LR-14.needling: Oblique medial or lateral insertion (along the intercostal space), 0.5–1.0 cun.
LR-14.safetyWarning: High risk of pneumothorax. Deep perpendicular insertion is strictly contraindicated. Deep insertion may also puncture the liver (right side).
actions: regulates and harmonizes the Liver and Stomach
tcmIndications: pain, distension, and fullness in the chest and lateral costal region
LR-14.etymology: Qi (期), cycle; Men (门), gate. The Qi and Xue (Blood) of the twelve meridians begin to circulate from the Yun Men point (LU-2) and end at Qi Men (LR-14), completing a cycle.
LR-14.clinicalNotes:
1. Qi Men (LR-14) is the Front-Mu point of the Liver Meridian, Foot Jue Yin, and has the function of dispersing stagnation of Gan (Liver) Qi and of tonifying the Pi (Spleen). For this reason, this point is the first choice in the treatment of hepatitis, cholecystitis, and other diseases of the digestive system caused by hyperactivity of Gan (Liver) Qi assaulting the Pi (Spleen).

2. Qi Men (LR-14) is effective in the treatment of interruption of menstruation caused by external pathogenic factors, or in cases of febrile state with persistent symptoms of chest oppression, anguish, and agitation.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-1.category: Luo-Connecting Point of the Governing Vessel
GV-1.locationClassical: In the perineum, at the midpoint between the tip of the coccyx and the anus.
howToFind: In the knee-chest position or in prone decubitus, locate the point at the midpoint of the line connecting the tip of the coccyx and the anus.
GV-1.anatomy: Anococcygeal ligament, external anal sphincter. Innervated by the coccygeal nerve and the anal branch of the pudendal nerve.
GV-1.needling: Perpendicular insertion, or oblique insertion directed anteriorly and superiorly, 0.5–1.0 cun.
GV-1.safetyWarning: Strict hygiene is mandatory due to proximity to the anus. Deep insertion may perforate the rectum.
actions: benefits the two lower Yin (genitalia and anus)
activates the channel and relieves pain
tcmIndications: pain in the lumbar region and coccyx
GV-1.etymology: The collateral pathway of the Du Mai runs laterally along the vertebral column and ascends to the vertex of the head. Its distribution is long (長 Chang), and its function very strong (強 Qiang).
GV-1.clinicalNotes:
Chang Qiang (GV-1) is indicated to treat diarrhea and dysentery due to its proximity to the anus. Needling Chang Qiang (GV-1) treats constipation and rectal "prolapse" caused by chronic diarrhea and dysentery.

  The Du Mai governs the Yang Qi of the entire body. The neuropsychiatric disorders cited are caused by hyperactivity of the Yang. Therefore, Chang Qiang (GV-1) is a useful point for mania and epilepsy.

It is a Crossing Point with the Kidney Meridian, Foot Shao Yin. The Shen (Kidney) governs water metabolism and Pang Guang (Bladder) accumulates the excretion. Thus, the point is indicated to treat disorders of the genitourinary system.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-2.locationClassical: On the sacrum, on the posterior midline, in the center of the sacral hiatus.
howToFind: In prone or lateral decubitus, locate the sacral prominence above the coccyx. Then locate the point at the intersection of the posterior midline with the horizontal line passing through the two sacral prominences.
GV-2.anatomy: Sacrococcygeal ligament. The needle penetrates the sacral canal. Innervated by branches of the coccygeal and sacral nerves.
GV-2.needling: Oblique insertion directed superiorly into the sacral canal, 0.5–1.0 cun.
GV-2.safetyWarning: Aseptic technique is essential, as the needle penetrates the epidural space of the sacral canal.
actions: Benefits the lumbar region and the lower limbs
tcmIndications: pain and stiffness in the lumbar and sacral region
weakness and paralysis of the lower limbs
GV-2.etymology: Su Wen: "The point is located in the sacral hiatus (GV-2)."
GV-2.clinicalNotes:
The Du Mai governs the Yang Qi of the entire body, and its points may be used to treat disorders of the vertebral column.

  The genitourinary system lies anterior to Yao Shu (GV-2). According to the principle of treatment along the meridian pathway, it is indicated for disorders of the genitourinary system and for reproductive function.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-3.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4). At the same level as the iliac crests.
howToFind: In prone or lateral decubitus, on the posterior midline, locate the point in the depression below the spinous process of the fourth lumbar vertebra, at the level of the iliac crest.
GV-3.anatomy: Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the lumbar nerves.
GV-3.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion directed superiorly, 0.5–1.0 cun.
GV-3.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
actions: benefits the lumbar region and the lower limbs
tcmIndications: weakness and motor impairment of the lower limbs
GV-3.etymology:
Guan means important, strategic. It is the strategic point of the lumbar Yang.

The point is located at the level of the waist and connects internally with the Dan Tian (field of the quintessence), where primordial Yin and Yang converge. It belongs to the Du Mai, "Sea of the Yang Meridians," which sends Yang Qi throughout the body, hence its name Yao Yang Guan.
GV-3.clinicalNotes: The point is located in the lower lumbar region, in the projection of the digestive and genitourinary systems. According to the principle of local action of the points, Yao Yang Guan (GV-3) may be indicated in the treatment of disorders of both systems, with intestinal disorders being its principal indication. Lumbosacral pain and motor deficit of the lower extremities may also be treated based on this principle.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-4.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the second lumbar vertebra (L2). At the same level as the umbilicus (CV-8) and BL-23.
howToFind: In lateral decubitus or seated, locate the point in the depression between the spinous processes of the second and third lumbar vertebrae.
GV-4.anatomy: Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the lumbar nerves.
GV-4.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion directed superiorly, 0.5–1.0 cun.
GV-4.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
tcmIndications: Stiffness and pain in the lumbar region
sensation of cold in the lower body
GV-4.etymology: The Qi of the Shen (Kidney) is the basic origin of the entire body. The point is located between the kidneys and is considered the "Gate of Life."
GV-4.clinicalNotes:
The Shen (Kidney) stores Yin and Yang and possesses the properties of water and fire. The point is located between the kidneys and belongs to the Du Mai, which is Yang. It is related to the fire of the "Gate of Life," reinforcing it — that is, tonifying the Yang of the Shen (Kidney). It is used especially in disorders of the digestive and genitourinary systems resulting from Yang deficiency. Disorders or syndromes caused by Yang deficiency, such as cold extremities, aversion to cold, insomnia, vertigo, and tinnitus, are usually treated by needling Ming Men (GV-4).

  The point has a dual regulatory function. In addition to treating Yang deficiency syndromes, it may also be used to treat syndromes caused by excess Heat, with high fever and malaria-like symptoms.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-5.locationClassical: In the lumbar region, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the first lumbar vertebra (L1).
howToFind: In prone decubitus or seated, locate the point in the depression between the spinous processes of the first and second lumbar vertebrae.
GV-5.needling: Perpendicular or slightly oblique insertion directed superiorly, 0.5–1.0 cun.
GV-5.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
tcmIndications: Pain and stiffness in the lumbar region
GV-5.etymology: Xuan (懸), suspended; Shu (樞), pivot. The point is located in the lumbar region, between the two San Jiao Shu points, which are responsible for the circulation and transport of Qi. For this reason, Xuan Shu (GV-5) carries the meaning of a pivot suspended between the two San Jiao Shu.
GV-5.clinicalNotes: According to the principle of local point treatment, Xuan Shu (GV-5) is indicated for gastrointestinal disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-6.locationClassical: In the mid-back region, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the eleventh thoracic vertebra (T11). At the same level as BL-20 (Spleen Shu).
howToFind: In prone decubitus or seated upright, locate the point in the depression between the spinous processes of the eleventh and twelfth thoracic vertebrae.
GV-6.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
actions: Strengthens the Spleen and drains Dampness
tcmIndications: stiffness and pain in the back
GV-6.etymology: Ji (脊), spine; Zhong (中), middle. The point is located at the midpoint between the thoracic spine and the sacrum.
GV-6.clinicalNotes: See Xuan Shu (GV-5) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-7.locationClassical: On the back, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the tenth thoracic vertebra (T10). At the same level as BL-19 (Gallbladder Shu).
howToFind: Seated upright or in prone decubitus, locate the point in the depression between the spinous processes of the tenth and eleventh thoracic vertebrae.
GV-7.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
GV-7.etymology: Zhong (中), middle; Shu (樞), pivot. The point is located at the center of the vertebral column, like a pivot.
GV-7.clinicalNotes: See Xuan Shu (GV-5) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-8.locationClassical: On the back, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the ninth thoracic vertebra (T9). At the same level as BL-18 (Liver Shu).
howToFind: Seated upright or in prone decubitus, locate the point in the depression between the spinous processes of the ninth and tenth thoracic vertebrae.
GV-8.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
tcmIndications: stiffness and spasms of the vertebral column
GV-8.etymology: Jin (筋), muscle and tendon; Suo (縮), contracture. Lateral to this point are the Gan Shu (BL-18) points. The point is useful in the treatment of muscular contractures.
GV-8.clinicalNotes: Jin Suo (GV-8) is located anterior to the Gan (Liver), and lateral to it are the Gan Shu (BL-18) points. For this reason, this point is indicated to treat disorders of the Gan (Liver), which manifest as psychiatric disorders. Jin Suo (GV-8) is internally related to the stomach, so it may treat gastric disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-9.locationClassical: On the back, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the seventh thoracic vertebra (T7). At the same level as the inferior angle of the scapula and BL-17.
howToFind: In prone or lateral decubitus, locate the point between the spinous processes of the seventh and eighth thoracic vertebrae.
GV-9.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
tcmIndications: stiffness and pain in the back and chest
GV-9.etymology: Zhi (至), reaching; Yang (陽), Yang of Yin-Yang. The point is located at the seventh thoracic vertebra. The upper part of the thoracic spine is "Yang within Yang." The point belongs to the Du Mai and lies below the seventh thoracic vertebra, and seven is a Yang number; for this reason, this point receives the name "Reaching Yang."
GV-9.clinicalNotes: Anterior and superior to the point are the lungs. Inferior to it is the stomach. The Fei (Lung) is responsible for respiration, and the Pi (Spleen) for the transformation and transport of nutrients and the trophism of the four limbs. According to the principle of local point treatment, Zhi Yang (GV-9) may be used in disorders of the digestive and respiratory systems. General deficiency and dyspnea result from dysfunction of the Pi (Spleen) and Wei (Stomach).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-10.locationClassical: On the back, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the sixth thoracic vertebra (T6). At the same level as BL-16.
howToFind: In prone decubitus or seated upright, locate the point in the depression between the spinous processes of the sixth and seventh thoracic vertebrae.
GV-10.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
westernIndications: pain in the upper back region
tags: pain in the upper back region
GV-10.etymology:
Ling (靈), spirit; Tai (台), tower or platform.

The point is located between Shen Dao (GV-11) and Xin Shu (BL-15) and lies near the heart, like a platform for the spirit of the Xin (Heart).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-11.locationClassical: On the back, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the fifth thoracic vertebra (T5). At the same level as BL-15 (Heart Shu).
howToFind: In prone decubitus or seated with the back flexed, locate the point in the depression between the spinous processes of the fifth and sixth thoracic vertebrae.
GV-11.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
actions: Tonifies the Heart and calms the spirit
GV-11.etymology: Shen (神), the mind of the Xin (Heart); Dao (道), path. The Xin (Heart) houses the mind, and the point is located lateral to the Xin Shu (BL-15), like a path of the mind.
GV-11.clinicalNotes:
The Xin (Heart) governs the blood vessels, the circulation of blood, and the mind. Disorders of the Xin may result in cardiovascular and psychic disorders.

The lungs are near the Shen Dao (GV-11) point, so the point may be used to treat respiratory disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-12.locationClassical: On the back, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra (T3). At the same level as BL-13 (Lung Shu).
howToFind: Seated with the back flexed or in prone decubitus, locate the point in the depression below the spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra — that is, at the intersection of the posterior midline with the line passing through the spines of the scapulae.
GV-12.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
actions: Clears Heat from the Lung and Heart
GV-12.etymology: Shen (身), body; Zhu (柱), pillar. The point is located between the Shu points of the Fei (Lung) (Fei Shu, BL-13). It means "pillar of the body" and is associated with Lung Qi.
GV-12.clinicalNotes: This point may be used to eliminate heat and relieve contractures.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-13.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel and the Bladder channel
GV-13.locationClassical: On the upper back, on the posterior midline, in the depression below the spinous process of the first thoracic vertebra (T1).
howToFind: Seated with the back flexed or in prone decubitus, first locate Da Zhui (GV-14) for reference. Locate (GV-13) in the depression below the spinous process of the first thoracic vertebra.
GV-13.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
GV-13.etymology: Tao (陶), kiln in which ceramic vessels are made; Dao (道), path or passage. The passage of Yang Qi is compared to the chimney of a kiln.
GV-13.clinicalNotes: Crossing Point of the Du Mai and the Bladder Meridian, Foot Tai Yang. Clinical experiments show that the point has effects similar to Da Zhui (GV-14), being able to lower fever, promote bronchodilation, and increase phagocytic capacity. Therefore, it is frequently used to treat disorders of the respiratory system and febrile conditions. It is also applied to treat cervical pain, difficulty raising the arm due to shoulder pain, and cervical stiffness with headache (cervicogenic headache).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-14.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel with the six Yang channels of the hand and foot. Point of the Sea of Qi
GV-14.locationClassical: On the posterior midline, in the depression directly below the spinous process of the seventh cervical vertebra (C7). (C7 is typically the most prominent vertebra with the neck flexed.)
howToFind: Seated with the back flexed or in prone decubitus, locate the point below the seventh cervical vertebra, at the largest prominence in the cervical region.
GV-14.anatomy: Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, trapezius. Innervated by the dorsal branches of the eighth cervical nerve.
GV-14.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may reach the spinal canal.
actions: Clears Heat and releases the exterior (master point for high fever)
regulates the Defensive (Wei) Qi and the Nutritive (Ying) Qi
clears the brain and calms the spirit
tcmIndications: stiffness of the neck and back
GV-14.etymology: Da (大), great; Zhui (椎), vertebra. The point is located below the prominence of the seventh cervical vertebra, the largest of the vertebrae.
GV-14.clinicalNotes: Crossing Point of all Yang Meridians. As a point of pure Yang, it dominates the Biao. It is commonly used to relieve Biao (superficial) syndromes, reduce fever, spontaneous sweating, and urticaria. According to the famous master Zhang Jing Yue, the best way to tonify Yin is to know how to treat Yang to support Yin. Thus, night sweats, consumptive fever (febre tísica), and other symptoms of Yin deficiency may be treated with this point. According to the principle of treatment along the meridian pathways, the point is indicated for pain in the shoulder, thoracic, and lumbar regions.

combinations.indication: High fever, heat clearing, immune regulation

GV-15.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel. Point of the Sea of Qi
GV-15.locationClassical: At the nape of the neck, on the posterior midline, 0.5 cun directly above the midpoint of the posterior hairline, in the depression below the spinous process of the first cervical vertebra (C1).
howToFind: Seated with the neck slightly flexed (Fig.
5), locate the point
5 cun above the hairline, on the posterior midline.
GV-15.anatomy: Nuchal ligament. Innervated by the third occipital nerve. The spinal cord and medulla oblongata lie deep to this point.
GV-15.needling: Perpendicular insertion, directed strictly toward the patient's lower jaw, 0.5–0.8 cun.
GV-15.safetyWarning: CRITICAL HIGH RISK. Deep insertion or directing the needle superiorly is strictly forbidden. Puncture of the medulla oblongata may cause respiratory arrest and death.
actions: Benefits the tongue and treats mutism
GV-15.etymology: Ya (啞), mutism; Men (門), gate. This point can treat mutism.
GV-15.clinicalNotes: This point penetrates the root of the tongue and is intimately related to it. It is used in the treatment of disorders of tongue motility, with motor aphasia, dysphonia, and sublingual swelling. As a Crossing Point of the Yang Wei Mai with the Du Mai, it has the function of awakening the mind and regulating the meridians. It is frequently used to treat disorders of the nervous system.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-16.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel with the Yang Linking (Yang Wei) vessel. Window of Heaven Point
GV-16.locationClassical: At the nape of the neck, on the posterior midline, 1 cun directly above the posterior hairline, in the depression immediately below the external occipital protuberance.
howToFind: Seated with the neck slightly flexed, locate the point 1 cun above the hairline, on the posterior midline, in the depression immediately below the external occipital protuberance.
GV-16.anatomy: Nuchal ligament, between the trapezius muscles. The cisterna magna and medulla oblongata lie deep to this point.
GV-16.needling: Perpendicular insertion, directed strictly toward the patient's lower jaw, 0.5–0.8 cun.
GV-16.safetyWarning: CRITICAL HIGH RISK. Deep insertion or superior angulation will perforate the cisterna magna and medulla oblongata, resulting in severe neurological injury or death.
actions: Eliminates Wind (principal point for internal and external Wind invading the head)
GV-16.etymology: Feng (風), pathogenic wind; Fu (府), place. A point for eliminating pathogenic wind.
GV-16.clinicalNotes: This point is located where pathogenic wind attacks and possesses the property of eliminating it. Therefore, this point is important for treating the disorders mentioned. It belongs to the Du Mai and is a Crossing Point of the Foot Tai Yang and the Yang Wei Mai, with the property of resolving Biao (surface) syndromes and eliminating pathogenic wind.

combinations.indication: Headache, neck stiffness, wind disorders, occipital pain

GV-17.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel with the Bladder channel
GV-17.locationClassical: On the posterior part of the head, on the posterior midline, 1.5 cun directly superior to GV-16, in the depression superior to the external occipital protuberance.
howToFind: Seated or in prone decubitus, locate the point at the upper border of the external protuberance, on the posterior midline.
GV-17.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve.
GV-17.etymology: Nao (腦), brain; Hu (戶), door. The Du Mai runs an ascending course along the vertebral column and penetrates the brain. The point is like a door in the occipital region for the Qi of the Du Mai to enter the brain.
GV-17.clinicalNotes: The point has the function of awakening the mind and improving vision. As the Du Mai connects with the brain, it is commonly used to treat disorders of the face and head, and psychiatric disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-18.locationClassical: On the posterior part of the head, on the posterior midline, 1.5 cun directly superior to GV-17 (at the midpoint between GV-16 and GV-20).
howToFind: Seated or in prone decubitus, locate the point
5 cun, immediately above the upper margin of the external occipital protuberance, on the posterior midline.
GV-18.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve.
GV-18.etymology: Qiang (強), stiffness; Jian (間), middle. The point is located between the parietal and occipital bones. Indicated to treat headache and cervical stiffness.
GV-18.clinicalNotes: It awakens and tranquilizes the mind, and is frequently used for psychiatric disorders, vertigo, and vomiting.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-19.locationClassical: On the top of the head, on the posterior midline, 1.5 cun directly posterior to GV-20 (and 1.5 cun superior to GV-18).
howToFind: Seated, with the back supported, locate the point
5 cun posterior to the Bai Hui (GV-20) point, on the posterior midline.
GV-19.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve.
GV-19.etymology: Hou (後), posterior; Ding (頂), vertex. The point is located posterior to the vertex.
GV-19.clinicalNotes: Like most points of the Du Mai, it treats psychiatric disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-20.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel with the Bladder
GV-20.locationClassical: At the vertex of the head, on the midline, 5 cun posterior to the anterior hairline (and 7 cun superior to the posterior hairline) — directly at the intersection of the midline with the line connecting the auricular apices
howToFind: With the patient seated, locate the point 1 cun anterior to the midpoint of the line connecting the anterior and posterior hairlines. Alternatively, locate it at the intersection of the median line of the head with the line connecting both auricular apices, with the ears folded forward.
GV-20.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the greater occipital nerve and the frontal nerve
GV-20.needling: Transverse (subcutaneous) insertion, directed anteriorly or posteriorly, 0.5–1.0 cun
actions: Raises Yang and reverses prolapse (principal point for organ prolapse)
Clears the brain and calms the spirit
GV-20.etymology: Bai (百), hundred; Hui (會), meeting. The point sits at the vertex where the three Hand and Foot Yang meridians, the Hand and Foot Jue Yin meridians, and the Du Mai all converge.
GV-20.clinicalNotes:
Located at the highest point of the body, GV-20 is where Yang Qi converges. It is used to regulate Yang Qi and is indicated in the treatment of visceral prolapses. Prolonged diarrhea and dysentery, enuresis, erectile dysfunction, coma, and syncope are all associated with deficient Yang Qi failing to ascend to the brain; needling this point promotes that ascent.

As the Crossing Point of the Three Hand and Foot Yang Meridians with the Hand and Foot Jue Yin Meridians, GV-20 has broad connections with the five sense organs of the face and head, and may be used to treat disorders of the ears, eyes, and nose.

Clinical practice supports the use of this point in cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and post-stroke sequelae, based on its properties of regulating excess Yang Qi, lowering blood pressure, and improving circulation. It is also indicated for raising blood pressure in patients presenting in shock.

combinations.indication: Hypertension, dizziness, loss of consciousness, calming the mind

GV-21.locationClassical: On the top of the head, on the midline, 1.5 cun anterior to GV-20 (3.5 cun posterior to the anterior hairline).
howToFind: Seated upright or with the neck in extension, locate the point
5 cun anterior to Bai Hui (GV-20).
GV-21.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the frontal nerve.
GV-21.safetyWarning: In infants, do not insert the needle if the fontanelle has not closed.
GV-21.etymology: Qian (前), anterior; Ding (頂), vertex. The point is located in front of the vertex.
GV-21.clinicalNotes:
The point has the function of awakening and tranquilizing the mind. It is used to treat disorders of the nose and eyes. Unlike Bai Hui (GV-20), it is not used to treat ear disorders.

Due to the natural characteristic of the Du Mai, this point may treat psychiatric disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-22.locationClassical: On the top of the head, on the midline, 2 cun anterior to GV-20 (3 cun posterior to the anterior hairline).
howToFind: Seated upright or with the neck in extension, locate the point 3 cun anterior to Bai Hui (GV-20) or 1 cun posterior to Shang Xing (GV-23).
GV-22.anatomy: Epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the frontal nerve.
GV-22.safetyWarning: Strictly contraindicated in infants whose anterior fontanelle has not yet closed.
GV-22.etymology: Xin (囟), fontanelle; Hui (會), closed. The point is located at the major fontanelle.
GV-22.clinicalNotes: See Bai Hui (GV-20) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-23.locationClassical: On the head, on the midline, 1 cun posterior to the anterior hairline.
howToFind: Seated, with the neck in extension and the head supported, locate the point 1 cun immediately above the anterior hairline.
GV-23.anatomy: Frontalis muscle and epicranial aponeurosis. Innervated by the frontal nerve.
GV-23.safetyWarning: In infants, do not insert the needle if the fontanelle has not closed.
actions: Benefits the nose and the eyes (principal point for nasal disorders)
GV-23.etymology: Shang (上), upper; Xing (星), star. The head is considered the sky. The point is located on the head like a star in the sky.
GV-23.clinicalNotes: See Bai Hui (GV-20). Currently the point is used to treat febrile and nasal disorders.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-24.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel with the Bladder and Stomach channels
GV-24.locationClassical: On the head, on the midline, 0.5 cun posterior to the anterior hairline.
howToFind: 1. Palpate the anatomical landmarks for GV-24 along the Governing Vessel (Du Mai) meridian.
2. Feel for the characteristic depression or inter-muscular groove at the specified Cun measurement.
3. Verify patient sensation (De Qi — soreness, numbness, distention, or heaviness upon palpation).
GV-24.anatomy: Frontalis muscle. Innervated by the frontal nerve.
actions: benefits the nose and the eyes
GV-24.etymology: Shen (神), mind; Ting (庭), court or vestibule. "The brain is the mansion of the primordial mind." The point is located on the forehead, like a vestibule of the brain.
GV-24.clinicalNotes: See Bai Hui (GV-20) for further details.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-25.locationClassical: On the face, at the tip of the nose.
howToFind: Seated, with the neck in extension and the head supported, or in supine decubitus, locate the point at the tip of the nose.
GV-25.anatomy: Cartilage of the nose. Innervated by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve.
GV-25.needling: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun, or pricked to bleed.
westernIndications: First aid for hypovolemic and anaphylactic shock
GV-25.etymology: Su (素), nasal cartilage; Liao (髎), foramen. The point is located on the nasal cartilage.
GV-25.clinicalNotes:
According to the principle of treatment by local point action, it is used in the treatment of nasal disorders.

According to current clinical research, it has the properties of raising blood pressure and improving respiratory function, and may be indicated to treat shock and neonatal asphyxia. Su Liao (GV-25) induces recovery of consciousness, relieves convulsions, and calms the mind. In cases of coma due to convulsion, infantile convulsion, or clonic convulsion, this point shows good therapeutic effect.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-26.category: Meeting Point of the Governing Vessel with the Large Intestine and Stomach channels. Sun Si-miao Ghost Point
GV-26.locationClassical: On the face, on the midline, at the junction of the upper third and the lower two-thirds of the philtrum.
howToFind: Seated, with the neck in extension, or in supine decubitus, locate the point at the upper third of the nasolabial groove.
GV-26.anatomy: Orbicularis oris muscle. Innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve and by the infraorbital nerve (trigeminal).
tcmIndications: deviation of the mouth and eye
westernIndications: acute lumbar sprain (the patient walks while the needle is stimulated)
GV-26.etymology: Shui (水), water; Gou (溝), trough. The point is located in a place that resembles a water trough.

combinations.indication: Acute low back pain, emergency resuscitation

GV-27.locationClassical: On the face, on the midline, at the junction of the upper lip margin with the philtrum (tubercle of the upper lip).
howToFind: With the patient seated, with the neck in extension, or in supine decubitus, locate the point at the intersection between the lower border of the nasolabial groove and the upper lip.
GV-27.anatomy: Orbicularis oris muscle. Innervated by the upper labial branch of the facial nerve and by the infraorbital nerve.
tcmIndications: pain and edema of the gums
GV-27.etymology: Dui (兌), mouth; Duan (端), summit. The point is located on the upper lip.
GV-27.clinicalNotes: According to the principle of treatment by local point action, it is used to treat disorders of the mouth, teeth, and nose. The treatment of pain at the tip of the coccyx with this point is based on the anatomic correspondence action of the points. Dui Duan (GV-27) and the coccyx are located at opposite extremities of the digestive system (mouth and anus).

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

GV-28.locationClassical: Inside the mouth, at the junction of the frenulum of the upper lip with the upper gum.
howToFind: Seated, with the neck in extension, lift the upper lip and locate the point where the upper frenulum meets the gum.
GV-28.anatomy: Frenulum of the upper lip. Innervated by the superior alveolar branches of the maxillary nerve (trigeminal).
GV-28.needling: Oblique insertion directed superiorly, 0.1–0.2 cun, or pricked to bleed.
GV-28.safetyWarning: Very sensitive point. Oral hygiene must be ensured before puncture.
actions: benefits the gums and the mouth
tcmIndications: Edema and pain of the gums
redness and edema of the eyes
GV-28.etymology: Yin (齦), gum; Jiao (交), meeting. The point is located on the incisive suture of the upper gum, where the Du Mai and the Ren Mai meet.
GV-28.clinicalNotes: According to the principle of treatment by local point action, it is indicated in disorders of the face and head. As the point is located at the convergence of the Du Mai and Ren Mai, it is indicated for the control of psychiatric disorders. (Qian Jin Yi Fang)

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

CV-1.locationClassical: In the perineum, at the midpoint between the anus and the posterior labial commissure in women, or the root of the scrotum in men.
howToFind: In supine decubitus, locate the point between the anus and the posterior root of the scrotum in men, and between the anus and the posterior commissure of the labia majora of the vulva in women.
CV-1.anatomy: Bulbospongiosus muscle, central tendon of the perineum. Innervated by the perineal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve).
actions: Resuscitation in drowning, coma, or manic episodes
regulates the anterior and posterior Yin (genitalia and anus)
tcmIndications: prolapse of the uterus or rectum
CV-1.etymology: Hui (會), crossing; Yin (陰), genitalia. The point is located in the region between the genitalia and the anus, called Hui Yin.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

CV-2.category: Meeting Point of the Conception Vessel with the Liver channel
CV-2.locationClassical: In the lower abdomen, on the anterior midline, on the superior border of the pubic symphysis.
howToFind: In supine decubitus, locate the point on the upper border of the pubic bone, on the midline.
CV-2.anatomy: Linea alba, pyramidalis muscle. Innervated by the iliohypogastric nerve.
CV-2.safetyWarning: Empty the bladder before needling. Deep insertion may perforate a full bladder. Contraindicated in pregnancy.
CV-2.etymology: Qu (曲), curved; Gu (骨), bone. Qu Gu refers to the pubic bone; the point is located on the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

CV-3.locationClassical: In the lower abdomen, on the anterior midline, 4 cun inferior to the umbilicus (1 cun superior to the pubic symphysis).
howToFind: In supine decubitus, locate the point 1 cun above Qu Gu (CV-2), or 4 cun below the center of the umbilicus.
CV-3.anatomy: Linea alba. Innervated by the iliohypogastric nerve.
CV-3.safetyWarning: Empty the bladder before needling. Contraindicated in pregnancy.
actions: drains Damp-Heat from the Lower Jiao (principal point for urogenital Damp-Heat)
CV-3.etymology: Zhong (中), center; Ji (極), exactly. The point is located exactly at the center of the body.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

CV-4.category: Front-Mu Point of the Small Intestine
CV-4.locationClassical: In the lower abdomen, on the anterior midline, 3 cun inferior to the umbilicus.
howToFind: In supine decubitus, locate the point 1 cun above Zhong Ji (CV-3), or 3 cun below the center of the umbilicus.
CV-4.anatomy: Linea alba. Innervated by the twelfth intercostal nerve (subcostal nerve).
CV-4.safetyWarning: Empty the bladder before needling. Contraindicated in pregnancy.
actions: Strengthens the Original Qi (Yuan Qi) and benefits the Essence (Jing)
regulates the uterus. (One of the most important tonification points of the body)
tcmIndications: asthma (Kidney fails to grasp the Qi)
CV-4.etymology: Guan (關), important strategic pass; Yuan (元), primordial Qi. Strategic point of storage of the primordial Qi of the body.

combinations.indication: Qi and Yang deficiency, fatigue, urogenital disorders

CV-5.category: Front-Mu Point of the Sanjiao (Triple Burner)
CV-5.locationClassical: In the lower abdomen, on the anterior midline, 2 cun inferior to the umbilicus.
howToFind: 1. Palpate the anatomical landmarks for CV-5 along the Conception Vessel (Ren Mai) meridian.
2. Feel for the characteristic depression or inter-muscular groove at the specified Cun measurement.
3. Verify patient sensation (De Qi — soreness, numbness, distention, or heaviness upon palpation).
CV-5.anatomy: Linea alba. Innervated by the eleventh intercostal nerve.
CV-5.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may penetrate the peritoneal cavity. Classically contraindicated in women, as it was believed to cause infertility.
actions: Moves and regulates the water passages
CV-5.etymology: Shi (石), stone; Men (門), gate. Stone signifies "obstruction." In ancient times, it was erroneously believed that needling this point would cause infertility.
CV-5.clinicalNotes:
The points Shi Men (CV-5), Qi Hai (CV-6), and Guan Yuan (CV-4) may be called Dan Tian, the site of tonification of the Yuan Qi. By tonifying the Yuan Qi, this point treats the diseases caused by its deficiency, namely the diseases of the genitourinary and digestive systems.

Shi Men (CV-5) is located in the lower abdomen, near the reproductive system, bladder, and small intestine. According to the principle of local function, the point is indicated in the treatment of disorders of the Zang Fu organs of the region, in both deficiency and excess syndromes.

combinations.indication: Synergistic reinforcement of channel regulation and targeted pain relief.

CV-6.locationClassical: In the lower abdomen, on the anterior midline, 1.5 cun inferior to the umbilicus.
howToFind: 1. Palpate the anatomical landmarks for CV-6 along the Conception Vessel (Ren Mai) meridian.
2. Feel for the characteristic depression or inter-muscular groove at the specified Cun measurement.
3. Verify patient sensation (De Qi — soreness, numbness, distention, or heaviness upon palpation).
CV-6.anatomy: Linea alba. Innervated by the eleventh intercostal nerve.
CV-6.safetyWarning: Deep insertion may penetrate the peritoneal cavity.
actions: Tonifies and strengthens the Original Qi
tcmIndications: Prolapse of the uterus or rectum
CV-6.etymology: Qi (氣), Qi; Hai (海), sea. The point is located below the umbilicus; it is the sea of the Qi of the body.
